# Breton Civil War (1341–1343)

The Breton Civil War of 1341–1343 was a pivotal conflict that originated as a dynastic succession crisis within the Duchy of Brittany but rapidly escalated into a major theatre of the broader Hundred Years' War between England and France , . The death of Duke John III without a direct heir on April 30, 1341, triggered a dispute between two rival claimants: his younger half-brother, John of Montfort, and his niece, Joan of Penthièvre, whose husband, Charles of Blois, represented her claim , . This internal Breton struggle was immediately co-opted by the external powers of the time. John of Montfort secured the backing of his feudal overlord, King Edward III of England, while Charles of Blois received strong support from his uncle, King Philip VI of France , . This intervention transformed the conflict from a localized civil war into a proxy war, with the outcome having significant implications for both the balance of power in Western Europe and the future trajectory of the Hundred Years' War . The war's opening phase was defined by swift territorial gains, dramatic military reversals, the decisive application of English naval power, and a series of crucial battles where tactical innovation proved more important than sheer numbers , . After a period of intense campaigning and a temporary diplomatic resolution, the fragile peace collapsed under the weight of political ambition and brutal reprisals, setting the stage for further decades of conflict , .

## Genesis of Conflict: A Succession Crisis Amplified

The conflagration known as the Breton Civil War erupted from the ashes of a dynastic uncertainty created by the death of Duke John III of Brittany on April 30, 1341 , . Having died childless after three marriages, he left no clear successor, plunging the duchy into a crisis that quickly transcended its borders , . The ambiguity of his final wishes was central to the ensuing dispute; sources record conflicting accounts of his intentions, with some stating he had reconciled with his half-brother John of Montfort in 1340 and appointed him heir in a will, while others note he had previously favored his niece Joan of Penthièvre, the daughter of his younger brother Guy , , . His reported last words to his peers—"For God's sake leave me alone and do not trouble my spirit with such things"—underscore the lack of a definitive testamentary decision, leaving the field open for competing interpretations and legal arguments , . This vacuum of authority set the stage for a conflict rooted in both personal ambition and deeply entrenched legal doctrines concerning inheritance.

The core of the conflict lay in the competing claims of John of Montfort and Charles of Blois, which hinged on differing interpretations of Breton customary law versus French feudal law . John of Montfort, born around 1295, asserted his right based on proximity of blood and male-line descent from their father, Arthur II, Duke of Brittany , . He championed a "semi-Salic" mode of inheritance that, while permitting female-line succession in the absence of a direct male heir, prioritized the nearest male relative , . This argument was bolstered by Brittany's status as a *duché-pairie*—a member and part of the French crown since 1297—which made its succession subject to royal law, a principle that Philip VI himself would later invoke inconsistently , . In contrast, Charles of Blois, nephew of King Philip VI, derived his claim through his wife, Joan of Penthièvre , . Joan was the daughter of Duke John III's brother, Guy, Count of Penthièvre, and she inherited the county in her own right , . Her claim rested on the principle of "representation," whereby a female heir could pass on the rights of her deceased father, a practice permitted under Breton custom but explicitly barred by the strict Salic Law of Capetian France , . On July 4, 1337, Joan and Charles had married in Paris, an act orchestrated by Duke John III to secure French royal backing for her succession, thus creating a powerful dynastic alliance against Montfort's claim , .

John of Montfort acted with remarkable speed and decisiveness upon learning of Duke John III's death. He seized the initiative by moving swiftly across Brittany, conducting what chroniclers called a "great ride" to consolidate his position before his rival could react , . In May 1341, he arrived outside Nantes with a small force of around 200 men-at-arms and secured the city without bloodshed, subsequently seizing the ducal treasury which was stored in the cathedral sacristy in Limoges , . On May 20, 1341, he was proclaimed duke by an assembly composed of townspeople and minor nobles, extracting oaths of homage from them , . By mid-August 1341, his control had expanded dramatically to include most of southern and western Brittany, with key towns such as Rennes, Vannes, Hennebont, Brest, and Dinan falling under Montfortist control , , . This early momentum established a foothold for his faction and demonstrated the effectiveness of proactive seizure of power in a contested environment. However, his control remained precarious, resting primarily on urban centers and lesser nobility, as the upper echelons of the Breton nobility largely supported Joan of Penthièvre and her husband , . This growing tension came to a head when rumors reached King Philip VI of France that John of Montfort had been negotiating with English emissaries about recognizing Edward III as king of France in exchange for support . This perceived betrayal prompted Philip VI to accelerate proceedings at the Parlement de Paris, which had been deliberating the matter since late August . On September 7, 1341, the Parlement issued its formal ruling, declaring Charles of Blois the legitimate successor to Duke John III, citing feudal overlordship and a desire to bring Brittany under tighter royal control , . This decision effectively sealed the fate of John of Montfort's nascent regime, forcing him to seek refuge with his new patron, Edward III of England, and paving the way for a full-scale French invasion , .

## The French Counteroffensive and Montfort's Captivity

Following the Parlement de Paris's ruling on September 7, 1341, which officially recognized Charles of Blois's claim, King Philip VI of France moved with swift and decisive action to enforce the verdict and quell the Montfortist rebellion , . The French royal court convened at Conflans, and Philip VI summoned John of Montfort to appear before the Court of Peers to renounce his title or face confiscation of his lands , . Unwilling to submit, John of Montfort fled Paris in early September, prompting Philip VI to withdraw all remaining support for him and formally accept the liege homage of Charles of Blois on behalf of his wife, Joan of Penthièvre , . This act marked the beginning of the end for Montfort's brief tenure as duke. Philip VI simultaneously ordered the sequestration of John of Montfort's French lands—the County of Montfort-l'Amaury and the Viscounty of Limoges—and began assembling a large army to invade Brittany and impose Charles of Blois's rule by force , .

The French response was formidable. An army of over 7,000 strong, commanded by the Prince of Wales, John, Duke of Normandy, with oversight from royal advisors, assembled at Angers in late September 1341 . Charles of Blois led this Franco-Breton force into Brittany, laying siege to Montfort's key strongholds . The first major confrontation occurred in early October 1341 near Champtoceaux, where Montfort's forces were defeated in the Battle of Champtoceaux , . This defeat shattered Montfort's military strength and forced him to retreat to the coastal city of Nantes, which he had earlier garrisoned . There, Charles of Blois laid siege to the city, trapping John of Montfort inside . The siege of Nantes was a brutal affair. Montfort attempted several sorties to break the blockade, but they failed, and as the situation grew dire, the citizens of Nantes, weary of the fighting and likely influenced by promises of clemency from Charles of Blois, pressured Montfort to surrender , . On November 2, 1341, John of Montfort capitulated and was taken prisoner , . Following his capture, he was imprisoned in the Louvre in Paris, where he remained for the next four years, effectively removing the leader of the Montfortist faction from the conflict , , .

The capture of John of Montfort was a catastrophic blow to the Montfortist cause. It collapsed the territorial gains he had so laboriously won in the preceding months and handed a decisive victory to the Blois faction . With their leader imprisoned, the Montfortist resistance fragmented, and Charles of Blois consolidated his control over much of Brittany . By fall 1342, the Montfortists retained only the port city of Brest, which served as their last bastion of hope . The war now entered a new phase, characterized by the "War of the Two Jeannes," a conflict between Joan of Penthièvre and Joan of Flanders (Montfort's wife), as each sought to assert authority over the duchy in the absence of their husbands . The narrative of the war shifted decisively away from John of Montfort's direct command and towards a guerrilla struggle for survival, led by his wife from the fortress of Hennebont . Meanwhile, Philip VI's victory seemed complete. He had successfully imposed his preferred candidate on the Duchy of Brittany, secured a strategic buffer state against English Aquitaine, and crippled his rival, John of Montfort . However, the English king, Edward III, had not yet abandoned his vassal. The news of Montfort's capture ignited a firestorm of outrage in England and signaled the beginning of a direct and escalating Anglo-French confrontation that would transform the Breton Civil War into a major international conflict , . The French victory of 1341 was therefore not a final settlement but merely the prelude to a larger war fought over the contested duchy.

## The Decisive Role of English Intervention

The imprisonment of John of Montfort in November 1341 galvanized King Edward III of England into direct military intervention, transforming the Breton Civil War from a local succession dispute into a formal theatre of the Hundred Years' War , . Edward III viewed the French seizure of Brittany as an act of aggression against his vassal and a direct threat to English economic interests, particularly the lucrative wool trade and maritime supply chains connecting England to Gascony . Furthermore, Philip VI's inconsistent application of Salic Law principles in the Breton case provided Edward with a potent ideological weapon, allowing him to frame his support for Montfort as a defense of legal precedent . English intervention began in earnest in the spring of 1342 with a small expedition led by Sir Walter Manny, who landed a force at Brest, securing the vital port for the Montfortist cause , . Brest's strategic importance was immense; controlling it meant controlling access to the rest of Brittany and providing a secure base for English reinforcements . The surrender of Brest to the English in 1342 marked a critical turning point, establishing a permanent foothold that would endure for decades and symbolize the deep entanglement of Breton politics with the wider Anglo-French rivalry , .

The tide of the war turned dramatically in favor of the Montfortists in the summer of 1342 with the arrival of a much larger English force under the command of William de Bohun, Earl of Northampton , . Landing at Brest in August 1342 with approximately 1,100 troops, Northampton's expedition was a significant show of English resolve , . His campaign included the recapture of the strategically important city of Vannes, which had fallen to Charles of Blois , . The culmination of Northampton's campaign was the Battle of Morlaix on September 30, 1342, a clash that would prove to be a watershed moment in the early Hundred Years' War , . Facing a numerically superior Franco-Breton army, possibly numbering up to 30,000, the English army under Northampton, estimated at around 1,500 to 3,000 men, employed a series of tactical innovations that proved devastatingly effective , , . They deployed a defensive formation of dismounted men-at-arms and archers, using concealed trenches dug across the main road to disrupt French cavalry charges , . As the French knights charged, they were thrown from their horses into the pits, where they were picked off by volleys of arrows from the massed English longbowmen . Contemporary accounts describe how one arrow volley repelled armed peasants, and another killed fifty knights and captured 150 others, including Geoffrey de Charni . This victory, achieved through disciplined tactics rather than overwhelming numbers, demonstrated the superiority of English archery and defensive formations, foreshadowing the even greater triumphs at Crécy and Poitiers , .

The success at Morlaix emboldened Edward III to commit his personal presence to the Breton campaign. In late October 1342, he landed in Brittany with a large army estimated at between 3,600 and 3,700 men , , . His objectives were ambitious: to reassert Montfortist control over the entire duchy and deliver a crippling blow to Charles of Blois's forces. His campaign was initially successful; he retook Vannes and laid siege to Rennes, the capital of Brittany , . For a time, Charles of Blois was forced onto the defensive, and the balance of power in Brittany appeared to have definitively shifted in favor of the English-backed Montfortists . However, the war's momentum was about to be checked once more by diplomacy. The high cost of maintaining such a large army in Brittany, combined with the looming prospect of renewed hostilities with France elsewhere, prompted Edward III to seek a cessation of hostilities. This led to the negotiations that culminated in the Truce of Malestroit, signed on January 19, 1343, which temporarily froze the territorial status quo and mandated the release of prisoners, including John of Montfort , . While the English campaigns of 1342 had undeniably reversed the fortunes of the Montfortists, the war was far from over. The conflict had matured into a conventional European war, where victory depended less on simple seizure of territory and more on sustained logistics, naval supremacy, and innovative battlefield tactics. The interventions of 1342 had proven that England possessed the military capability to dominate the Breton theater, but achieving a final, lasting victory would require overcoming not only French and Bloisist resistance but also the inherent fragility of negotiated peace in an age of relentless dynastic conflict.

## Leadership and Resistance in the Breton Heartland

With the capture and imprisonment of John of Montfort in late 1341, the mantle of leadership for the Montfortist cause fell squarely upon his wife, Joanna of Flanders, a woman whose courage, strategic acumen, and martial prowess would become legendary , . Seizing the remnants of the Montfortist movement, she established her headquarters at the fortified port of Hennebont in western Brittany, a region that remained loyal to her faction , . From there, she became the embodiment of the Montfortist resistance, personally commanding the defense of the town against the determined siege laid by Charles of Blois in the spring of 1342 , . Her leadership was not confined to administrative duties; she actively participated in the fight for her husband's duchy. Chroniclers recount that she donned armor, rode through the streets summoning defenders, and rallied both soldiers and civilians to the cause , . When the siege intensified and supplies dwindled, she famously directed women and children to break up the town pavements to provide stones for ammunition, demonstrating a resourcefulness that inspired her followers , .

The climax of the siege at Hennebont occurred in April 1342 when Joanna executed a daring and brilliantly conceived cavalry sally , . Leading a force of 300 horsemen, she broke out of the besieged town, attacked Charles of Blois's camp, and set it ablaze, causing chaos and inflicting significant damage before retreating back to the safety of Hennebont , . This audacious maneuver shattered the morale of the besieging army and forced Charles of Blois to lift the siege in June 1342 , . Her actions during the siege were widely credited with earning her the epithet "Jeanne la Flamme" ("Joanna the Flame") and were instrumental in preserving the last major Montfortist stronghold , . The arrival of English naval reinforcement shortly thereafter, lifting the siege entirely, was the ultimate vindication of her steadfast resistance , . Beyond her defense of Hennebont, Joanna's contributions to the war effort were multifaceted. She dispatched her cousin, Amaury of Clisson, to England to solicit financial aid and military support from Edward III, a mission that proved successful . Later, in mid-1342, she sailed from England to Brittany with a contingent of English men-at-arms but was intercepted near Guernsey by a French fleet . During the ensuing shipboard combat, she reportedly fought with a glaive, slew multiple enemies, and helped repel the ambush, ensuring the safe passage of her reinforcements to Brittany . Her leadership during this dark period for the Montfortists was nothing short of heroic, sustaining the cause through sheer determination and military skill, and cementing her place as one of the most remarkable female figures of the Hundred Years' War era.

While Joanna of Flanders was the public face of Montfortist resistance in Brittany, the war also saw significant activity from French-aligned Breton nobles who defected to the English side. One of the most prominent among them was Olivier de Clisson, the head of a powerful noble house in north-western Poitou . In November 1342, he brought his vast network of clients and retainers, including notable lords like Girard Chabot and Girard de Machecoul, into allegiance with Edward III . De Clisson's defection was a significant blow to the Blois faction, as his annual income was estimated at 20,000 livres and his estates spanned western France, giving him considerable military and economic resources to contribute to the English war effort . Another notable figure was Godfrey of Harcourt, lord of Saint-Sauveur-le-Vicomte, who launched a personal rebellion against Philip VI in early 1343 over a dispute involving a local heiress . Although his rebellion was quickly suppressed and he was forced to flee to Brabant, he later performed liege homage to Edward III in England, further illustrating the fractious nature of the Breton and Norman nobility during this period . These defections highlight that the Breton Civil War was not simply a binary conflict between two external-backed factions. It was a complex web of loyalties, ambitions, and grievances, where individual lords made calculated choices based on self-interest, fealty, and opportunity. The willingness of powerful Breton magnates to switch sides underscores the fluidity of allegiances and the extent to which the war was a genuine civil conflict, pitting neighbor against neighbor in a struggle for the soul of the duchy.

## Diplomacy and the Collapse of the Truce of Malestroit

After years of escalating violence and shifting fortunes, the prospect of a negotiated peace emerged in early 1343. The immense cost of waging war, particularly for King Edward III who had invested heavily in his campaign in Brittany, made a temporary cessation of hostilities politically and economically attractive . This desire for peace was facilitated by Pope Clement VI, who, despite his general sympathies for the French, saw the utility of brokering a truce between the warring Christian monarchs . Mediated by Papal legates Cardinal Annibaldo Caetani di Ceccano and Cardinal Pierre Desprès, the Truce of Malestroit was signed on January 19, 1343, in the chapel of Malestroit , . The agreement aimed to freeze the ongoing conflict between England and France, stipulating a three-and-a-half-year cessation of hostilities scheduled to expire on September 29, 1346 , . The truce's terms were significant and carefully crafted. Both sides were required to retain all territories held at the inception of the truce, effectively freezing the map of Brittany . The strategically vital city of Vannes was placed under papal custody for the duration of the truce , . Furthermore, the agreement mandated a general exchange of prisoners and required King Philip VI to immediately free John of Montfort from his prison in the Louvre , . Historian Jonathan Sumption described the terms as being "astonishingly favourable" to England, as it allowed Edward III to achieve his primary goal of securing his vassal's freedom without conceding any ground on the underlying question of succession .

Despite the optimism surrounding its signing, the Truce of Malestroit was inherently fragile. It was a pragmatic ceasefire designed to buy time, not a treaty resolving the fundamental dispute over the Duchy of Brittany . Its provisions contained loopholes that allowed for continued localized fighting. Charles of Blois, in particular, argued that his war was separate from the truce between the kings of France and England, thereby justifying his continued military operations against Montfortist strongholds within Brittany , . This interpretation ensured that the civil war aspect of the conflict would continue beneath the surface of the official Anglo-French truce. John of Montfort's release from captivity on September 1, 1343, was a major victory for the Montfortist cause, but it was not a restoration of his former power , . He was released only after posting a huge bond and agreeing to remain on his eastern estates, effectively neutralizing his ability to directly command military operations in the west , . This restriction fueled his growing frustration and resentment towards Philip VI, who he felt had broken his word.

The truce's veneer of peace was shattered in a brutal display of political murder in the latter half of 1343. On August 2, 1343, King Philip VI ordered the arrest and execution of Olivier IV de Clisson, the powerful Breton noble who had defected to the English side , . His head was impaled above the main gate of Nantes as a warning to others . This act was a direct violation of the spirit, if not the letter, of the truce. It was followed by an even more shocking atrocity in November 1343, when Philip VI ordered the execution of fourteen other Breton lords who had supported John of Montfort . These executions were not only a cynical attempt to eliminate opposition but also a calculated provocation designed to destroy any possibility of reconciliation. They demonstrated that Philip VI was not interested in a lasting peace but in total victory. The news of these massacres enraged John of Montfort and solidified his resolve to return to Brittany and fight for his duchy. Unable to bear his confinement and spurred by the atrocities committed in his name, he broke parole in March 1345 and fled back to England . Upon his arrival, he found Edward III prepared to renew the war. The Truce of Malestroit was formally renounced, and open hostilities resumed, marking the end of the 1341–1343 phase of the conflict and the beginning of a new, more vicious chapter in the Breton Civil War . The failure of diplomacy underscored a grim reality: in the ruthless world of 14th-century European politics, agreements brokered by popes were often less durable than the swords of kings and their vassals.

Controlling Brest meant controlling access to the rest of Brittany and providing a secure base for English reinforcements.

The surrender of Brest to the English in 1342 marked a critical turning point, establishing a permanent foothold that would endure for decades and symbolize the deep entanglement of Breton politics with the wider Anglo-French rivalry.
The tide of the war turned dramatically in favor of the Montfortists in the summer of 1342 with the arrival of a much larger English force under the command of William de Bohun, Earl of Northampton.
Landing at Brest in August 1342 with approximately 1,100 troops, Northampton's expedition was a significant show of English resolve.
His campaign included the recapture of the strategically important city of Vannes, which had fallen to Charles of Blois.
The culmination of Northampton's campaign was the Battle of Morlaix on September 30, 1342, a clash that would prove to be a watershed moment in the early Hundred Years' War.

Facing a numerically superior Franco-Breton army, possibly numbering up to 30,000, the English army under Northampton, estimated at around 1,500 to 3,000 men, employed a series of tactical innovations that proved devastatingly effective.
They deployed a defensive formation of dismounted men-at-arms and archers, using concealed trenches dug across the main road to disrupt French cavalry charges.
As the French knights charged, they were thrown from their horses into the pits, where they were picked off by volleys of arrows from the massed English longbowmen.
Contemporary accounts describe how one arrow volley repelled armed peasants, and another killed fifty knights and captured 150 others, including Geoffrey de Charni.

This victory, achieved through disciplined tactics rather than overwhelming numbers, demonstrated the superiority of English archery and defensive formations, foreshadowing the even greater triumphs at Crécy and Poitiers.
The success at Morlaix emboldened Edward III to commit his personal presence to the Breton campaign.
In late October 1342, Edward III landed in Brittany with a large army estimated at between 3,600 and 3,700 men.
Edward III's objectives were ambitious: to reassert Montfortist control over the entire duchy and deliver a crippling blow to Charles of Blois's forces.
His campaign was initially successful; he retook Vannes and laid siege to Rennes, the capital of Brittany.
For a time, Charles of Blois was forced onto the defensive, and the balance of power in Brittany appeared to have definitively shifted in favor of the English-backed Montfortists.
However, the war's momentum was about to be checked once more by diplomacy.
The high cost of maintaining such a large army in Brittany, combined with the looming prospect of renewed hostilities with France elsewhere, prompted Edward III to seek a cessation of hostilities.

This led to the negotiations that culminated in the Truce of Malestroit, signed on January 19, 1343, which temporarily froze the territorial status quo and mandated the release of prisoners, including John of Montfort.
While the English campaigns of 1342 had undeniably reversed the fortunes of the Montfortists, the war was far from over.

The conflict had matured into a conventional European war, where victory depended less on simple seizure of territory and more on sustained logistics, naval supremacy, and innovative battlefield tactics.

The interventions of 1342 had proven that England possessed the military capability to dominate the Breton theater, but achieving a final, lasting victory would require overcoming not only French and Bloisist resistance but also the inherent fragility of negotiated peace in an age of relentless dynastic conflict.

With the capture and imprisonment of John of Montfort in late 1341, the mantle of leadership for the Montfortist cause fell squarely upon his wife, Joanna of Flanders, a woman whose courage, strategic acumen, and martial prowess would become legendary.
Seizing the remnants of the Montfortist movement, Joanna of Flanders established her headquarters at the fortified port of Hennebont in western Brittany, a region that remained loyal to her faction.
From there, she became the embodiment of the Montfortist resistance, personally commanding the defense of the town against the determined siege laid by Charles of Blois in the spring of 1342.
Her leadership was not confined to administrative duties; she actively participated in the fight for her husband's duchy.
Chroniclers recount that she donned armor, rode through the streets summoning defenders, and rallied both soldiers and civilians to the cause.

When the siege intensified and supplies dwindled, she famously directed women and children to break up the town pavements to provide stones for ammunition, demonstrating a resourcefulness that inspired her followers.
The climax of the siege at Hennebont occurred in April 1342 when Joanna executed a daring and brilliantly conceived cavalry sally.

Leading a force of 300 horsemen, she broke out of the besieged town, attacked Charles of Blois's camp, and set it ablaze, causing chaos and inflicting significant damage before retreating back to the safety of Hennebont.
This audacious maneuver shattered the morale of the besieging army and forced Charles of Blois to lift the siege in June 1342.
Her actions during the siege were widely credited with earning her the epithet "Jeanne la Flamme" ("Joanna the Flame") and were instrumental in preserving the last major Montfortist stronghold.
The arrival of English naval reinforcement shortly thereafter, lifting the siege entirely, was the ultimate vindication of her steadfast resistance.
Beyond her defense of Hennebont, Joanna's contributions to the war effort were multifaceted.
She dispatched her cousin, Amaury of Clisson, to England to solicit financial aid and military support from Edward III, a mission that proved successful.
Later, in mid-1342, she sailed from England to Brittany with a contingent of English men-at-arms but was intercepted near Guernsey by a French fleet.
During the ensuing shipboard combat, she reportedly fought with a glaive, slew multiple enemies, and helped repel the ambush, ensuring the safe passage of her reinforcements to Brittany.

Her leadership during this dark period for the Montfortists was nothing short of heroic, sustaining the cause through sheer determination and military skill, and cementing her place as one of the most remarkable female figures of the Hundred Years' War era.
While Joanna of Flanders was the public face of Montfortist resistance in Brittany, the war also saw significant activity from French-aligned Breton nobles who defected to the English side.
One of the most prominent among them was Olivier de Clisson, the head of a powerful noble house in north-western Poitou.
In November 1342, Olivier de Clisson brought his vast network of clients and retainers, including notable lords like Girard Chabot and Girard de Machecoul, into allegiance with Edward III.

De Clisson's defection was a significant blow to the Blois faction, as his annual income was estimated at 20,000 livres and his estates spanned western France, giving him considerable military and economic resources to contribute to the English war effort.
Another notable figure was Godfrey of Harcourt, lord of Saint-Sauveur-le-Vicomte, who launched a personal rebellion against Philip VI in early 1343 over a dispute involving a local heiress.

Although his rebellion was quickly suppressed and he was forced to flee to Brabant, he later performed liege homage to Edward III in England, further illustrating the fractious nature of the Breton and Norman nobility during this period.
These defections highlight that the Breton Civil War was not simply a binary conflict between two external-backed factions.
It was a complex web of loyalties, ambitions, and grievances, where individual lords made calculated choices based on self-interest, fealty, and opportunity.

The willingness of powerful Breton magnates to switch sides underscores the fluidity of allegiances and the extent to which the war was a genuine civil conflict, pitting neighbor against neighbor in a struggle for the soul of the duchy.
After years of escalating violence and shifting fortunes, the prospect of a negotiated peace emerged in early 1343.

The immense cost of waging war, particularly for King Edward III who had invested heavily in his campaign in Brittany, made a temporary cessation of hostilities politically and economically attractive.
This desire for peace was facilitated by Pope Clement VI, who, despite his general sympathies for the French, saw the utility of brokering a truce between the warring Christian monarchs.
Mediated by Papal legates Cardinal Annibaldo Caetani di Ceccano and Cardinal Pierre Desprès, the Truce of Malestroit was signed on January 19, 1343, in the chapel of Malestroit.
The agreement aimed to freeze the ongoing conflict between England and France, stipulating a three-and-a-half-year cessation of hostilities scheduled to expire on September 29, 1346.
The truce's terms were significant and carefully crafted.
Both sides were required to retain all territories held at the inception of the truce, effectively freezing the map of Brittany.
The strategically vital city of Vannes was placed under papal custody for the duration of the truce.
Furthermore, the agreement mandated a general exchange of prisoners and required King Philip VI to immediately free John of Montfort from his prison in the Louvre.

Historian Jonathan Sumption described the terms as being "astonishingly favourable" to England, as it allowed Edward III to achieve his primary goal of securing his vassal's freedom without conceding any ground on the underlying question of succession.
Despite the optimism surrounding its signing, the Truce of Malestroit was inherently fragile.
It was a pragmatic ceasefire designed to buy time, not a treaty resolving the fundamental dispute over the Duchy of Brittany.
Its provisions contained loopholes that allowed for continued localized fighting.

Charles of Blois, in particular, argued that his war was separate from the truce between the kings of France and England, thereby justifying his continued military operations against Montfortist strongholds within Brittany.
This interpretation ensured that the civil war aspect of the conflict would continue beneath the surface of the official Anglo-French truce.
John of Montfort's release from captivity on September 1, 1343, was a major victory for the Montfortist cause, but it was not a restoration of his former power.
He was released only after posting a huge bond and agreeing to remain on his eastern estates, effectively neutralizing his ability to directly command military operations in the west.
This restriction fueled his growing frustration and resentment towards Philip VI, who he felt had broken his word.
The truce's veneer of peace was shattered in a brutal display of political murder in the latter half of 1343.
On August 2, 1343, King Philip VI ordered the arrest and execution of Olivier IV de Clisson, the powerful Breton noble who had defected to the English side.
His head was impaled above the main gate of Nantes as a warning to others.
This act was a direct violation of the spirit, if not the letter, of the truce.
It was followed by an even more shocking atrocity in November 1343, when Philip VI ordered the execution of fourteen other Breton lords who had supported John of Montfort.
These executions were not only a cynical attempt to eliminate opposition but also a calculated provocation designed to destroy any possibility of reconciliation.
They demonstrated that Philip VI was not interested in a lasting peace but in total victory.
The news of these massacres enraged John of Montfort and solidified his resolve to return to Brittany and fight for his duchy.
Unable to bear his confinement and spurred by the atrocities committed in his name, he broke parole in March 1345 and fled back to England.
Upon his arrival, he found Edward III prepared to renew the war.

The Truce of Malestroit was formally renounced, and open hostilities resumed, marking the end of the 1341–1343 phase of the conflict and the beginning of a new, more vicious chapter in the Breton Civil War.

The failure of diplomacy underscored a grim reality: in the ruthless world of 14th-century European politics, agreements brokered by popes were often less durable than the swords of kings and their vassals.

Brittany") [**†**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killed_in_action "Killed in action") [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre") | [![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/Guerre_de_Succession_de_Bretagne_1341-1364.png/500px-Guerre_de_Succession_de_Bretagne_1341-1364.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Guerre_de_Succession_de_Bretagne_1341-1364.png) Funeral of [John III, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany"), depicted in the Chronicles of [Jean Froissart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Froissart "Jean Froissart") The **War of the Breton Succession** ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _guerre de Succession de Bretagne_; [Breton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_language "Breton language"): _Brezel hêrezh dugelezh Breizh_) or **Breton Civil War** was a conflict between the [Counts of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counts_of_Blois "Counts of Blois") and the [Montforts of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montfort_of_Brittany "Montfort of Brittany") for control of the [Duchy of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brittany "Duchy of Brittany"), then a [fief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fief "Fief") of the [Kingdom of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France"). It was fought between 1341 and 12 April 1365.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#cite_note-FritzeRobison2002-1) It is also known as the **War of the Two Joans** ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _guerre des deux Jeannes_) due to the involvement of two rival duchesses of that name, [Joan of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort") and [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#cite_note-2) The war formed an integral part of the early [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") due to the proxy involvement of the French and English monarchs in the conflict; the French supported the Blois (female heir) whilst the English backed the Montforts (male heir). The rival kings supported the duke of the principle opposite to their own claims to the French throne—the [Plantagenet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Plantagenet "House of Plantagenet") having claimed it by female succession, and the [Valois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Valois "House of Valois") by male succession. Montfort was ultimately successful following the [Battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray") in 1364 but, in a surprising turn of events, pledged his loyalty to the king of France and not to the Plantagenet king of England who had supported him. The Breton dukes had both a historical and ancestral connection to Britain and were also [earls of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earls_of_Richmond "Earls of Richmond") in [Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire "Yorkshire"). Duke [Arthur II of Dreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "Arthur II, Duke of Brittany") married twice, first to Mary of Limoges (1275–1291), then to [Yolande of Dreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yolande_of_Dreux,_Queen_of_Scotland "Yolande of Dreux, Queen of Scotland") (1263–1322), countess of Montfort and widow of King [Alexander III of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_III_of_Scotland "Alexander III of Scotland"). From his first marriage, he had three sons, including his heir [John III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany") and Guy, [count of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counts_and_dukes_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Counts and dukes of Penthièvre") (d. 1331). From Yolande, Arthur had another son, also named John, who became Count of Montfort. (See [Dukes of Brittany family tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dukes_of_Brittany_family_tree "Dukes of Brittany family tree").) John III strongly disliked the children of his father's second marriage. He spent the first years of his reign attempting to have this marriage annulled and his half-siblings bastardized. When this failed, he tried to ensure that [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort") would never inherit the duchy. Since John III was childless, his heir of choice became [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre"), _la Boiteuse_, daughter of his younger brother Guy. In 1337 she married [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois"), the second son of a powerful French noble house whose mother's brother was King [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"). But in 1340, John III reconciled himself with his half-brother, and made a will that appointed John of Montfort the heir of Brittany. On 30 April 1341, John III died. His last words on the succession, uttered on his deathbed, were, "For God's sake leave me alone and do not trouble my spirit with such things". First stage of the war ---------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=War_of_the_Breton_Succession&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: First stage of the war")\] Most of the nobility supported Charles of Blois, so if John of Montfort was to have any chance, it was dependent upon swift action before organized resistance could be made. John quickly took possession of the [ducal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke "Duke") capital [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes") and then seized the Ducal treasury at [Limoges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limoges "Limoges"). By the middle of August, John of Montfort was in possession of most of the Duchy, the three principal cities of Nantes, [Rennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes "Rennes") and [Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes "Vannes"). Up to this point, the succession crisis had been a purely internal affair. But to complicate things further, the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") between England and France had broken out four years earlier, in 1337. In 1341, there was a truce between the two countries, but there was little doubt that hostilities would be renewed when the truce ended in June 1342. Thus, when rumours reached [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") that John of Montfort had received English agents, the French Crown naturally took a more direct interest in their small neighbors situation. Charles of Blois became the official French candidate. Whatever had been his original intentions, John of Montfort was now forced to support [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") as King of France. Edward III was bound by the truce not to take any offensive action in France. Nothing in it, however, hindered France from subduing rebellious vassals. In November, after a short siege and defeat at the [Battle of Champtoceaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux "Battle of Champtoceaux"), John of Montfort was forced to surrender at [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes") by the citizens. He was offered safe conduct to negotiate a settlement with Charles of Blois, but when this led nowhere he was thrown in prison. It now fell upon John's wife, [Joan of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), to lead the Montfortist cause. Deeming her possessions in the east indefensible, she set up headquarters at [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont") in western Brittany but was driven into Brest and besieged, the siege being broken by the arrival of an English army under the [Earl of Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton") at the [naval battle of Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Brest_/(1342/) "Battle of Brest (1342)") on 18 August 1342. Northampton then made his way inland and besieged Morlaix after an unsuccessful initial attack. The siege was lifted after the [battle of Morlaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix "Battle of Morlaix") on 30 September. In Paris it was feared that Edward III would land at [Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calais "Calais") once the truce ran out. The major part of the French army was therefore withdrawn, and Charles of Blois was left to pursue his claim on his own. Charles soon proved himself to be an able soldier: Rennes and Vannes were taken and many of the Montfortist captains defected. In late November, [Edward III arrived with his army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III%27s_Breton_campaign,_1342%E2%80%931343 "Edward III's Breton campaign, 1342–1343") at [Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brest,_France "Brest, France"). He almost at once marched against Vannes. [The siege dragged on](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sieges_of_Vannes_/(1342/) "Sieges of Vannes (1342)") and a French army was assembled to meet him, but on 19 January 1343, before any major engagements could be fought, the two kings agreed the [Truce of Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit "Truce of Malestroit"). Vannes was taken into papal custody. With John of Montfort in prison, his son an infant, and his wife recently gone mad, the places under Montfortist control were in practice administered from London, with a large permanent English garrison at Brest. The truce was to last until 29 September 1346 with the hopes that in the meantime the disputes between the two kingdoms could be permanently settled, but in Brittany it made little difference. The truce bound the two kings and their followers, but Charles of Blois claimed to be fighting his own separate war and was therefore not bound by any truce. The brutal small-scale fighting continued at the same pace. In Paris, John of Montfort was released from prison on 1 September 1343 in return for a huge bond and a promise to stay on his estates in the east. The English coastal garrisons held firm, but the Montfortist party continued to crumble. They had some successes, such as the expulsion of the papal custodians from Vannes, but with no unifying leadership, mostly they were reduced to pleading for men and money from London. To hamper communication between Brest and Vannes, Charles of Blois laid siege to [Quimper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quimper,_Finist%C3%A8re "Quimper, Finistère") in early March 1344. The city fell by assault on 1 May and, as usual at that time, this meant the slaughter of civilians in huge numbers, estimated between 1,400 and 2,000. The English prisoners were held for ransom, but the Breton and Norman captives were dispatched to Paris where they were executed for treason. During the summer and autumn, the Montfortist party fell apart. Even those who had been John of Montfort's staunchest allies now considered it futile to continue the struggle. It, therefore, mattered little that in March 1345 John finally managed to escape to England. With no adherents of note of his own, he was now little more than a figurehead for English ambitions in Brittany. Edward III decided to repudiate the truce in summer 1345, a year before it was due to run out. As part of his larger strategy, a force was dispatched to Brittany under the joint leadership of the [Earl of Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton") and John of Montfort. Within a week of their landing in June, the English had their first victory when Sir [Thomas Dagworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Dagworth "Thomas Dagworth"), one of Northampton's lieutenants, raided central Brittany and defeated Charles of Blois at Cadoret near [Josselin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josselin "Josselin"). The follow-up was less impressive. Further operations were delayed until July when Montfort attempted the recapture of Quimper. However, news had reached the French government that Edward's main campaign had been canceled and they were able to send reinforcements from Normandy. With his strengthened army, Charles of Blois broke the siege. Routed, Montfort fled back to Hennebont where he fell ill and died on 16 September. The heir to the Montfortist cause was his five-year-old son, [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"). During the winter, Northampton fought a long and hard campaign with the apparent objective of seizing a harbour on the north side of the peninsula. Edward III had probably planned to land here with his main force during summer 1346. However, the English achieved very little for their efforts. Northern Brittany was Joan of Penthièvre's home region and resistance there was stiff. In the end, Edward decided upon Normandy as the landing spot for his 1346 campaign. Northampton was recalled and Thomas Dagworth was appointed as deputy lieutenant. It was during a tour through the English strongholds on 9 June that Dagworth and his escort were trapped by Charles of Blois and his army near [Saint-Pol-de-Léon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Pol-de-L%C3%A9on "Saint-Pol-de-Léon"). They dug in on a hilltop and fought off all attacks until nightfall when Charles was forced to retreat leaving many of his wounded behind. Tide turns against Charles -------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=War_of_the_Breton_Succession&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Tide turns against Charles")\] [![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Capture_Charles_de_Blois.jpg/250px-Capture_Charles_de_Blois.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Capture_Charles_de_Blois.jpg) Capture of Charles of Blois At this point events outside Brittany started to have an effect on the war. The French suffered a major defeat at the [Battle of Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy "Battle of Crécy") in 1346, and at Calais in 1347. Without French support, Charles of Blois gradually began to lose ground to the English captains. The memory of the massacre at Quimper increased his unpopularity, and Breton traders had an economic interest in strengthening links with England due to Brittany's strategic position between the Atlantic and English Channel. At the [Battle of La Roche-Derrien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_La_Roche-Derrien "Battle of La Roche-Derrien") in 1347, Charles was taken prisoner as he tried to recapture the town, which had just been taken by the English. He was jailed for five years in the Tower of London. The English now controlled Brest, Quimper, and Vannes. Under pressure from [Pope Innocent VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Innocent_VI "Pope Innocent VI"), the English, French, and Bretons negotiated a peace, while both factions maintained an uneasy balance of power within the duchy. It was during this period that the [Combat of the Thirty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combat_of_the_Thirty "Combat of the Thirty") took place, a famous episode in medieval chivalry. Conflicts between the French and English strongholds of [Josselin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josselin "Josselin") and [Ploërmel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plo%C3%ABrmel "Ploërmel") were resolved in a duel between thirty Montfortist knights led by [Robert Bemborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bemborough "Robert Bemborough"), and thirty supporters of Charles de Blois led by [Jean de Beaumanoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_de_Beaumanoir "Jean de Beaumanoir"). The combat took place midway between the two towns on 26 March 1351. By nightfall the Anglo-Breton Montfortists had lost nine dead against six of the pro-French knights; the surviving Montfortists were forced to surrender. Though renowned at the time, and later highly romanticised, the combat had no effect on the outcome of the war. [![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Le_Combat_des_Trente_%281857%29.jpg/250px-Le_Combat_des_Trente_%281857%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Le_Combat_des_Trente_/(1857/).jpg) A 19th-century painting depicting the _[The Combat of the Thirty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Combat_of_the_Thirty "The Combat of the Thirty")_ ([Octave Penguilly L'Haridon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octave_Penguilly_L%27Haridon "Octave Penguilly L'Haridon"), 1857) Edward III signed the Treaty of Westminster on 1 March 1353, accepting Charles of Blois as Duke of Brittany if the latter undertook to pay a ransom of 300,000 crowns, and that Brittany signed a treaty of alliance "in perpetuity" with England; this alliance was to be sealed by the marriage of the Montfortist claimant John of Montfort (son of the earlier John of Montfort) with Edward's daughter Mary. The marriage required the approval of the King of France and a papal dispensation. [Charles de la Cerda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_la_Cerda "Charles de la Cerda"), the [Constable of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constable_of_France "Constable of France"), negotiated the deal, but [Charles II of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_Navarre "Charles II of Navarre"), who needed to continue the war between England and France to maintain his own power, decided to intervene by assassinating the Constable. He then switched his support to France in exchange for territory. The treaty was negated, but Charles of Blois had been freed, and returned to Brittany as Duke. [![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Battle_of_Auray_2.jpg/250px-Battle_of_Auray_2.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Battle_of_Auray_2.jpg) The Battle of Auray, 1364 The situation remained in stalemate for some time, with Charles of Blois as _de facto_ Duke, but with significant territory still controlled by the Montfortists. Outside events again began to have an effect on the conflict. A plague struck France and the King himself was captured by the English at the [Battle of Poitiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Poitiers "Battle of Poitiers") in 1356. The French state was virtually paralysed. In 1362, when the younger John de Montfort reached 22 years of age, King Edward permitted him to return to Brittany. His return was conditioned by a covenant not to marry without permission, given in pledge of several fortresses. On arrival, John attempted to reach agreement with Charles of Blois to make peace and share Brittany, but Charles's wife Joan urged him to resist and crush John. The war resumed in 1363 when Charles de Blois, assisted by [Bertrand du Guesclin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand_du_Guesclin "Bertrand du Guesclin"), had some successes, but when Bertrand left to take control of strongholds in Navarre and Normandy, Charles's advance halted at the unsuccessful siege of Bécherel. Another opportunity to negotiate an agreement arose, but again Joan blocked negotiations. John de Montfort moved to besiege [Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auray "Auray") with renowned English warlord [John Chandos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Chandos "John Chandos"). Charles of Blois and Bertrand du Guesclin came to the rescue of the besieged city, but they were decisively defeated at the [Battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray") on 29 September 1364. This battle marked the end of this long conflict: Charles of Blois was killed and Joan of Penthièvre, finding herself a widow, saw her cause collapse. Du Guesclin was captured and [ransomed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ransom "Ransom") by Charles V for 100,000 [francs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franc "Franc"). Peace was concluded on 12 April 1365 by the [First Treaty of Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_/(1365/) "Treaty of Guérande (1365)") which established John of Montfort as Duke of Brittany. He did not reject completely the claims of the Penthièvre family, and established the following law of succession in Brittany: * The Duchy would be transmitted from male to male in the family of Montfort. * In the absence of male offspring, it would switch to males of the family of Penthièvre. * Joan retained the prerogative of Penthièvre and the Viscouncy of Limoges. * She would also receive 10,000 livres of annual rent taken from the French territories of the enemy. King [Charles V of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V_of_France "Charles V of France") did not oppose the elevation of John, fearing that he might declare homage to Edward of England, his protector and former father-in-law (Mary having died in 1361). In addition, France was clearly depleted in the context of the Hundred Years' War. He therefore recognized John as Duke. By this action, he won the friendship of the Breton nobility. In December 1366, he received the oath of the new duke who surprisingly did not pledge allegiance to Edward, recognizing Charles as his sovereign instead. The provisions of the treaty were later repudiated by the Montfortists when a later duke, [John V, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_V,_Duke_of_Brittany "John V, Duke of Brittany") was kidnapped by the Penthièvres in 1420, in violation of the treaty. The Montfortists declared that the treaty had been broken, and as such were no longer required to accept its succession provisions. This became significant when [Francis II, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "Francis II, Duke of Brittany") failed to produce a male heir, allowing the duchy to pass to his daughter [Anne of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_of_Brittany "Anne of Brittany") in 1488. * **30 April 1341**: John III dies without heirs. Joan of Penthièvre and Charles of Blois became Duchess and Duke of Brittany. John of Montfort refuses to accept and calls for the help of King [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England"). * **1343**: John of Montfort is taken prisoner, but is released shortly afterwards. Charles tries to take advantage and attacks Hennebont, but the city is defended with success by [Joan of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), wife of Montfort. An English army relieves the siege and forces the Blois to a truce, broken shortly afterwards. * **1344**: Charles takes Quimper with the help of a French army, courtesy of King [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"), and slaughters 2000 civilians. * **1345**: John of Montfort fails to recover Quimper and dies. His ambitions over Brittany are inherited by his son [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"). His mother, Joan of Flanders, becomes the political and military commander of the Montfort faction. * **Between 1346 and 1364**, several minor battles are won and lost by both parts, several truces are signed and broken. Joan of Flanders becomes mentally ill and is institutionalized in a convent. * **27 March 1351**: [Combat of the Thirty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combat_of_the_Thirty "Combat of the Thirty") * **29 September 1364**: [Battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray"). [Bertrand du Guesclin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand_du_Guesclin "Bertrand du Guesclin") and Charles of Blois are heavily defeated by John IV and the English warlord [John Chandos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Chandos "John Chandos"). Charles is killed in action, ending the Blois pretensions in Brittany. * **1365**: John IV is recognized as Duke of Brittany and Joan of Penthièvre gives up any claim to the duchy in the [Treaty of Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_/(1365/) "Treaty of Guérande (1365)"). Surprisingly, the new duke declares himself as a vassal, not to the English king who helped him, but to King [Charles V of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V_of_France "Charles V of France"). * [List of rulers of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_rulers_of_Brittany "List of rulers of Brittany") * [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") * [List of wars of succession in Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_wars_of_succession_in_Europe "List of wars of succession in Europe") * [War of the Two Pedros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Two_Pedros "War of the Two Pedros") 1. ^ [_**a**_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#cite_ref-FritzeRobison2002_1-0) [_**b**_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#cite_ref-FritzeRobison2002_1-1) Ronald H. Fritze; William Baxter Robison (2002). [_Historical Dictionary of Late Medieval England, 1272–1485_](https://books.google.com/books?id=INmdwCSkvIgC). Greenwood Publishing Group. p. 231. [_Medieval Elite Women and the Exercise of Power, 1100–1400: Moving beyond the Exceptionalist Debate_](https://books.google.com/books?id=HxyDDwAAQBAJ&q=%22war+of+the+two+jeannes%22+1385). Springer.
