The **Truce of Malestroit** was [sealed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seal_/(emblem/) "Seal (emblem)") by King [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") and King [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") on 19 January 1343 in [Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malestroit "Malestroit"), [Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany "Brittany"), with the intention of pausing the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") until 29 September 1346. It laid down that a peace conference was to be held in the interim to negotiate an end to the war. The war had broken out in 1337 and Edward had formally laid claim to the French crown in 1340, possibly as a diplomatic manoeuvre. On 25 September 1340 the [Truce of Espléchin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Espl%C3%A9chin "Truce of Espléchin"), which was mediated by emissaries of [Pope Benedict XII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Benedict_XII "Pope Benedict XII"), was agreed. This was intended to pause hostilities until 24 June 1341 but was later extended to 24 June 1342. During 1341 [a succession war broke out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_campaign_of_the_Breton_Civil_War "Initial campaign of the Breton Civil War") in the [Duchy of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brittany "Duchy of Brittany"), a semi-autonomous province of France. Philip VI backed one of the factions – led by [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois") – and early in 1342 Edward III backed the other – led by [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort"). [Edward landed in Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III%27s_Breton_campaign "Edward III's Breton campaign") in October 1342 with a small army; a lack of shipping prevented many of the available English troops from crossing [the Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Channel "The Channel") with him. This English force struck at the important town of [Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes "Vannes"). A naval attack in November failed to take the town, and an assault by the main English army later in the month was also beaten off. The French raised a much larger army and marched it into Brittany, but halted at Malestroit, 20 miles (32 km) from Vannes. There two [cardinals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_/(Catholic_Church/) "Cardinal (Catholic Church)") mediated a truce in the course of a few days. This was sealed on 9 January 1343 and was due to last until 29 September 1346. Both monarchs pledged to send delegations to negotiate in [Avignon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon "Avignon"), then the [seat of the Papacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon_Papacy "Avignon Papacy"). There, mediated by [Pope Clement VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_VI "Pope Clement VI"), a treaty to permanently end the war would be drafted. In reality each king saw the truce as a mere pause and neither intended to negotiate in good faith; the truce had only been agreed because each felt it was beneficial to him. When the conference finally convened in late 1344 the proposals made by each side were unacceptable to the other, with neither displaying any willingness to compromise, and it rapidly collapsed. After mutual provocations Edward formally renounced the truce on 15 June 1345 and full-scale war resumed. [![Image 3: a map of France showing only a small part of the south-west under English control](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Francia1328-Shepherd-Simplificado.svg/250px-Francia1328-Shepherd-Simplificado.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Francia1328-Shepherd-Simplificado.svg) France in 1328: English-controlled Gascony is shown in blue in the south west Since the [Norman Conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Conquest "Norman Conquest") of 1066, English monarchs had held titles and lands within France, the possession of which made them [vassals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vassal "Vassal") of the kings of France. By the first quarter of the fourteenth century, the only sizeable French possession still held by the English in France was [Gascony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gascony "Gascony") in the south west.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption199039%E2%80%9340-1) Following a series of disagreements between [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") and [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England"), on 24 May 1337 Philip's [Great Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conseil_du_Roi "Conseil du Roi") agreed that the lands held by Edward III in France should be taken back into Philip's hands on the grounds that Edward was in breach of his obligations as a vassal. This marked the start of the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War"), which was to last 116 years.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990184-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger200479-3) On 26 January 1340 Edward formally [claimed the French throne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_claims_to_the_French_throne "English claims to the French throne"). The immediate effect was to allow the [Flemings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flemish_people "Flemish people") to join his cause without technically disowning their fealty to the French crown and therefore becoming rebels. The extent to which Edward considered the claim more than a negotiating position is unclear. In June the French navy was annihilated by the English fleet at the [battle of Sluys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sluys "Battle of Sluys") and in July Edward [invaded France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tournaisis_campaign_of_1340 "Tournaisis campaign of 1340") at the head of a large, heavily subsidised, allied army. The allies [laid siege to Tournai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Tournai_/(1340/) "Siege of Tournai (1340)") on 1 August. On 7 September the French army arrived, but Philip held it back to ensure there was no risk of a battle occurring. He was probably aware that the allied army was falling apart, with the English unable to pay their allies what they had been promised, or even to feed them. Negotiations for a pause in the fighting were opened, mediated by emissaries of [Pope Benedict XII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Benedict_XII "Pope Benedict XII"). The [Truce of Espléchin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Espl%C3%A9chin "Truce of Espléchin") was rapidly agreed, to last from 25 September 1340 to 24 June 1341. The allied armies left France thereafter.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200235%E2%80%9336-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006299%E2%80%93300-5) Edward was unable to meet his commitments, the English Crown was bankrupt, and Edward fled the continent in order to avoid his envisaged in 1621[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBritannica2018-7) During the early 14th century [Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany When the [Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_rulers_of_Brittany "List of rulers of Brittany"), [John III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany"), died on 30 April 1341 he left a disputed succession, with both his niece, [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre"), and his France.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990370%E2%80%93371-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199966%E2%80%9367-12)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraham-Goering202047%E2%80%9349-13) The French king correctly suspected that John was negotiating with the English, and had Charles declared the rightful heir on 7 September, despatching an army to support him.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand200114-14)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990377%E2%80%93378-15)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007203-16) On 12 September 1341 the Truce of Espléchin was extended to 24 June 1342. Edward and his [council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privy_Council_of_England "Privy Council of England") agreed that the English army would be disbanded for the winter and the fleet paid off. Meanwhile, the French army swiftly overran all of eastern Brittany apart from [Rennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes "Rennes") and captured John.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990385%E2%80%93386,_389-17) John's wife, [Joanna of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), fled west with the ducal treasury and their two-year-old son, also named [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), whom she set up as the faction's figurehead and heir to his father's claim to the duchy. She despatched a senior counsellor to England with a large sum in cash, to encourage rapid English military intervention.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990389%E2%80%93390,_409-18)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-19)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVisserSnijder201433%E2%80%9334-20) ### English intervention \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Truce_of_Malestroit&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: English intervention")\] [![Image 5: Colour photograph of a small medieval-era single-masted sailing ship](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Ubena_von_Bremen_Kiel2007_1_%28cropped%29.jpg/330px-Ubena_von_Bremen_Kiel2007_1_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ubena_von_Bremen_Kiel2007_1_/(cropped/).jpg) In 1962 a well-preserved wreck of a [cog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cog_/(ship/) "Cog (ship)") dated to 1380 was found near Bremen, Germany. This is a full-size reproduction. Merchant vessels such as these formed the bulk of the English fleet.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004120-21)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTERose200716-22) On 21 February 1342 Edward sealed a treaty to support the Montfort cause, as an extension of the war with France.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod199017-23)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990390-24) Edward planned to land in Brittany himself with a substantial force, after the expiry of the Truce of Espléchin in June, but had extreme difficulty in mustering ships.[\[note 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-27) Eventually the English impressed 440 ships,[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011112-28) but then contrary winds caused their departure to be repeatedly put back.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990391,_393-29)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-19)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011109%E2%80%93111-30) In May 1342 [Clement VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_VI "Pope Clement VI") became pope. He was strongly pro-French and had previously been one of Philip's senior advisers. He despatched two cardinals – [Annibaldo Caetani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annibaldo_Caetani "Annibaldo Caetani"), [bishop of Frascati–Tusculum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Suburbicarian_Diocese_of_Frascati "Roman Catholic Suburbicarian Diocese of Frascati"); and [Pierre Desprès](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Despr%C3%A8s "Pierre Desprès"), [bishop of Palestrina–Praeneste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Suburbicarian_Diocese_of_Palestrina "Roman Catholic Suburbicarian Diocese of Palestrina") – to attempt to broker a permanent settlement of the Anglo-French war. They were well received by Philip in June, but Edward would not even allow them to cross [the Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Channel "The Channel").[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990395%E2%80%93396-31)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZutshi2000658-32)[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTED%C3%A9prez1967302-33) Instead he continued to gather ships and troops.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFriel200375-34) Meanwhile, the flow of events went against the Montfortists in the face of the huge military superiority of the French. By July [Joanna was besieged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Brest_/(1342/) "Siege of Brest (1342)") in the port of [Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brest,_France "Brest, France"), the only fortified place still held by her faction.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004101-35) This was on the brink of surrender when the English advance force, commanded by [William, Earl of Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton"), arrived on 18 August. The French commander, Charles of Blois, promptly broke off the siege, abandoned western Brittany and withdrew 70 miles (110 km) to [Guingamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guingamp "Guingamp").[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199970-36)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990399%E2%80%93401-37)[\[note 2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-39) The English marched 30 miles (50 km) from Brest to Morlaix, a port on the north coast of Brittany with strong fortifications and a secure harbour, and laid siege to it.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199970-36)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990399%E2%80%93401-37) Edward's contingent was still in England waiting for the ships which had transported Northampton's echelon to return. The French mistakenly believed Edward's army would be used in northern France, probably disembarking in [Picardy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picardy "Picardy"). A French army was gathered to confront this imagined threat, including many men transferred from Brittany. Charles became aware his force greatly outnumbered the English, despite the detachments to Picardy, and took his army west in an attempt to relieve Morlaix. He was [defeated by Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix "Battle of Morlaix") on 30 September, suffering heavy losses.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990401%E2%80%93402-40)[\[note 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-43) On 6 October Edward abandoned his [siege train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Train_/(military/) "Train (military)") on the beach and set sail with those troops he was able to embark onto the available shipping. They reached Brittany after a storm-wracked three-week passage.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011112%E2%80%93113-44)[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990401,_403-45) A map of Brittany, with modern administrative boundaries, showing the locations of some of the places mentioned in the text After concentrating at Brest, the English and Montfortist forces moved on the major city of [Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes "Vannes"), the second most populous settlement in Brittany, with a good harbour and strong walls. From Vannes a strong detachment could control much of southern Brittany. On 7 November both the navy and the army set off. The fleet was depleted by the desertion of most of its ships; their masters and crews were unhappy at not being paid and at being forced out to sea in dangerous winter weather.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011113-46)[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990403%E2%80%93404-47)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFr%C3%A9laut200535-48) Those left sailed to Vannes, enduring a winter storm en route. They attempted to take the town with a surprise attack; this came close to success but was defeated.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990404%E2%80%93405-49)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011113-46)[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004102-38) In England the [King's Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curia_regis "Curia regis") attempted to organise a further fleet to carry supplies and reinforcements. Fifty-six ships sailed on or after 3 November carrying 600 men, but were driven ashore in the [Isles of Scilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isles_of_Scilly "Isles of Scilly") by further storms. They and 800 men who had not sailed waited for a break in the weather, fruitlessly: they were finally [stood down](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/stand_down "wikt:stand down") in February 1343.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990406-50)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011113-46) The main Anglo-Breton army marched unopposed some 120 miles (190 km) through southern Brittany and on 29 November attempted to take Vannes by storm. The French garrison had been newly reinforced and repelled this assault; a regular siege began.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990405%E2%80%93406-51) The siege did not require the entire army and large detachments were sent on [chevauchees](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/chevauchee "wikt:chevauchee") across eastern Brittany to devastate the region and capture the fortified places. The outskirts of [Dinan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinan "Dinan") and the area around [Dol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dol-de-Bretagne "Dol-de-Bretagne") were devastated, 100 miles (160 km) north of Vannes.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990405%E2%80%93406-51) [Ploërmel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plo%C3%ABrmel "Ploërmel"), [Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malestroit "Malestroit") and [Redon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redon,_Ille-et-Vilaine "Redon, Ille-et-Vilaine") were captured and [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes"), the ducal capital, was besieged.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200660,_207-52) Increasing numbers of Breton knights and lords switched their allegiance to the Montfortist cause. However, there were fewer than 5,000 English troops in Brittany, and the term of service of many was running out.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990406-50) No food supplies were arriving for Edward by sea, and although he sent out foraging columns over a broad area, living off the land in winter yielded thin returns. Edward's army was in difficulty.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007206-53)[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004102-38) [![Image 6: See caption](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Malestroit_-_Chapelle_de_la_Madeleine_plaque.JPG/250px-Malestroit_-_Chapelle_de_la_Madeleine_plaque.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Malestroit_-_Chapelle_de_la_Madeleine_plaque.JPG) The commemorative plaque on the ruins of the [Chapel of the Madeleine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_the_Madeleine,_Malestroit "Chapel of the Madeleine, Malestroit") where the truce was sealed,[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006207-54) reads: "Historic ruins of the Magdalene chapel, where was signed on 19th January 1343 during the Hundred Years' war by representatives of the Kings of France and England, the Truce of Malestroit, in the presence of Papal Legates the Cardinals of Clermont and Prenets."[\[note 4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-55) The French were perturbed by Edward's landing in Brittany, when he was expected to invade further east, and by his taking the field so late in the season, when their armies had been disbanded. During November they struggled to put together an army and to accumulate sufficient supplies to feed and equip it. The army was based at the major French supply centre of [Angers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angers "Angers")[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990386,_406%E2%80%93407-56) with King Philip's eldest son, [John, Duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France"), in command.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006207-54) There are no contemporary figures on the size of the French army, but it was several times larger than the Anglo-Breton force.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007207-57) It was 14 December before the French began the 50-mile (80 km) journey west to the Breton border. Edward was sufficiently alarmed to invite the two cardinals he had brushed off in the summer to present their credentials. They had been observing events from [Avranches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avranches "Avranches"), just over the Breton border, and were allowed no closer than Malestroit, 18 miles (29 km) from the main English camp. Edward suspected that details of everything they saw would be passed on to the French and took great care not to betray the small size and poor state of his army.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990406%E2%80%93407-58)[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006207-54) Once started, the French advance was rapid; it was Christmas Day (25 December) 1342[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199984-59) when the French relieved Nantes. Redon, Ploërmel and Malestroit were recaptured during early January and the French encamped around the latter. The two cardinals were probably in Malestroit when it fell to the French, on or shortly after 10 January.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990386,_406%E2%80%93407-56) As in 1340 the French were content to threaten the English, without moving close enough for serious fighting to be a possibility. With both sides disinclined to commit to battle, negotiations were entered into.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich1980174-60) Philip VI set up his court at Redon from where he sent emissaries to the cardinals. By 19 January 1343 the terms of a truce had been agreed and it was sealed; the break in hostilities was to last until 29 September 1346.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990407%E2%80%93408-61) The historian [Jonathan Sumption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Sumption,_Lord_Sumption "Jonathan Sumption, Lord Sumption") describes the terms as "astonishingly favourable" to the English.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990407%E2%80%93408-61) Both France and England were to retain the territory they held when the truce came into effect: this applied to Brittany, Gascony, [Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flanders "Flanders") and [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland").[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990409-62) Vannes was to be held by the papacy for the duration of the truce, Philip was to immediately free John of Montfort[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006207-54)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007207-57) and there was a general exchange of prisoners.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones1988208,_n._30-63)[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEB%C3%A1r%C3%A1ny1997225-64) Both monarchs pledged to negotiate in [Avignon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon "Avignon"), mediated by Clement, a treaty to permanently end the war. In reality each saw the truce as a mere pause and neither intended to negotiate in good faith; the truce had only been agreed because each king felt it was beneficial to him.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990408-65)[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006110-66) Edward left for England, enduring another winter storm which scattered the fleet and sank several ships, and arrived on 1 March.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007209-67) Philip believed that with the fighting ended, all the English would leave for home, as they had left north-east France after the Truce of Espléchin. He was mistaken, and the Breton Civil War ground on as a disjointed and inconclusive series of petty sieges and skirmishes, despite the truce.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich1980174-60)[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200245-68) The English and their Montfortist allies held almost the whole of Brittany by 1345.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoskins201113-69)[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESadler2013211-70) John of Montfort was not released until September, despite the stipulation of the treaty.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990409,_432-71) Late in 1343 the citizens of Vannes rose against the Pope's authority, expelled his garrison and delivered the town to the English, who held it until the end of the Breton Civil War in 1364.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990432-72)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFr%C3%A9laut200535-48) [![Image 7: a water colour image of the head and shoulders of a man wearing a white papal hat](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/01_Cl%C3%A9ment_VI_%28Fresque_de_la_chapelle_Saint-Martial_du_palais_des_papes%29.jpg/250px-01_Cl%C3%A9ment_VI_%28Fresque_de_la_chapelle_Saint-Martial_du_palais_des_papes%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:01_Cl%C3%A9ment_VI_/(Fresque_de_la_chapelle_Saint-Martial_du_palais_des_papes/).jpg) Pope Clement VI, pictured on the wall of the Chapel of Saint-Martial in the [Papal Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_des_Papes "Palais des Papes") in Avignon. Clement commissioned the decoration of the chapel, which was completed during his lifetime.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTELuyster2011334-73) English quibbling over the arrangements for the peace conference at Avignon delayed its start until 22 October 1344. Both the French and the English sent delegations, as they had agreed at Malestroit. The English were represented by [John of Offord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_de_Ufford "John de Ufford"), Edward's [lord privy seal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Privy_Seal "Lord Privy Seal") and a seasoned diplomat;[\[note 5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-75) the lawyer [Thomas Fastolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Fastolf "Thomas Fastolf"); [William Bateman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Bateman_/(bishop/) "William Bateman (bishop)"), the [dean of Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dean_of_Lincoln "Dean of Lincoln"); Hugh Neville; and Nicolino Fieschi.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200639-76)[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFowler196938-77)[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBombi2019111%E2%80%93112-78) The full roster of the French delegates is not known, but they included [Foulques of Chanac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foulques_de_Chanac "Foulques de Chanac"), [bishop of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Archdiocese_of_Paris "Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Paris"); the Dean of [Clermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Archdiocese_of_Clermont "Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Clermont"); [Louis of Cerda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_de_la_Cerda "Luis de la Cerda"), [prince of Fortuna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Fortuna "Prince of Fortuna"); [Louis of Poitiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_I_de_Poitiers,_Count_of_Valentinois "Louis I de Poitiers, Count of Valentinois"), count of Valentinois; and Simon Bucy, president of the [Parlement of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parlement_of_Paris "Parlement of Paris").[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTED%C3%A9prez1967305-79) They did not meet face to face, but each group talked to Clement, who conveyed messages between them. The terms of the truce required Clement to be neutral, but his behaviour outside the bounds of the conference was generally supportive of the French and the English were deeply distrustful of him. The proposals presented by each side to Clement were all unacceptable to the other, with neither displaying any willingness to compromise: the English demanded recognition of Edward as king of France as a starting point, the French insisted on acceptance of Philip's overlordship of Gascony. After four rounds of mediation Clement handed over the role of intermediary to a pair of cardinals. They made various proposals: one was that England accept the border of Aquitaine as agreed in 1303 by the [Treaty of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Paris_/(1303/) "Treaty of Paris (1303)"), but with Aquitaine held as sovereign English territory; the French would not accept any diminution of their kingdom. Several suggestions were put to the English delegation by which either England generally or Edward personally would give up the claim to Aquitaine in exchange for territorial compensation elsewhere, but all were rejected.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200639-76)[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich1980175-80)[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990436%E2%80%93443-81) Several members of the English delegation had left Avignon by December. Clement suggested that the largely [ecclesiastical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Church "Christian Church") and low-status English delegation be replaced by high-status nobles, such as Northampton and [Henry, Duke of Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_of_Grosmont,_Duke_of_Lancaster "Henry of Grosmont, Duke of Lancaster"); both had been among the English negotiators who had agreed the truce at Malestroit so rapidly. But his plea was to no avail. The last English delegate at Avignon – Offord – was forbidden from leaving by Clement, but he fled in February 1345.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200639-76)[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFowler196938-77)[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990436,_443-82) Neither monarch took the provisions of the truce agreement seriously. Edward was planning another major invasion of France long before the truce was due to expire in September 1346.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEB%C3%A1r%C3%A1ny1997225-64) During the summer of 1343 [Olivier of Clisson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olivier_IV_de_Clisson "Olivier IV de Clisson"), a senior Breton lord, was invited from England to a tournament on French soil. As he was protected by the treaty he attended, but on the orders of the French king was arrested for treason and executed without trial.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoveBiget2013131-83)[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBordonove200674-84) Edward formally renounced the truce on 15 June 1345. The fighting had continued much as before in Brittany and Gascony, and with Edward's repudiation of the truce Gascony [reverted to full-scale war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gascon_campaign_of_1345 "Gascon campaign of 1345").[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEB%C3%A1r%C3%A1ny1997225-64) Edward personally led another expedition to France in 1346, this time [landing in Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cr%C3%A9cy_campaign "Crécy campaign").[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006xxxvi%E2%80%93xxxvii,_39-85) His army was wholly English and Welsh this time and it laid waste to a 40-mile-wide (64 km) strip of some of the richest lands in France to within 2 miles (3 km) of Paris, [sacking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looting "Looting") many towns on the way. On 26 August 1346 Philip was finally provoked into attacking at the [battle of Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy "Battle of Crécy"), where the French were defeated with a heavy loss of life.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200239%E2%80%9340-86)[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006105%E2%80%93106-87)[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers2014252,_257-88) In the aftermath of this battle the English [laid siege to the port of Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Calais_/(1346%E2%80%931347/) "Siege of Calais (1346–1347)"), which fell in August 1347. The [Truce of Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Calais "Truce of Calais") was subsequently sealed on 28 September; originally due to expire on 7 July 1348, it was repeatedly extended until 1355, when full-scale war broke out once again.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200673%E2%80%9375-89) Notes, citations and sources ---------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Truce_of_Malestroit&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Notes, citations and sources")\] 1. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit#cite_ref-27)** Edward asserted the feudal right to the Crown to [impress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angary "Angary") English merchant ships into service. 7.content:
1341 saw a serious political crisis – Edward returned home determined to put his English administration, parliament and particularly Archbishop in their places. In fact it’s Edward who is forced to back down and accept a punitive legislative programme to rebuild his partnership with the political community. With a truce in place, Edward was saved from a life of fun and luxury by the start of civil war with a disputed succession to the Duchy of Brittany.

[103 The War in Brittany](https://thehistoryofengland.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/files/103-the-war-in-brittany-2.mp3)

### **The crisis of 1341**

[![Image 1: John Stratford](https://thehistoryofengland.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/files/6a0147e0fd1b4a970b019aff1f1a20970c.jpg)](https://thehistoryofengland.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/files/6a0147e0fd1b4a970b019aff1f1a20970c.jpg)Edward had returned and sacked his ministers, determined to show that his defeat was the result of incompetence on behalf of his ministers, not because it was a losing strategy. His household officials pretty much took the law into their own hands in trying to collect the tax approved in 1340 and getting the clergy to cough up. But the money was still not forthcoming, and a storm of protest, led by the Archbishop of Canterbury, arose at these methods.

In the end Edward had to give way, and call a parliament. He was forced to accept a series of new statutes from the Commons – although a year later in happier times to cancelled all of them. But it was a significant defeat for Edward – but also significant in the way Edward accepted the result, and re-established harmony with his magnates and parliament, not something his predecessor would have been able to do.

### **The topography of Brittany**

Think of Brittany in 2 parts. To the east, fertile country similar to neighbouring Maine and Anjou, easily accessible to the rest of France – Gallo-Brittany. To the west, Breton Brittany; a central rocky and hilly central spine (then heavily forested) and a coastal strip of communities.

[![Image 2: Brtittany in the 14th Century](https://thehistoryofengland.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/files/6a0147e0fd1b4a970b019aff1f4b46970d.jpg)](https://thehistoryofengland.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/files/6a0147e0fd1b4a970b019aff1f4b46970d.jpg)

### **The succession and start of the war**

The death of the Duke of Brittany led to a disputed succession:

1.  John Montfort and his wife Jeanne de Flandre.
2.  Jeanne de Penthievre, and her husband the French king’s nephew Charles of Blois

Almost to a man, with a few exceptions, the Bretons accepted Charles. But John and the Countess of Montfort reacted to the Duke’s death quickly, taking possession of key towns and the ducal treasury.

Charles of Bloix soon arrived with a large army and the backing of the French king, and before long had swept most of Brittany clear. Montfort was imprisoned in Paris. Just a few strongholds remained for the Montfort’s, including Auray, Brest and the castle of Hennebont, held by the Countess.

### **William Bohun, Earl of Northampton and the Battle of Morlaix**

[![Image 3: Battle of Morlaix](https://thehistoryofengland.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/files/6a0147e0fd1b4a970b019aff1f4b05970d.jpg)](https://thehistoryofengland.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/files/6a0147e0fd1b4a970b019aff1f4b05970d.jpg)Northampton finally arrived to help with an army of 2,400, split 50/50 men at arms and archers. At first Charles of Blois retreated but as Northampton advanced to besiege Morlaix he returned with an army of maybe 3 times the size. In the ensuing battle, Blois was driven off despite his superior numbers. [There’s a good description on Wikipedia here](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix).

Morlaix is significant becuase it’s the first real battle in the Hundred Years war, and it has many features of later English victories – a defensive well chosen position, dismounted knights/men at arms, the impact of the longbow in the hand of English archers.

### **The Truce of Malestroit, January 1343**

In the autumn of 1342, Edward arrived with an army that took the English presence to 5,000 men. He took over most of western Brittany, but was held up at Vannes. And then meanwhile Jean, Duke of Normandy and the French heir, arrived with a considerably larger army in Nantes.

Edward was vulnerable, with a much smaller army. But incredibly the Duke offered a Truce – and Edward almost snatched his hand off in enthusiasm to accept. The terms were generous – lands in all theatres to be held as they were at the date of the truce, January 1343. It meant that the Montfort claim had survived despite at one stage coming very close to extinction.

**Transcript**

Last week, Edward had arrived home in high dudgeon and full of righteous anger, ready to pillage and burn his way through the treacherous ministers who, according to his world view, had let him down so badly. In their place, he would use the trustworthy, doughty and reliable household staff who had worked with him so closely over the last 2 years, who had shared his pain and humiliation and had helped him write all those thorough reasonable and sensible letters while he’d been away.

His main anger focussed on the ABC. As we heard last week, Edward had rather nuttily decided that the ABC was out to kill him and bring him down.

As you can see, Edward’s world view was decidedly warped. This time, the magnates and the community of the realm, would un-warp it for him, sharpish, in the form of a bloody nose.

But I’m getting ahead of myself. Robert Stratford was the Chancellor from whom Edward had torn strips, and been summarily dismissed on Edward’s return. Now it just so happens that the ABC was none other than Robert’s brother, John. So unsurprisingly, the ABC caught wind of the direction of Edward’s thoughts – and legged it down to the relative safety of Canterbury.

Before you could say ‘full and frank exchange of views’ , a document had appeared from Edward detailing all the crimes of which he thought Stratford guilty. It is fair to say that it is not a balanced, objective document. Stratford is supposed to have withheld money, encouraged opposition to taxes, impoverished the crown and abused his authority to his own advantage.

While Edward launched his attack on Stratford, he confidently embarked on a new approach to government – using his own household officers to do the things he was convinced had been simple, but that the incompetent and evil guys in England had simply decided they couldn’t be bothered to do. Now he had his top team back in England, Edward was confident things would soon fall into place.

Let me introduce you briefly to two men that play a bit part in today’s story then – John Darcy and William Kilsby. These are two professional administrators who have been at Edward’s side night and day while he’s been abroad – they have his ear, and his confidence.

Darcy would have been in his late 50’s at this time. He’s been an administrator all his life, in the service of Edward II as well as Edward III, and he’s become the Keeper of the Privy Seal. That means that he looks after the king’s private signet ring, which is more important than it sounds. It sounds frankly, a little menial – ‘John, where have you put my rings?’ that sort of thing.

Of course we have two seals at this time, and as I think we have discussed before, these are not large aquatic mammals. The Great Seal is the official seal of state, the Privy seal the King’s personal one. Both of them authorise things to be done and are a symbol and practical expression of power. So John is always by the king’s side. As a youth, before I lost my callow, I always used to laugh at the role of Groome of the Stool, a post that appears in the reign of Henry VIII. The thought of building a career handing the king loo paper seemed the most ridiculous thing I could conceive of. But of course it became a most powerful position – because you were constantly at the king’s side. What better time could there be to press for some favour on behalf of one of your clients.  Which same principle very much holds true for John Darcy.

The other chap was William Kilsby, Steward of the royal Household, and like Darcy, a close confidente of the king. Both of these men were not from the magnate class, and probably not from the baronial class – they were next to the king because they were good at their jobs. Both became knights and bannerets, but from royal advancement not birth. These days, that’s a good thing. In those days, that meant that in the eyes of chroniclers and magnates, they were dodgy.

And in all likelihood, they had probably fuelled the King’s fury, and encouraged the view that those blokes in England were rubbish, and given half a chance they’d put that right. They might well have been slightly horrified that bluff was to be called.

So between January and March 1341, the King let’s slip his dogs of tax collection, Darcy and Kilsby among them. Sheriffs were replaced,  chief justices was appointed for each shire to enforce collection of previous tax subsidies, they hammered the  clergy for the collection of a nineth, which was probably illegal. Basically, the king had lost patience with due process, and tried to cut out all that pfaff.

While this was going on a good old slanging match was developing between the king and his ABC. Stratford did not take this lying down, Oh dearie me no. Stratford had plenty of experience of dealing with kings; he was 65 years old, he’d been a bishop and diplomat under Edward II, had represented the old earl of Lancaster at court in spite of the threat that posed to him, he’d been a chancellor of England and since 1333 ABC. He was no pushover. And in front of him, in his mind’s eye was the saintly figure of Thomas Beckett, a light and a model to show him the way. Here was his chance to be the new Beckett.

So Stratford hit straight back with a letter to Edward. This is in effect a pamphletting war now, a struggle to influence  public opinion. Stratford was not without defences; he was a member of the church and at a very high position. Strafford went for the jugular. I mean all wrapped in sweetie wrappers and all – we love you, it wasn’t you it was the evil counsellors and so on – but in the middle there’s this bit:

You begin to seize various clerks, peers and other people of the land, and to make unseemly process against the law of the land, and against the great charter, which you are bound to keep and maintain by the oath at your coronation

Even worse, he reminded Edward what had happened to his father:

And sire you may remember …by the evil counsel which our lord your father had, he caused to be taken, against the law of the land and of the great charter, the peers and other people of the land and put to some shameful death…

The message is pretty straightforward – look, sir, you are acting the same as you dad, and I think we both remember what happened to him, eh? And note again yet another generation referring to Magna Carta as the touchstone of all liberties.

Edward wasn’t used to this kind of opposition, and he kept straight on going. But it wasn’t happening – the revenues weren’t coming in, against all expectation it was beginning to look as though there wasn’t some magic answer. It slowly began to dawn on him that he’d made a mistake – the lack of money had nothing to do with the relative merits of his household and government in England – it had more to do with genuine problems.

So in desperation, Edward allowed himself to back down and call a parliament. But he’d be darned if that weasel the ABC would come. So on the first day of parliament, when Stratford arrived, he was met at the door and quietly but firmly told to go to the exchequer to answer some minor charges against him. The next day the same thing happened. Third day, Stratford patiently presented himself, but this time any pretence was dropped – this time the serjeant at arms told him he was no longer invited to this particular party, and would he please stop turning up and making everyone feel awkward?

Stratford dug his heels in. If this had been the ‘60s, he have waved a placard above his head, sung ‘we shall not be moved’ and quite probably produced some magic mushrooms, but as it was he insisted that he wouldn’t move until the king himself came and told him to go. The king’s croneys gathered around – Darcy and his son, and Kilsby. These guys just made Stratford even stroppier. Then William Bohun came to try and pour oil on the waters to no avail – the ABC was not to be emolled or maneuvered.

This became the focus of the struggle. If Edward had to cave in and re-admit the ABC, he was going to lose a lot of face, and he’d already had to lose a cheek or two by calling the parliament at all. And then at this point up stood John Warenne. A man with a chequered sort of life and reputation, but 6 generations ago, his ancestor had been at the side of William the Conqueror in his great enterprise, and at 54 he was the elder statesman of the magnates in the parliament. He would have been well aware by this stage that he was likely to be the last Warenne Earl of Surrey. Here’s what he said:

Sir king, how goes this parliament? Parliaments are not wont to be like this. For here those who should be foremost are shut out, while there sit other men of low rank who have no business to be here. Such right belongs only to the peers of the land. Sir King, think of this.

You’ll note the subtle dig at Kilsby and Darcy there. Hardworking maybe, in with the king, certainly, members of the club – no chance.

And so we come to the difference between Edward II and Edward III. Edward II would have retired hurt, and plotted his revenge. Edward smiled graciously, and set up a face saving process to review Stratford’s case, which of course exonerated him. He accepted all the reforms parliament demanded of him – magnates must only be tried in parliament; an audit was to be carried out of the king’s finances; the great officers of the realm were to be appointed in parliament. And while Stratford was never re-admitted to the inner circle of Edward’s advisers, he genuinely played an active role as an elder statesman and adviser. As a result of all this, Edward got a wool tax that would yield £150,000, and set his finances on the path to recovery.

The crisis of 1341 was a serious defeat for Edward. It was a defeat not just because he’d been taxing his country without any reward, or just because he’d picked on the wrong guy, or even because he had imposed changes on the national administration without consent; but because he’d allowed a gap to open up between him and his magnates, his natural partners. The problem was that they were simply no longer sure how to play a role.

The magnates felt their role was still to fight and protect, and to advise the king. But over the last 10 years, this role had become muddied. Edward had recruited large, conscript armies paid for centrally, rather than using all the magnates with their traditional feudal levies. It gave him more control, they weren’t buzzing off to gather in the harvest all the time, and they were more professional soldiers.

And then also in the last 3 years, it had been Edward and his household who had run the show over on the continent – a small coterie of Edward’s mates – William Montague, the Earl of Salisbury; William Clinton, William Bohun – the Nottingham tunnel lot. People like Arundel and Surrey and the barons had felt cut out of their natural role.

Without getting maudlin, I played tennis quite a bit in my youth, and I remember as a lad playing with against my father and his group of cunning old crusties. On the many occasions when my youthful ambition had been soundly walloped by said crustie cunning, I didn’t always take it well. I remember on one occasion one of those crusties remarking that it is how we act in defeat that defines, us rather than how we act in victory.

Now my immediate reaction had been to resolve never ever to be in the position of being defeated by an old crustie, but my rather tenuous point is that the difference between Edward II and Edward III was that the latter learned from his mistake. EII had specifically been described as incorrigible. Edward III was corrigible. He had a generosity of spirit that allowed him to admit that he was wrong, and move on. He had the intelligence to know when he was beaten. And we should refute the old Victorian idea that he cared nothing for the rights he gave away, just so long as he could joust and make war. Because the final act in this drama came a year later in 1341, when in absence of a parliament and his relationships restored, Edward cancelled all these statutes, calmly saying that he’d been bullied into it. This time he’d judged the mood perfectly – there was not a whimper of protest, and the new reforms were consigned to the dustbin of history.

Edward never again allowed himself to forget the role of his magnates; until his dotage, he never allowed a distance to grow between him and them. A feature of his reign is that while his father and indeed his successor insisted on that distance as a feature of their kingship, Edward was happy to be primus inter pares, first among equals. All the tournaments and jousting and great councils were part of that process of building the link; he didn’t want anyone to forget that he was primus, but given acceptance of that, the pares bit was fine too.

And from here on the method of military recruitment also changed. Armies began to be recruited by indenture. Essentially under this process, the king agreed to pay a magnate or lord to provide x number of soldiers of type y for z amount of money – rather than raising conscripts. So all the Barons and knights were an integral part of the Edwardian army. They had a role, a sense of partnership in this great adventure. As a by the by, it means that we begin to see the development of uniforms in the army, in the form of the liveries of each lord with indentured men. A man would be given robes or a jupon to cover his armour with, bearing the lord’s insignia. Some groups went further towards full uniform; the first were the Welsh spearmen, with men from north Wales wearing the white and green of the Black Prince, and the Red and White of Arundel’s men from Chirkland.

Through 1340 and 1341, most of Edward’s old strategy came apart at the seams. His biggest so-called allies, the Duke of Brabant and the Emperor Ludwig declared that they were no longer interested in this alliance and in making war on France. Edward’s status as the vicar of the HRE was revoked, and a separate peace made. That just left Flanders who might be waiting for Edward once the current truce with France came to an end.

So there he was, our Edward, all truced up and nowhere to go. Scotland remained a running sore; Edinburgh castle fell to the Scots in April 1341, and in June David II was back from his extended exile in France.  With the standard of the Bruce raised again, the Scots came over the border and besieged Newcastle, and the war with Scotland was into a new and potentially far more painful phase.  Edward zipped up North – and the Scots melted away into the forests. So at least the siege was lifted – but nothing much else achieved. Edward’s Christmas was spent at Melrose Abbey in Scotland but was really nothing more than symbolic.

There was one feature of the campaign that rings a bell with the war in France – the jousts of war, or jousts a l’outrance. In a normal tournament, weapons were blunted – the lance had a thing called a coronal at the end of it. Personally, I still wouldn’t like one hitting my face with the weight of a charging knight behind it, but it was in principle blunt. In joust of war, there was no blunting going on. Everything was as sharp as a knife sort of thing. So you get this rather remarkable event where William Douglas appeared out of the forests and came to Roxburgh with 11 Scottish knights and challenged the Earl of Derby to a joust. Possibly, there was something riding on it – no pun intended of course – such as the right to spend Christmas at Melrose Abbey. Either way, the Scots on this occasion got a drubbing, Douglas being carried home after his joust with the Earl of Derby. This is chivalry for you. Throughout the war, in all but the darkest days of the routiers, there is a connection and shared culture between the noble classes, an agreed way of carrying on. There is a remarkable adherence to the rules of war that are understood by all, but could be so easily broken, but very rarely are. The idea that you could just wander out of the forest and be offered a fair fight for fun is another such rule. These days of course you’d be offered the services of a psychiatrist.

Now then, as I say there’s our Edward, all truced up and nowhere to go. But he will be saved from the boredom of endless tournaments and hunting by Brittany.

Brittany was as semi autonomous collective, sorry a semi autonomous Dukedom under the homage of the French king. There was a succession dispute brewing, always a cause of trouble in the world medieval. The old Duke was getting long in the tooth, and would at some point pop his proverbial clogs. There were two possible successors. On the one hand a chap called John Montfort. Montfort had little to do with Brittany; he was very much oriented toward the French court with land in the Isle de France, and he knew little of the yokels. Although Montfort probably had the best claim, the old Duke didn’t appear to like him. We don’t know why. But he didn’t.

So there was another option, his niece Jeanne de Penthievre. So he bolstered her claim, marrying her in 1337 to the nephew of Phillip VI, a man called Charles of Blois. Charles will be a figure in our story for many years. He was austere, pious but also a fine and intelligent soldier who inspired the loyalty of people around him. There is no two ways about it – as far as the Bretons were concerned, Jeanne and Charles were going to inherit, Montfort was a busted flush and good thing too.

Let me briefly give you a tour of Brittany – and there is a map on the website of course. Think of it as two bits – an east and West. Eastern Brittany was the Gallo-Brittany, very much oriented towards the rest of France; it had prosperous fertile lowlands, and was easy to get to from Paris and therefore pretty open to any invading army from France. The West was very different. The interior is inhospitable, rocky and at the time heavily forested, and around it is a narrow coastal fringe where most people live. This is Breton Brittany rather than Gallo Brittany, a region dominated by complicated local loyalties, and difficult to get at.

Breton Breton they might be, but pro Montfort they were not – they agreed entirely with their Eastern Cousins on that score. So when the Old Duke died in 1341, an assembly of Breton notable met to discuss the claims. They ruled overwhelmingly in favour of Charles. Game over, presumably.

No, Game on, let me introduce you to john Montfort’s wife, Jeanne de Flandre. She was in all likelihood the dominant personality in the Montfort camp – she was tough, rich and ambitious. In Froissart’s words

She had the spirit of a man and the heart of a Lion

Incidentally, I think Froissart was being complimentary with the spirit of a man thing by the way. I don’t think he meant that she lay on the sofa all weekend watching football and had an unfortunate weakness for an excess of wind at inappropriate moments. But I could be wrong. The Countess of Montfort had the same ability to inspire fierce loyalty, and in the dark days ahead would keep the Montfort claim alive. And it was probably her that inspired what happened next.

And what happened next was that Montfort’s acted with verve and energy. As the assembly of notables dispersed, Montfort appeared with 200 men outside Nantes, the major town of eastern Brittany. And told them he’d come because he was the new Duke. The inhabitants were confused – hang on a minute, aren’t you supposed to be called Charles? While they were asking this question they turned round and found Montfort had squeezed past them and like an unwanted relative was ensconced in the castle. He did the same in Limoges and seized the Ducal treasury. He announced that he would hold a party where all the nobles and towns should come and do homage. As it happens everyone stayed away, except for the good burgers of Nantes who saw the opportunity for a free meal. So there was a slightly uncomfortable evening where Montfort sat in a half empty hall with a bunch of locals concentrating on finishing off the food, but the Montfort’s were making their point – possession was after all 9/10ths of the law.

And so it went on. While Charles of Blois and Philip stared bemused like scared rabbits, the Montforts went on – they took the major centres of Rennes and Vanne, and the south and West coasts in July and August 1341, sometimes being accepted by the confused, sometimes having to fight. By the time Philip and Charles realised what was going on, Montfort did in fact have 9/10th s of the country, not just of the law.

Charles of course complained. Philip then summoned the Parlement of Paris to make a judgement on the best claim and called Montfort to attend. Montfort, however got a pretty clear idea of the way the wind was blowing when he went to meet the king. Philip accused him of talking treasonably to the English, was probably true. He told him to wait until the Parlement had pronounced, and not on any account to leave Paris.

So Montfort promptly left Paris.

As you would. It was pretty clear he was to be held hostage when the Parlement duly returned the king’s preferred verdict. In September, the parlement met and returned the preferred verdict – Charles was to be the official candidate, Montfort was to be confiscated of his other lands as well, and 25 years of civil war, death and destruction in Brittany was a go.

By October Montfort and Edward had signed a military alliance, and Edward was making plans to come and visit, accompanied by an army of hard faced archers. For Edward all this was a real windfall. Brittany was well placed for a naval descent, it set up a new front in Philip’s backyard.

Philip’s spies told him all about these conversations and at last the French were ready to march. Command of the armies was given to the king’s eldest and favourite son, Jean, the Duke of Normandy, a man of who, we will hear much more. Jean and Charles marched into Brittany in October. When the French armies appeared in front of the Eastern Breton towns, they took one look and said  – A yes, that’s right – Charles. They threw open their gates and invited them in. In Nantes, the inhabitants told Montfort this was exactly what they intended to do when Jean and Charles arrived there so….that was going to be awkward.

So Montfort negotiated while he had something to negotiate with. He was given a safe conduct to Paris, and he and the Duke of Normandy hopped off to talk turkey. Before you could say jack robinson, the safe conduct had been repealed, and Montfort was imprisoned in the Louvre.

At which point the Countess of Montfort came into her own. There was going to be no rolling over as far as she was concerned. Though she was dealt a bad hand  – places like Rennes, big rich towns in the East were set to declare for Charles, so she had to run for the west. But the Countess made a stand, at Hennebont in South Western Brittany. The Montfort’s 2 year old son was declared as the nominal head of the party should his Dad be put to death in Paris. Her Noble ally, Amaury de Clisson was sent to England to get help.

When Clisson arrived, Edward was having a party – the largest tournament of his reign at Dunstable. It was attended by over 250 knights, and Edward fought as what’s described as ‘a simple knight’. Edward had a love of symbols and grandeur, and at this event everything was embroidered with a motto, ‘It is as it is’, a habit we’ll see repeated with the Order of the Garter.

Clisson fixed up a deal with Edward, which would see Edward arrive with an army as soon as the Truce with France expired in June 1342. Obviously, the problem was to get there before the Countess’s cause was swept away. As ever they struggled with the logistics of getting fleet and army together, but in May, with the news of the fall of Brittany’s biggest town, Rennes to the French, a teensy weensy army arrived in Brittany under the command of one Walter Manny. We are talking 34 men at arms and 200 mounted archers, and even the redoubtable Manny could do little as Charles of Blois invested Vannes and Hennbont. Resistance was fierce, with the Countess to be seen riding through the streets of Hennebont, haranguing her men from a charger, with every attempt to take the town by storm thrown back. But outside, the French spread out in small detachments and started the killing and looting of the inland towns and villages.

About this time, by the way, a new Pope took over in Avignon, taking the name of Clemont. Just in case we had any doubt about the quality of Papal independence and morality, here was a man of princely tastes, great style and richness. As far as he was concerned, France _was_ Christendom, Edward was a rebel and aggressor. At his inauguration knees-up, the Duke of Normandy took the honour of holding the reins of the Pope’s horse and sitting at the Pope’s RH side. Point taken. It’s no wonder the English deeply distrusted papal negotiators.

Meanwhile in the South West, England had some success during the truce when the inhabitants of Bourg in the Saintonge, had thrown out their French garrison. But with the end of the truce, the Bishop of Beauvais launched an offensive that essentially saw Ingham and the English pinned back into their heartlands around Bordeaux.

In Brittany, following Montfort’s treatment in Paris and the blatant disregard for his safe conduct, the Breton’s now also distrusted the French, and in western Brittany were more reluctant to open their gates; but without a proper English army in the field, the French were dominant. In July Vannes surrendered, and the inhabitants of the besieged town of Auray were reduced to eating their horses. Finally, finally the English started to arrive. The Earl of Northampton, William Bohun, arrived with a small army of 2,400 men, split roughly 50/50 between MAA and Archers. Charles of Blois immediately lifted the siege of Brest and withdrew. Bohun  followed him, and started the siege of the small town of Morlaix.

In September 1342 Charles of Blois returned to raise the siege, with a substantial army; 3,000 cavalry, 1,500 Genoese and a large local contingent of Bretons. We don’t know how many that made his army in total – estimates go up to 30,000, which is clearly daft. But whatever – several time the size of the English army and its Breton allies. But finally, after dancing round their handbags for the last 5 years, the English and the French were going to get it on, as it were.

Northampton left enough men to keep an eye on the garrison of Morlaix, and drew up the rest of his men across the main road at the top of a rise, so that to relieve the garrison at Morlaix, Charles would have to get through him. At his back was a wood. In the centre of the English line Northampton placed his armoured knights and MAA, not as cavalry as had been the tradition for so long, but dismounted. On the flanks, he placed his archers, each with 36 arrows. In front of the line, taking a leaf from the Scottish book at Bannockburn, they dug a hidden trench. And then they waited.

Charles of Blois came on in 3 columns, each considerably bigger than Northampton’s army. The first were the Bretons, recently recruited, probably most kindly described as irregular infantry, the kind of people who wore red shirts in the original star trek series. As they approached the English they were met by a storm of arrows, and they ran away.

A conference took place on the French side about what to do next. And as a result, on came the next column this time in a mounted attack. Horses fell into the concealed traps, the same storm of arrows took out the horses and chaos ensued. Only about 200 managed to reach the English MAA, but for a moment the line was broken – until Northampton committed his reserve and captured the commander of the 2nd wave.

There was now a considerable pause, but finally the 3rd column came on. Northampton now faced a real problem. His archers were almost out of ammo, his men were exhausted from 2 waves of attack, the attacking column had extended its line beyond the English line so they were in danger of being flanked. But Northampton wasn’t ready to give up. So instead they retreated into the wood, and lined all four sides into what you might describe as a hedgehog.

Charles’s forces were non-plused. They couldn’t attack on horse because of the wood. As they approached, the archers used their final ammo carefully, picking off individual targets. Those who did get in the wood found it difficult to link up and use the advantage of their greater numbers. And so Charles called the retreat, and is next heard of in the siege of Hennebont.

Morlaix isn’t on the roll call of famous battles of the 100 year’s war – Crecy, Poitier, Agincourt. So why cover this poxy, two bit, no good battle?

There are two answers to that. Firstly, I like battles. I’d hate to be in one, but at the safe distance of over 600 years I’m ok with them. But secondly, here’s our first sight of the key attributes of English tactics, forged on the battlefield of Scotland, for which the French take 20 years to develop an effective response. Here’s an English commander’s notebook:

1.  You fight on foot, not mounted. Not in the chivalric tradition, but stuff that 

1.  Wait for them to attack you. They are bigger than us 

1.  Choose the ground carefully, and don’t fight unless you’ve done so 

1.  Archers on the flank, MAA in the middle 

I should note that the positioning of the Archers by the way is a matter of deep controversy. I have gone for this, but there are equally valid views that say that archers were often dispersed among the MAA. I’m assuming we don’t want to go into this in depth.

There are a couple of other wrinkles about Morlaix specifically worth noting. The French attacked in columns which was handy for the archers – they didn’t need to worry about range, and packed together there’s an easy target. And secondly, the English had learnt the lessons of Bannockburn, and learnt them well.

Finally in October Edward himself arrived in Brittany. Before long, most of southern Brittany was his. The town of Vannes held the army up, but raids into the surrounding countryside broke the morale of Charles forces and captured a number of towns and castles.

But in December, Jean the Duke of Normandy finally arrived with a far larger army – Edward had no more than 5,000. Stuck outside Vannes, Edward was vulnerable.  Jean entered Nantes, preventing it falling to a force commanded by the Earl of Warwick, and then advanced on Edward. The clever money would have been on the French, although in the light of Crecy who knows.

And then remarkably, the French agreed to a truce. A what? Yes, a truce – overwhelming force, just driven off your enemies from a key castle, enemy stranded with nowhere to run to – seems like the obvious choice. And the terms of the truce were remarkably generous – it basically said everyone held on to what they had at the time. Which meant all Edward’s gains stayed with Montfort, and the Montfort faction was basically saved from extinction. It also said that John Montfort should be released – which didn’t happen but hey.

This truce of Malestroit brought to an end the first phase of the war in Brittany, and gave both French and English another chance to draw breath. The countess of Montfort took a ship for England, but although she lived for another 30 years she went mad soon after arriving, and played no further part.
