The Monstrous Regiment of Women: Jeanne de Penthièvre: "the Courage of a Man and of a Lion" =============== [The Monstrous Regiment of Women](https://www.monstrousregimentofwomen.com/) ============================================================================ A Women's History Daybook Christine de Pizan ------------------ [![Image 1: Christine de Pizan](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiLi-PM6B40Lzxd8MeR0w9bB8ANd44KIIbyoRWCrA4LAd_YyZWcCrHAU44ko4Fikb-kfhXlb9nK9asM6n00pOj3cqB5nLl7Qc2mdRySlEn7SjuKCwyhGsqdLzEJ1jDBgfhqO7p2FMMB46w/s1600/master-of-the-cite-des-dames-workshop-the-book-of-the-queen-f4-christine-de-pizan-in-her-study-at-the-beginning-of-the-book-cent-balades-detail-france-1410-4.jpg)](https://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/115672/Christine-de-Pisan) The Writer Christine de Pizan at Her Desk Tuesday, September 10, 2024 --------------------------- ### Jeanne de Penthièvre: "the Courage of a Man and of a Lion" ### Jeanne de Penthièvre, duchess of Brittany (died 10 September 1384) A year ago, I wrote about [Joanna of Flanders](https://www.monstrousregimentofwomen.com/2023/09/joanna-of-flanders-becomes-jeanne-la.html), countess of Montfort, and her involvement in the War of the Breton Succession, and just last month, I posted an essay about another Jeanne, [Jeanne de Belleville](https://www.monstrousregimentofwomen.com/2024/08/jeanne-de-belleville-lioness-of-brittany.html), who was also caught up in the conflict over the duchy of Brittany, an independent state. Both of these women gained a reputation for their activities during the war, Joanna of Flanders as "la flamme" (or, "fiery Joanna") and Jeanne de Belleville as an avenger of her husband's death.  But there is a third woman caught up in this conflict over Brittany, Jeanne de Penthièvre. She did not have quite as colorful a life as her two contemporaries, though the trauma and tragedy she faced were much like the traumas and tragedies the other women suffered.
An imagined portrait of 
Jeanne de Penthièvre
from Jacques de Boucq's 
Receuil de portraits historiques
(image 107, fol. 045r)

Born about the year 1325,\* Jeanne de Penthièvre was the daughter of Guy II de Bretagne and Jeanne d'Avaugour, the daughter of Henri d'Avaugour, count of Penthièvre.  Guy de Bretagne was the younger son of Arthur II, duke of Brittany, and his wife, Marie of Limoges. Guy's elder brother, John (or Jean) III, became duke of Brittany after the death of Arthur II.  But Arthur of Brittany had remarried after the death of his wife, and his second wife bore him another son, John de Montfort. Notably, John III detested his father's second wife and after his father's death, John III attempted to have the marriage annulled posthumously and to have his half siblings declared illegitimate. Remember John de Montfort . . .  Meanwhile, following his wife's death in 1327, Guy de Bretagne married Jeanne de Belleville--but, as you may already know if you've read the earlier post for Jeanne de Belleville, this marriage was annulled by the pope in 1330 after complaints by Guy's family about its legitimacy--and there was also some involvement by Charles of Blois, nephew of the king of France, Philip VI, in the annulment of this marriage. (Even though Jeanne de Belleville's marriage to Guy was annulled, she was still pulled into the Breton war of succession by her marriage to Olivier de Clisson.) After the failure of his marriage to Jeanne de Belleville, Guy tried again, this time allying himself with Marie of Blois--who just so happened to be Philip VI's niece and Charles of Blois' sister. A dispensation for the two to marry during Lent was issued on 12 February 1331. But on 26 March, just a few weeks later, Guy de Bretagne died. His only child, his daughter Jeanne de Penthièvre, was his heir.  After her father's death, which occurred when she was about eleven years old, Jeanne became countess of Penthièvre in her own right. From her father, she also inherited a claim to the duchy of Brittany. But in 1331, her uncle, John III, was still alive, and although his first two marriages had been childless, he had married for a third time in 1330.  In the meantime, arrangements were being made for Jeanne de Penthièvre's marriage. In 1335, [negotiations](https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/BRITTANY.htm#_Toc480020741) for her match to John, earl of Cornwall, King Edward III's younger brother, were begun, but the projected alliance with England did not materialize. (In any case, John of Cornwall died in September of 1336--maybe his death is the reason the negotiations were abandoned.) Instead, on 4 June 1337, Jeanne was married to Charles of Blois, the French king's nephew. (Remember him? He was involved in having Guy of Penthièvre's marriage to Jeanne of Belleville annulled, and his sister, Marie of Blois, would have been married to Guy of Penthièvre if he had not died . . . hmm.) With her marriage to Charles of Blois, Jeanne, countess of Penthièvre, became countess of Blois.  I've spent a lot of time here noting all of these relationships and interrelationships because after John III, duke of Brittany, died on 30 April 1341, still childless, all hell broke loose about who would succeed him--the result was the so-called War of the Breton Succession.  Without a direct male heir to succeed John III as duke of Brittany, who was to inherit the duchy? The two claimants were Jeanne de Penthièvre, only heir of John III's younger brother Guy, and John de Montfort, John III's half brother.  The critical question was to be which of these claims [took precedence](https://archive.org/details/leguay-martin-fastes-et-malheurs-de-la-bretagne-ducale/page/98/mode/2up?view=theater). When Arthur II, duke of Brittany, died, he had been succeeded by John III, his eldest son by his first wife. When John III died, himself childless, his younger brother Guy was also dead, and Guy's daughter, Jeanne de Penthièvre, was her father's heir. But Arthur II of Brittany had a third son, still living, John de Montfort, the child of Arthur and his second wife.  So, did John III's younger brother, Guy, have a right of succession to the duchy of Brittany? And, if so, could a daughter--in this case, Guy's daughter--inherit her father's rights of succession? Or did the succession belong to the next eldest male heir in the line? That is, did John de Montfort, as the only surviving son of Arthur II, have a right of succession? In sum: since John III had no direct male heir, who had the better claim: his half brother or his niece? Here is an analysis of the problem from [historian](https://thehundredyearswar.co.uk/jeanne-de-penthievre-duchess-of-brittany/) Dan Moorhouse: since John III died childless, the question of inheritance "reverted back to his father \[Arthur II\], with claims being made against lineage from him." Arthur had been married twice--John III and Guy were the sons of his first wife, Marie, countess of Limoges. Although Guy had died before his elder brother, he had an heir, Jeanne; if her right to inherit was recognized, she would become duchess of Brittany, and her husband, Charles of Blois, would become duke of Brittany "by right of her claim." Moorhouse continues: Arthur II of Brittany had been married a second time, to Yolande de Dreux, and with her he had another son, John de Montfort. If the right of inheritance was "to the male with the closest lineage, then he would inherit."  It was not as if John III were unaware of the explosive situation. According to the contemporary chronicler Jean Froissart, [the duke's intentions](https://archive.org/details/b24872799_0001/page/86/mode/2up?q=Montfort&view=theater) were for his niece to succeed him: "It seemed to the duke, that the daughter of his brother-german ought, by reason of her proximity, to have the duchy after his death, in preference to the earl of Montfort, his \[half\] brother. And as he had long had his suspicions that the earl of Montfort would, after his decease, enforce his claim, to the prejudice of his young niece, with all his \[Montfort's\] power, he had married her to the lord Charles of Blois, with the intent that the king of France, his \[Charles of Blois'\] uncle, might more powerfully assist him in preserving his rights, should the earl of Montfort attempt to encroach on them."  So that was the state of affairs after the death of John III, duke of Brittany. The succession of Jeanne de Penthièvre was recognized by the _parlement_ of Paris and by the king of France--Philip VI accepted the _homage_ of her husband, his nephew Charles of Blois, on 7 September 1341. Although Jeanne's right to inherit Brittany would trigger decades of war, she would assert her right to be recognized as duchess of Brittany for twenty-three years, from this date until she was forced to relinquish the title in 1364.  Despite the French king's recognizion of Jeanne's claims to Brittany, John de Montfort had arrived in Nantes after John III's death and seems to have been recognized there as duke in May of 1341. According to Froissart, he "held a solemn court, and a great feast at Nantes. Summons were ordered to be sent to all the barons and nobles of Brittany, and to the councils of the great towns. Inviting them to attend this court, to do their fealty and homage as to their true lord, which was done." But by October 1341, Charles of Blois and his forces reached Nantes, and the city surrendered to him. John de Montfort was captured and imprisoned in the Louvre, his wife, Joanna of Flanders, carrying on the fight without him. Although John de Montfort was eventually released, he died in 1345, leaving his wife to continue the struggle, claiming the inheritance of Brittany for her son.
Jeanne de Penthièvre's seal
1369
As for Jeanne de Penthièvre. Her husband, Charles of Blois, was initially successful in pursuing her claims to Brittany, and after John de Montfort's capture and imprisonment, it seemed as if the pair had been victorious. Joanna of Flanders, however, continued to pursue war, in her son's name, and Charles of Blois was taken captive by the English in 1347. He was taken to England, where he was imprisoned in the Tower of London. Although there are records documenting Jeanne's role in the administration of Brittany from the time she claimed the title of duchess, it was after her husband's capture that she played a more active role. She took command of Charles of Blois' troops, leading them into battle. In Froissart's [words](https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/61126196.pdf), she "takes the war with a great will." In a later version of his chronicle, he adds that she "held the bridle to the teeth and showed the courage of a man and of a lion," reminding her husband's forces that they fought for her two sons.  At this point, the war for Brittany had become a fight between two women, two Jeannes, as the chronicler noted: "\[Jeanne de Penthièvre\] waged as good and strong a war against \[Joanna, or Jeanne,\] the Countess of Montfort and her people as had my lord Charles, her husband, and his people before." During her husband's captivity, Jeanne de Penthièvre also sought assistance from the pope, attempted to engage Edward III in negotiations to settle the Breton conflict, and even suggested a marriage between one of the English king's daughters and one of her sons. She attended peace talks in Calais in 1351, one of the results of which was the marriage of her daughter, Marguerite, to Charles de la Cerda ("Charles of Spain"), who was appointed constable of France by his cousin, John II, who had succeeded Philip VI in 1350. Jeanne also involved Breton religious leaders, barons, and citizens of the towns as she negotiated for her husband's release--for one thing, she would have to pay a huge ransom, and she would need support in Brittany from all these groups.  In 1353, three of Jeanne de Penthièvre's children were sent to England as part of the negotiations for her husband's release--her daughter Marie, and her two sons, Jean and Guy. Charles of Blois was finally relieased from captivity--after nine years, he was ransomed in 1356. When he returned to Brittany, he was accompanied only by his daughter. His sons would remain in England for decades. Back in Brittany, Charles of Blois resumed the title of duke, and the war for control of Brittany recommenced. But within three years he was dead; Charles of Blois was killed on 29 September 1364 at the battle of Auray, after which Jeanne de Penthièvre was forced to relinquish her claims to the duchy, ceding them to the son of Joanna of Flanders and John de Montfort (he was also named John, becoming John IV of Brittany).  Jeanne de Penthièvre did not lose everything, however. She may have lost the title of duchess of Brittany, but by the [terms](https://thehundredyearswar.co.uk/jeanne-de-penthievre-duchess-of-brittany/) of the first treaty of Guérande, she retained her rights to Penthièvre and Avaugour, she was exempt from paying _homage_ to the new duke, and she received a pension. She also retain _some_ claim to Brittany--if the Montfort dukes failed to produce an heir, her descendants would inherit.\*\*  In the years following the loss of her title, Jeanne de Penthièvre endeavored to have her husband, Charles of Blois, [canonized](https://cottesimple.com/articles/tailoring-grande-assiette/the-pourpoint-of-charles-de-blois-moyen-age-article/#:~:text=In%201364%2C%20Charles%20de%20Blois,was%20preserved%20as%20a%20relic.). Charles had always been a pious man (despite all the fighting!), and as early as 1366, groups had begun traveling to the monastery of the Cordeliers in Guincamp to pray at his tomb. A few cures were attributed to him, as were a miracle or two. An investigation into his case began in 1368 and continued until 1371, after which the report was sent to Avignon. The case was under review throughout the papacies of Gregory XI, Clement VII, and Urban VI, but Charles was never canonized. His case was reopened in 1894, and Charles of Blois was beatified in 1904. During this same period, Jeanne struggled to repay debts that she and her husband had incurred in their long struggle for Brittany. After the Montfort duke of Brittany, John IV, was forced into exile in 1373--he had tried to strike a balance between his English allies and the Breton lords, and he had failed--she also attempted to reclaim her rights in the duchy, actions which brought her into increasing conflict with Charles V, now king of France (he was Philip VI's grandson).  When the king attempted to bring the independent duchy of Brittany under French control in 1379, Jeanne de Penthièvre briefly united with her old enemies. The combined efforts of the barons of Brittany brought the Montfort duke back to the duchy and preserved its independence.
Cenotaph of
Jeanne de Penthièvre

After Charles V's death in 1380, a second treaty of Guérande was negotiated with his son and successor, Charles VI. Jeanne signed the second treaty on 2 May 1381. It confirmed the terms which the earlier treaty had laid out.  Although no longer duchess of Brittany, Jeanne de Penthièvre lived in a peaceful Brittany for the rest of her life. Jeanne spent the last years of her life in La Roche-Darrien, where her husband had been fighting when he was taken captive by the English in 1347.  She died on 10 September 1384. Notice of her death is preserved in a [contemporary chronicle of Brittany](https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/BRITTANY.htm#_ftnref453): "Lady Jeanne, daughter of Guy of Brittany, count of Penthièvre, and Jeanne of Avaugour, duchess of Brittany, wife of Charles of Blois of good memory (_Pendomina Johanna filia D. Guidonis de Britannia Penthevriæ comitiis, Johannæque de Avalgorio...ducissa Britanniæ uxor bonæ memoriæ Caroli de Blesis_). The necrology of Notre Dame de Beauport (Brittany) also [records](https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/BRITTANY.htm#_ftnref454) the death of Jeanne, duchess of Brittany, in 1384.  She is buried at the Franciscan monastery, the [Cordeliers à Guingamp](https://patrimoine-guingamp.net/la-ville/eglises-et-monasteres-a-guingamp-du-xe-au-debut-du-xxe-siecles/les-ordres-a-guingamp/les-cordeliers-a-guingamp/), where her father, mother, and husband are also buried. Jeanne de Penthièvre had six children: Marguerite de Blois-Châtillon (1339-c. 1354), Marie de Blois-Châtillon (1343-1404), Jean I de Blois-Châtillon, comte de Penthièvre (1345-1404), Guy de Blois-Châtillon (b. before 1347-d. 1385), Henri de Blois-Châtillon (c. 1356-c. 1400), and Charles de Blois-Châtillon (b. and d. before 1364). * In 1352, Marguerite de Blois-Châtillon married Charles de la Cerda, who was given the title count of Angoulême. Charles "the Spaniard" was a descendant of both Alfonso X of Spain and of Louis IX of France.  * Marie de Blois-Châtillon married Louis I, duke of Anjou, son of John II of France, in 1360. Historian Erika Graham-Goering [notes](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/princely-power-in-late-medieval-france/career-of-jeanne-de-penthievre/F3D3D679151C7F5C01E15CD671B76001) that Marie was sent to England, along with her brothers Jean and Guy, as a hostage. She was the only one of the three to return to Brittany when her father was ransomed in 1356. * Jean de Blois-Châtillon became count of Penthièvre and continued to claim the duchy of Brittany. He remained as a hostage in England until 1387--Graham-Goering [notes](https://www.amazon.com/Princely-Power-Late-Medieval-France/dp/1108489095/ref=sr_1_1?crid=1WZBY53IT8K7Z&dib=eyJ2IjoiMSJ9.QlGT3leSWZdkm-CLkKBqgw.IEnUgD8YdeOCXTgE4kYrCwXuca8o7LKA-_NhtwAFfiM&dib_tag=se&keywords=princely+power+in+late+medieval+france&qid=1725401846&sprefix=Princely+Power+%2Caps%2C452&sr=8-1&asin=1108489095&revisionId=&format=4&depth=1) that he was finally released with the assistance of Olivier de Clisson, and the following year he married Olivier's daughter, Marguerite de Clisson (Jeanne de Belleville's granddaughter!). * A [reference](https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/brittcope.htm#CharlesBloisChatillondied1364A) in his father's canonization file indicates that Guy de Blois-Châtillon was still a hostage in England. Graham-Goering [indicates](https://www.amazon.com/Princely-Power-Late-Medieval-France/dp/1108489095/ref=sr_1_1?crid=1WZBY53IT8K7Z&dib=eyJ2IjoiMSJ9.QlGT3leSWZdkm-CLkKBqgw.IEnUgD8YdeOCXTgE4kYrCwXuca8o7LKA-_NhtwAFfiM&dib_tag=se&keywords=princely+power+in+late+medieval+france&qid=1725401846&sprefix=Princely+Power+%2Caps%2C452&sr=8-1&asin=1108489095&revisionId=&format=4&depth=1) that he died there in 1385, a year after his mother's death. * Henri de Blois-Châtillon was likely born after his father was released from captivity in 1356. Graham-Goering [notes](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/princely-power-in-late-medieval-france/career-of-jeanne-de-penthievre/F3D3D679151C7F5C01E15CD671B76001) a reference, dated 1365, that says he is in the care of _nourrices_, suggesting that he was still a small child_._ Graham-Goering also writes that along with his mother, Henri swore on 2 May 1381 to uphold the terms of the seconed treaty of Guérande. In 1382, when his brother-in-law Louis, duke of Anjou, went to Italy to claim the crown of Naples, Henri went with him. There, at some point after 1385 (when her first husband died), he married Giacobella Caetani. Henri is named in a legal document dated 31 July 1400, the last surviving reference to him. * Charles de Blois-Châtillon (d. before 1364). According to Graham-Goering, this child "probably died in infancy." In her assessment Jeanne de Penthièvre, Graham-Goering concludes that she "was an active and determined ruler who maintained her claim to the duchy throughout a war of succession and even after her eventual defeat."  \*The years given for Jeanne de Penthièvre's birth vary widely--here, I have used the date provided by Erika Graham-Goering in [her full-length study](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/princely-power-in-late-medieval-france/career-of-jeanne-de-penthievre/F3D3D679151C7F5C01E15CD671B76001), _Princely Power in Late Medieval France: Jeanne de Penthièvre and the War for Brittany._ She notes that a 1337 betrothal contract indicates that Jeanne will be "of an age to bear children in a year or two" and that her "intelligence" could "make up for age," suggesting she is "about 10 or 12 years old" at the time. Twelve was the [canonical age](https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01206c.htm) for marriage for girls: "The marriageable age is fourteen full years in males and twelve full years in females, under penalty of nullity (unless natural puberty supplies the want of years)." \*\*Although the treaty of Guérande was intended to settle the War of the Breton Succession, it was not quite successful. In 1420, another John de Montfort, duke of Brittany (this one is John V, John IV's son) was abducted by Olivier, the count of Penthièvre, and his brother, Charles de Avaugour (the grandsons of Jeanne). They held John for five months before his release was negotiated. As a result of his abduction and captivity, John V declared that the treaty settling the Breton War of Succession had been abrogated, thus ending any future Penthièvre claims. So, when Francis II, duke of Brittany (John IV's grandson), died in 1488 _without a male heir_, the rights of inheritance to the duchy of Brittany did not revert to the Penthièvres--Francis II was succeeded by his daughter, [Anne of Brittany](https://www.monstrousregimentofwomen.com/2015/01/anne-of-brittany-twice-queen-of-france.html). (approx.) French and English soldiers killed in combat,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-2) ~556,000 total French and English military deaths | The **Hundred Years' War** ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _Guerre de Cent Ans_; 1337–1453) was a conflict between the kingdoms of [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") and [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France") and a civil war in France during the [Late Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Middle_Ages "Late Middle Ages"). It emerged from feudal disputes over the [Duchy of Aquitaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Aquitaine "Duchy of Aquitaine") and was triggered by [a claim to the French throne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_claims_to_the_French_throne "English claims to the French throne") made by [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England"). The war grew into a broader military, economic, and political struggle involving factions from across [Western Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Europe "Western Europe"), fuelled by emerging nationalism on both sides. The periodisation of the war typically charts it as taking place over 116 years. However, it was an intermittent conflict which was frequently interrupted by external factors, such as the [Black Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death "Black Death"), and several years of truces. The Hundred Years' War was a significant conflict in the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages"). During the war, five generations of kings from two rival [dynasties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynasties "Dynasties") fought for the throne of France, then the wealthiest and most populous kingdom in Western Europe. The war had a lasting effect on European history: both sides produced innovations in military technology and tactics, including professional standing armies and artillery, that permanently changed European warfare. [Chivalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chivalry "Chivalry") reached its height during the conflict and subsequently declined. Stronger national identities took root in both kingdoms, which became more centralized and gradually emerged as global powers.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-3) The term "Hundred Years' War" was adopted by later historians as a historiographical periodisation to encompass dynastically related conflicts, constructing the longest military conflict in [European history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_history "European history").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-4)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-5) The war is commonly divided into three phases, separated by truces: the [Edwardian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwardian_War "Edwardian War") (1337–1360), the [Caroline War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caroline_War "Caroline War") (1369–1389), and the [Lancastrian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancastrian_War "Lancastrian War") (1415–1453). Each side drew many allies into the conflict, with English forces initially prevailing; however, the French forces under the [House of Valois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Valois "House of Valois") ultimately retained control over the Kingdom of France. The French and English monarchies thereafter remained separate, despite the monarchs of England and Great Britain styling themselves as [sovereigns of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_claims_to_the_French_throne "English claims to the French throne") until 1802. [![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/TimeLine100YearsWar_%28cropped%29.png/500px-TimeLine100YearsWar_%28cropped%29.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TimeLine100YearsWar_/(cropped/).png) A [timeline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_the_Hundred_Years%27_War "Timeline of the Hundred Years' War") of the key events of the Hundred Years' War The root causes of the conflict can be traced to the [crisis of 14th-century Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_of_the_late_Middle_Ages "Crisis of the late Middle Ages"). The outbreak of war was motivated by a gradual rise in tension between the kings of France and England over territory; the official pretext was the interruption of the direct male line of the [Capetian dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capetian_dynasty "Capetian dynasty"). Tensions between the French and English crowns had gone back centuries, dating to the [Norman Conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Conquest "Norman Conquest") of 1066 had put a king of (Norman) French origins, [William, duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William,_duke_of_Normandy "William, duke of Normandy"), on the throne of England. Since that time, English monarchs had held [titles and lands within France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angevin_Empire "Angevin Empire"), which made them [vassals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vassal "Vassal") to the kings of France. The status of the English king's French [fiefs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fief "Fief") was a significant source of conflict between the two monarchies throughout the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages").\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] According to military historian and author [Michael Livingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Livingston "Michael Livingston"), the conflict began in 1337, when [Philippe VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippe_VI_of_France "Philippe VI of France") claimed that [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") controlled English holdings in France.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-6) In 1328, [Charles IV of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_IV_of_France "Charles IV of France") died without any sons or brothers, initiating a succession crisis. A similar crisis in 1316 had resulted in the [Estates-General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estates_General_/(France/) "Estates General (France)") in 1317 deciding that "Women do not succeed in the kingdom of France". Charles's closest male relative was his nephew [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England"), whose mother [Isabella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_of_France "Isabella of France") was Charles's sister. Isabella [claimed the throne of France for her son](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_claims_to_the_French_throne "English claims to the French throne") by the rule of [proximity of blood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proximity_of_blood "Proximity of blood"), but the French nobility rejected this on the basis of the 1317 decision, declaring that Isabella [could not transmit a right she did not possess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nemo_dat_quod_non_habet "Nemo dat quod non habet"). An assembly of French [barons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baron "Baron") decided that a [native Frenchman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_people "French people") should receive the crown rather than Edward.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrevit%C3%A9-Orton1978872-7) The throne passed to Charles's [patrilineal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrilineal "Patrilineal") cousin instead, [Philip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"), [Count of Valois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Valois "Count of Valois") who had been made regent on the death of Charles IV. Edward protested but ultimately submitted and did homage for Gascony. Further French disagreements with Edward induced Philip during May 1337 to meet with his Great Council in Paris. It was agreed that Gascony should be taken back into Philip's hands, which prompted Edward to renew his claim for the French throne, this time by force of arms.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrevit%C3%A9-Orton1978873%E2%80%93876-8) In the early years of the war, the English, led by King Edward III and his son [Edward the Black Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_the_Black_Prince "Edward the Black Prince"), saw resounding successes, notably at the battles of [Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cr%C3%A9cy "Crécy") (1346) and [Poitiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Poitiers "Battle of Poitiers") (1356), where King [John II of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France") was taken prisoner. ### Caroline phase and Black Death \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Caroline phase and Black Death")\] By 1378, under King [Charles V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V_of_France "Charles V of France") the Wise and the leadership of [Bertrand du Guesclin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand_du_Guesclin "Bertrand du Guesclin"), the French had reconquered most of the lands ceded to King Edward in the [Treaty of Brétigny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Br%C3%A9tigny "Treaty of Brétigny") (signed in 1360), notably reducing English control on the continent, leaving them with few cities. The French victory of the Battle of the Castillion was not just a victory but a significant turning point in the Hundred Years' War. It characterized the end of English territorial claims in France and marked the dawn of the decline of English power in France.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-9) However, both countries faced challenges and problems. The Black Death, a deadly plague that spread through Europe between 1347 and 1351 caused catastrophic widespread damage. In France, 6 to 12 million people died, 30% to 60% of the population,[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-10) resulting in major labor shortages, economic collapse, and widespread social dislocation. England also suffered from the Black Death, but to a lesser extent, with roughly 2–3 million deaths. Economic consequences of the plague and the war led to major unrest in both kingdoms, widespread poverty, and a weakening of royal authority.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-11)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-12) These crises were resolved in England earlier than in France. ### Lancastrian phase and after \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: Lancastrian phase and after")\] King [Henry V of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_V_of_England "Henry V of England") seized the opportunity presented by the mental illness of King [Charles VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_VI_of_France "Charles VI of France") and the [French civil war between Armagnacs and Burgundians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armagnac%E2%80%93Burgundian_Civil_War "Armagnac–Burgundian Civil War") to revive the conflict. Overwhelming victories at the battles of [Agincourt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Agincourt "Battle of Agincourt") (1415) and [Verneuil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Verneuil "Battle of Verneuil") (1424)—as well as an alliance with the Burgundians—raised the prospects of an ultimate English triumph and persuaded the English to continue the war over many decades. A variety of factors prevented this, however. Notable influences include the deaths of both Henry and Charles in 1422, the emergence of [Joan of Arc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Arc "Joan of Arc") (which boosted French morale), and the loss of [Burgundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgundian_State "Burgundian State") as an ally (concluding the French civil war). The [Siege of Orléans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Orl%C3%A9ans "Siege of Orléans") (1429) made English aspirations for conquest all but unreal. Despite Joan's capture by the Burgundians and her subsequent execution in 1431, a series of crushing French victories concluded the siege, favoring the Valois dynasty. Notably, the battles of [Patay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Patay "Battle of Patay") (1429), [Formigny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Formigny "Battle of Formigny") (1450), and [Castillon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Castillon "Battle of Castillon") (1453) proved decisive in ending the war. England permanently lost most of its continental possessions, with only the [Pale of Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pale_of_Calais "Pale of Calais") remaining under its control on the continent until the [Siege of Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Calais_/(1558/) "Siege of Calais (1558)") in 1558. ### Related conflicts and after-effects \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=6 "Edit section: Related conflicts and after-effects")\] Local conflicts in neighbouring areas, which were contemporarily related to the war, including the [War of the Breton Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession "War of the Breton Succession") (1341–1364), the [Castilian Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castilian_Civil_War "Castilian Civil War") (1366–1369), the [War of the Two Peters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Two_Peters "War of the Two Peters") (1356–1369) in [Aragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_Aragon "Crown of Aragon"), and the [1383–1385 crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1383%E2%80%931385_crisis "1383–1385 crisis") in [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Portugal "Kingdom of Portugal"), were used by the parties to advance their agendas. By the war's end, feudal armies had mainly been replaced by professional troops, and aristocratic dominance had yielded to a democratization of the manpower and weapons of armies. Although primarily a [dynastic conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_succession "War of succession"), the war inspired [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_nationalism "French nationalism") and [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_nationalism#Medieval "English nationalism") nationalism. The broader introduction of weapons and tactics supplanted the [feudal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudal "Feudal") armies where [heavy cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_cavalry "Heavy cavalry") had dominated, and [artillery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artillery "Artillery") became important. The war precipitated the creation of the first [standing armies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standing_armies "Standing armies") in Western Europe since the [Western Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Roman_Empire "Western Roman Empire") and helped change their [role in warfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_science "Military science"). Civil wars, deadly epidemics, famines, and bandit free-companies of mercenaries reduced the population drastically in France. But at the end of the war, the French had the upper hand with their better weapon supply, such as small hand-held cannons. In England, political forces over time came to oppose the costly venture. After the war England was left insolvent, leaving the conquering French in complete control of all of France except Calais. The dissatisfaction of [English nobles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_British_peerage "History of the British peerage"), resulting from the loss of their continental landholdings as well as the general shock at losing a war in which investment had been so significant, helped lead to the [Wars of the Roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Roses "Wars of the Roses") (1455–1487). The economic consequences of the Hundred Years' War produced a decline in trade and led to a high collection of taxes from both countries, which played a significant role in civil disorder. ### Dynastic turmoil in France: 1316–1328 \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Dynastic turmoil in France: 1316–1328")\] The question of female succession to the French throne was raised after the death of [Louis X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_X_of_France "Louis X of France") in 1316. Louis left behind a young daughter, [Joan II of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_II_of_Navarre "Joan II of Navarre"), and a son, [John I of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I_of_France "John I of France"), although he only lived for five days. However, Joan's paternity was in question, as her mother, [Margaret of Burgundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_of_Burgundy,_Queen_of_France "Margaret of Burgundy, Queen of France"), was accused of being an adulterer in the [Tour de Nesle affair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_de_Nesle_affair "Tour de Nesle affair"). Given the situation, Philip, [Count of Poitiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Poitiers "Count of Poitiers") and brother of Louis X, positioned himself to take the crown, advancing the stance that women should be ineligible to succeed to the French throne. He won over his adversaries through his political sagacity and succeeded to the French throne as [Philip V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_V_of_France "Philip V of France"). When he died in 1322, leaving only daughters behind, the crown passed to his younger brother, [Charles IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_IV_of_France "Charles IV of France").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrissaud1915329%E2%80%93330-13) | * [v](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Template:Hundred_Years%27_War_family_tree "Template:Hundred Years' War family tree") * [t](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Template_talk:Hundred_Years%27_War_family_tree "Template talk:Hundred Years' War family tree") * [e](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:EditPage/Template:Hundred_Years%27_War_family_tree "Special:EditPage/Template:Hundred Years' War family tree") Royal families involved in the Hundred Years' War (1337–1453) | | --- | |

| Charles IV died in 1328, leaving behind his young daughter and pregnant wife, [Joan of Évreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_%C3%89vreux "Joan of Évreux"). He decreed that he would become king if the unborn child were male. If not, Charles left the choice of his successor to the nobles. Joan gave birth to a girl, [Blanche of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanche_of_France,_Duchess_of_Orl%C3%A9ans "Blanche of France, Duchess of Orléans") (later Duchess of Orleans). With Charles IV's death and Blanche's birth, the main male line of the [House of Capet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Capet "House of Capet") was rendered extinct. By [proximity of blood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proximity_of_blood "Proximity of blood"), the nearest male relative of Charles IV was his nephew, [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England"). Edward was the son of [Isabella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_of_France "Isabella of France"), the sister of the dead Charles IV, but the question arose whether she could transmit a right to inherit that she did not possess. Moreover, the French nobility balked at the prospect of being ruled by an Englishman, especially one whose mother, Isabella, and her lover, [Roger Mortimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Mortimer,_1st_Earl_of_March "Roger Mortimer, 1st Earl of March"), were widely suspected of having murdered the previous English king, [Edward II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_II "Edward II"). The French barons, prelates, and the [University of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Paris "University of Paris") assemblies decided that males who derive their right to inheritance through their mother should be excluded from consideration. Therefore, excluding Edward, the nearest [heir through the male line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnatic_primogeniture "Agnatic primogeniture") was Charles IV's first cousin, Philip, [Count of Valois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Valois "Count of Valois"), and it was decided that he should take the throne. He was crowned [Philip VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") in 1328. In 1340, the [Avignon papacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon_papacy "Avignon papacy") confirmed that, under [Salic law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salic_law "Salic law"), males would not be able to inherit through their mothers.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrissaud1915329%E2%80%93330-13)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrevit%C3%A9-Orton1978872-7) Eventually, Edward III reluctantly recognized Philip VI and paid him [homage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homage_/(feudal/) "Homage (feudal)") for the duchy of [Aquitaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Aquitaine "Duchy of Aquitaine") and [Gascony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Gascony "Duchy of Gascony") in 1329. He made concessions in [Guyenne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guyenne "Guyenne") but reserved the right to reclaim territories arbitrarily confiscated. After that, he expected to be left undisturbed while he made [war on Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_War_of_Scottish_Independence "Second War of Scottish Independence"). ### Dispute over Guyenne: a problem of sovereignty \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: Dispute over Guyenne: a problem of sovereignty")\] [![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/Hommage_d_%C3%89douard_Ier_%C3%A0_Philippe_le_Bel.jpg/500px-Hommage_d_%C3%89douard_Ier_%C3%A0_Philippe_le_Bel.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hommage_d_%C3%89douard_Ier_%C3%A0_Philippe_le_Bel.jpg) Homage of [Edward I of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_I_of_England "Edward I of England") (kneeling) to [Philip IV of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_IV_of_France "Philip IV of France") (seated), 1286. As [Duke of Aquitaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Aquitaine "Duke of Aquitaine"), Edward was also a vassal to the French king (illumination by [Jean Fouquet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Fouquet "Jean Fouquet") from the _[Grandes Chroniques de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandes_Chroniques_de_France "Grandes Chroniques de France")_ in the [Bibliothèque Nationale de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblioth%C3%A8que_Nationale_de_France "Bibliothèque Nationale de France"), Paris). Tensions between the French and English monarchies can be traced back to the 1066 [Norman Conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Conquest "Norman Conquest") of England, in which the [English throne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_throne "English throne") was seized by the [Duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Normandy "Duke of Normandy"), a [vassal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vassal "Vassal") of the [King of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_France "King of France"). As a result, the crown of England was held by a succession of nobles who already owned lands in France, which put them among the most influential subjects of the French king, as they could now draw upon the economic power of England to enforce their interests in the mainland. To the kings of France, this threatened their royal authority, and so they would constantly try to undermine English rule in France, while the [English monarchs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_monarchs "English monarchs") would struggle to protect and expand their lands. This clash of interests was the root cause of much of the conflict between the French and English monarchies throughout the medieval era. The [Anglo-Norman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Normans "Anglo-Normans") [dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Normandy "House of Normandy") that had ruled [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") since the Norman conquest of 1066 was brought to an end when [Henry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_II_of_England "Henry II of England"), the son of [Geoffrey of Anjou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_of_Anjou "Geoffrey of Anjou") and [Empress Matilda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empress_Matilda "Empress Matilda"), and great-grandson of [William the Conqueror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_the_Conqueror "William the Conqueror"), became the first of the [Angevin kings of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angevin_kings_of_England "Angevin kings of England") in 1154 as Henry II.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBartlett200022-14) The Angevin kings ruled over what was later known as the [Angevin Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angevin_Empire "Angevin Empire"), which included more French territory than that under the [kings of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kings_of_France "Kings of France"). The Angevins still owed [homage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homage_/(feudal/) "Homage (feudal)") to the French king for these territories. From the 11th century, the Angevins had autonomy within their French domains, neutralizing the issue.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBartlett200017-15) [King John of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_John_of_England "King John of England") inherited the Angevin domains from his brother [Richard I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_I "Richard I"). However, [Philip II of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_II_of_France "Philip II of France") acted decisively to exploit the weaknesses of John, both legally and militarily, and [by 1204 had succeeded in taking control of much of the Angevin continental possessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_invasion_of_Normandy_/(1202%E2%80%931204/) "French invasion of Normandy (1202–1204)"). Following John's reign, the [Battle of Bouvines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bouvines "Battle of Bouvines") (1214), the [Saintonge War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saintonge_War "Saintonge War") (1242), and finally the [War of Saint-Sardos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_Saint-Sardos "War of Saint-Sardos") (1324), the English king's holdings on the continent, as [Duke of Aquitaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Aquitaine "Duke of Aquitaine"), were limited roughly to provinces in Gascony (and [Bordeaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bordeaux "Bordeaux")).[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGormley2007-16) The dispute over Guyenne is even more important than the dynastic question in explaining the outbreak of the war. Guyenne posed a significant problem to the kings of France and England: Edward III was a vassal of Philip VI of France because of his French possessions and was required to recognize the [suzerainty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzerainty "Suzerainty") of the King of France over them. In practical terms, a judgment in Guyenne might be subject to an appeal to the French royal court. The King of France had the power to revoke all legal decisions made by the King of England in Aquitaine, which was unacceptable to the English. Therefore, sovereignty over Guyenne was a latent conflict between the two monarchies for several generations. During the War of Saint-Sardos, [Charles of Valois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Valois "Charles of Valois"), father of Philip VI, invaded Aquitaine on behalf of Charles IV and conquered the duchy after a local insurrection, which the French believed had been incited by [Edward II of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_II_of_England "Edward II of England"). Charles IV grudgingly agreed to return this territory in 1325. Edward II had to compromise to recover his duchy: he sent his son, the future [Edward III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III "Edward III"), to pay homage. The King of France agreed to restore Guyenne, minus [Agen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agenais "Agenais"), but the French delayed the return of the lands, which helped Philip VI. On 6 June 1329, Edward III finally paid homage to the King of France. However, at the ceremony, Philip VI had it recorded that the homage was not due to the fiefs detached from the duchy of Guyenne by Charles IV (especially Agen). For Edward, the homage did not imply the renunciation of his claim to the extorted lands. ### Gascony under the King of England \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=10 "Edit section: Gascony under the King of England")\] [![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Guyenne_1328-en2.svg/250px-Guyenne_1328-en2.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Guyenne_1328-en2.svg) France in 1330.France before 1214 French acquisitions until 1330 England and Guyenne/Gascony and other English territories as of 1330 In the 11th century, [Gascony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gascony "Gascony") in southwest France had been incorporated into Aquitaine (also known as _Guyenne_ or _Guienne_) and formed with it the province of Guyenne and Gascony (French: _Guyenne-et-Gascogne_). The [Angevin kings of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angevin_kings_of_England "Angevin kings of England") became [dukes of Aquitaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dukes_of_Aquitaine "Dukes of Aquitaine") after [Henry II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_II_of_England "Henry II of England") married the former Queen of France, [Eleanor of Aquitaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleanor_of_Aquitaine "Eleanor of Aquitaine"), in 1152, from which point the lands were held in vassalage to the French crown. By the 13th century the terms _Aquitaine_, _Guyenne_ and _Gascony_ were virtually synonymous.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-17) At the beginning of Edward III's reign on 1 February 1327, the only part of Aquitaine that remained in his hands was the Duchy of Gascony. The term _Gascony_ came to be used for the territory held by the Angevin ([Plantagenet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plantagenet "Plantagenet")) kings of England in southwest France, although they still used the title Duke of Aquitaine.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-18) For the first 10 years of Edward III's reign, Gascony had been a significant friction point. The English argued that, as Charles IV had not acted properly towards his tenant, Edward should be able to hold the duchy free of French [suzerainty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzerainty "Suzerainty"). The French rejected this argument, so in 1329, the 17-year-old Edward III paid homage to Philip VI. Tradition demanded that vassals approach their liege unarmed, with heads bare. Edward protested by attending the ceremony wearing his crown and sword.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson2011194-19) Even after this pledge of homage, the French continued to pressure the English administration.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2007394-20) Gascony was not the only sore point. One of Edward's influential advisers was [Robert III of Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_III_of_Artois "Robert III of Artois"). Robert was an exile from the French court, having fallen out with Philip VI over an inheritance claim. He urged Edward to start a war to reclaim France, and was able to provide extensive intelligence on the French court.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2007306-21) ### Franco-Scot alliance \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=11 "Edit section: Franco-Scot alliance")\] France was an ally of the [Kingdom of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Scotland "Kingdom of Scotland") as English kings had tried to subjugate the country for some time. In 1295, [a treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auld_Alliance "Auld Alliance") was signed between France and Scotland during the reign of [Philip the Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_the_Fair "Philip the Fair"), known as the Auld Alliance. Charles IV formally [renewed the treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Corbeil_/(1326/) "Treaty of Corbeil (1326)") in 1326, promising Scotland that France would support the Scots if England invaded their country. Similarly, France would have Scotland's support if its own kingdom were attacked. Edward could not succeed in his plans for Scotland if the Scots could count on French support.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2007304%E2%80%93305-22) Philip VI had assembled a large naval fleet off Marseilles as part of an ambitious plan for a [crusade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crusade "Crusade") to the [Holy Land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Land "Holy Land"). However, the plan was abandoned and the fleet, including elements of the Scottish navy, moved to the [English Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Channel "English Channel") off Normandy in 1336, threatening England.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2007306-21) To deal with this crisis, Edward proposed that the English raise two armies, one to deal with the Scots "at a suitable time" and the other to proceed at once to Gascony. At the same time, ambassadors were to be sent to France with a proposed treaty for the French king.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1991180-23) ### Beginning of the war: 1337–1360 \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=13 "Edit section: Beginning of the war: 1337–1360")\] [![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e0/Hundred_years_war.gif/250px-Hundred_years_war.gif)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hundred_years_war.gif) Animated map showing progress of the war (territorial changes and the most important battles between 1337 and 1453). At the end of April 1337, Philip of France was invited to meet the delegation from England but refused. The _[arrière-ban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arri%C3%A8re-ban "Arrière-ban")_, a call to arms, was proclaimed throughout France starting on 30 April 1337. Then, in May 1337, Philip met with his Great Council in Paris. It was agreed that the Duchy of Aquitaine, effectively Gascony, should be taken back into the King's hands because Edward III was in breach of his obligations as a vassal and had sheltered the King's "mortal enemy" [Robert d'Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_III_of_Artois "Robert III of Artois").[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1991184-24) Edward responded to the confiscation of Aquitaine by challenging Philip's right to the French throne. When Charles IV died, Edward claimed the succession of the French throne through the right of his mother, Isabella (Charles IV's sister), daughter of Philip IV. His claim was considered invalidated by Edward's homage to Philip VI in 1329. Edward revived his claim and in 1340 formally assumed the title "King of France and the French Royal Arms".[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2003149%E2%80%93150-25) On 26 January 1340, Edward III formally received homage from Guy, half-brother of the [Count of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Flanders "Count of Flanders"). The civic authorities of [Ghent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghent "Ghent"), [Ypres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ypres "Ypres"), and [Bruges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruges "Bruges") proclaimed Edward King of France. Edward aimed to strengthen his alliances with the [Low Countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Countries "Low Countries"). His supporters could claim that they were loyal to the "true" King of France and did not rebel against Philip. In February 1340, Edward returned to England to try to raise more funds and also deal with political difficulties.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2007307%E2%80%93312-26) Relations with Flanders were also tied to the [English wool trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_wool_trade "English wool trade") since Flanders' principal cities relied heavily on textile production, and England supplied much of the raw material they needed. Edward III had commanded that his [chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Chancellor "Lord Chancellor") sit on the [woolsack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolsack "Woolsack") in council as a symbol of the pre-eminence of the wool trade.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFriar2004480%E2%80%93481-27) At the time there were about 110,000 [sheep in Sussex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Sussex#Wool "History of Sussex") alone.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-darby160-28) The great medieval English monasteries produced large wool surpluses sold to mainland Europe. Successive governments were able to make large amounts of money by taxing it.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFriar2004480%E2%80%93481-27) France's sea power led to economic disruptions for England, shrinking the wool trade to [Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_Flanders "County of Flanders") and the wine trade from Gascony.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-29) #### Outbreak, the English Channel and Brittany \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=15 "Edit section: Outbreak, the English Channel and Brittany")\] [![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/BattleofSluys.jpeg/500px-BattleofSluys.jpeg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BattleofSluys.jpeg) The [Battle of Sluys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sluys "Battle of Sluys") from a [BNF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblioth%C3%A8que_nationale_de_France "Bibliothèque nationale de France") [manuscript](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Froissart_of_Louis_of_Gruuthuse_/(BnF_Fr_2643-6/) "Froissart of Louis of Gruuthuse (BnF Fr 2643-6)") of [Froissart's Chronicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Froissart%27s_Chronicles "Froissart's Chronicles"), Bruges, c. 1470. On 22 June 1340, Edward and his fleet sailed from England and arrived off the [Zwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zwin "Zwin") estuary the next day. The French fleet assumed a defensive formation off the port of [Sluis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sluis "Sluis"). The English fleet deceived the French into believing they were withdrawing. When the wind turned in the late afternoon, the English attacked with the wind and sun behind them. The French fleet was almost destroyed in what became known as the [Battle of Sluys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sluys "Battle of Sluys"). England dominated the English Channel for the rest of the war, preventing French [invasions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasions "Invasions").[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2007307%E2%80%93312-26) At this point, Edward's funds ran out and the war probably would have ended were it not for the death of the [Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany") in 1341 precipitating a succession dispute between the duke's half-brother [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort") and [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois"), nephew of Philip VI.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers201088%E2%80%9389-30) In 1341, this inheritance dispute over the [Duchy of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brittany "Duchy of Brittany") set off the [War of the Breton Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession "War of the Breton Succession"), in which Edward backed John of Montfort and Philip backed Charles of Blois. Action for the next few years focused on a back-and-forth struggle in Brittany. The city of [Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes "Vannes") in Brittany changed hands several times, while further campaigns in Gascony met with mixed success for both sides.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers201088%E2%80%9389-30) The English-backed Montfort finally took the duchy but not until 1364.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-31) #### Battle of Crécy and the taking of Calais \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=16 "Edit section: Battle of Crécy and the taking of Calais")\] [![Image 11](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/Cr%C3%A9cy_-_Grandes_Chroniques_de_France.jpg/330px-Cr%C3%A9cy_-_Grandes_Chroniques_de_France.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cr%C3%A9cy_-_Grandes_Chroniques_de_France.jpg) [Battle of Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy "Battle of Crécy"), 1346, from the [Grandes Chroniques de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandes_Chroniques_de_France "Grandes Chroniques de France"). [British Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Library "British Library"), London In July 1346, Edward mounted a major invasion across the channel, landing on Normandy's [Cotentin Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotentin_Peninsula "Cotentin Peninsula") at [St Vaast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Vaast-la-Hougue "Saint-Vaast-la-Hougue"). The English army [captured](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Caen_/(1346/) "Battle of Caen (1346)") the city of [Caen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caen "Caen") in just one day, surprising the French. Philip mustered a large army to oppose Edward, who chose to march northward toward the Low Countries, pillaging as he went. He reached the river Seine to find most of the crossings destroyed. He moved further south, worryingly close to Paris until he found the crossing at Poissy. This had only been partially destroyed, so the carpenters within his army were able to fix it. He then continued to Flanders until he reached the river Somme. The army crossed at a tidal ford at Blanchetaque, stranding Philip's army. Edward, assisted by this head start, continued on his way to Flanders once more until, finding himself unable to outmaneuver Philip, Edward positioned his forces for battle, and Philip's army attacked. [![Image 12](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Edward_III_counting_the_dead_on_the_battlefield_of_Cr%C3%A9cy.jpg/330px-Edward_III_counting_the_dead_on_the_battlefield_of_Cr%C3%A9cy.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Edward_III_counting_the_dead_on_the_battlefield_of_Cr%C3%A9cy.jpg) [Edward III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III "Edward III") counting the dead on the battlefield of Crécy The [Battle of Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy "Battle of Crécy") of 1346 was a complete disaster for the French, largely credited to the English [longbowmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_longbow "English longbow") and the French king, who allowed his army to attack before it was ready.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2007318%E2%80%93319-32) Philip appealed to his Scottish allies to help with a diversionary attack on England. King [David II of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_II_of_Scotland "David II of Scotland") responded by invading northern England, but his army was defeated, and he was captured at the [Battle of Neville's Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Neville%27s_Cross "Battle of Neville's Cross") on 17 October 1346. This greatly reduced the threat from Scotland.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers201088%E2%80%9389-30)[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers201055%E2%80%9345-33) In France, Edward proceeded north unopposed and [besieged the city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Calais_/(1346%E2%80%931347/) "Siege of Calais (1346–1347)") of [Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calais "Calais") on the English Channel, capturing it in 1347. This became an important strategic asset for the English, allowing them to keep troops safely in northern France.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2007318%E2%80%93319-32) Calais would remain under English control, even after the end of the Hundred Years' War, until the successful [French siege in 1558](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Calais_/(1558/) "Siege of Calais (1558)").[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrummitt20081-34) The [Black Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death "Black Death"), which had just arrived in Paris in 1348, ravaged Europe.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-35) In 1355, after the plague had passed and England was able to recover financially,[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHewitt20041-36) King Edward's son and namesake, the [Prince of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Wales "Prince of Wales"), later known as the [Black Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Prince "Black Prince"), led [a _chevauchée_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Prince%27s_chevauch%C3%A9e_of_1355 "Black Prince's chevauchée of 1355") from Gascony into France, during which he pillaged [Avignonet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignonet "Avignonet"), [Castelnaudary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castelnaudary "Castelnaudary"), [Carcassonne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carcassonne "Carcassonne"), and [Narbonne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narbonne "Narbonne"). The next year during [another _chevauchée_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Prince%27s_chevauch%C3%A9e_of_1356 "Black Prince's chevauchée of 1356") he ravaged [Auvergne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auvergne "Auvergne"), [Limousin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limousin "Limousin"), and [Berry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berry,_France "Berry, France") but failed to take [Bourges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourges "Bourges"). He offered terms of peace to King [John II of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France") (known as John the Good), who had outflanked him near Poitiers but refused to surrender himself as the price of their acceptance. This led to the [Battle of Poitiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Poitiers "Battle of Poitiers") (19 September 1356) where the Black Prince's army routed the French.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunt1903388-37) During the battle, the Gascon noble [Jean de Grailly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_III_de_Grailly,_captal_de_Buch "Jean III de Grailly, captal de Buch"), [captal de Buch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captal_de_Buch "Captal de Buch") led a mounted unit that was concealed in a forest. The French advance was contained, at which point de Grailly led a flanking movement with his horsemen, cutting off the French retreat and successfully capturing King John and many of his nobles.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-38) With John held hostage, his son the [Dauphin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dauphin_of_France "Dauphin of France") (later to become [Charles V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V_of_France "Charles V of France")) assumed the powers of the king as [regent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regent "Regent").[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuignebert1930Volume_1._pp._304%E2%80%93307-39) After the Battle of Poitiers, many French nobles and mercenaries rampaged, and chaos ruled. A contemporary report recounted: > ... all went ill with the kingdom and the State was undone. Thieves and robbers rose up everywhere in the land. The Nobles despised and hated all others and took no thought for usefulness and profit of lord and men. They subjected and despoiled the peasants and the men of the villages. In no wise did they defend their country from its enemies; rather did they trample it underfoot, robbing and pillaging the peasants' goods ... #### Reims campaign and Black Monday \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=18 "Edit section: Reims campaign and Black Monday")\] [![Image 13](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Black_Monday_hailstorm.jpg/330px-Black_Monday_hailstorm.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Black_Monday_hailstorm.jpg) A later engraving of [Black Monday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Monday_/(1360/) "Black Monday (1360)") in 1360: hailstorms and lightning ravage the English army outside [Chartres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chartres "Chartres") Edward invaded France, for the third and last time, hoping to capitalise on the discontent and seize the throne. The Dauphin's strategy was that of non-engagement with the English army in the field. However, Edward wanted the crown and chose the cathedral city of [Reims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reims "Reims") for his coronation (Reims was the traditional coronation city).[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2007326-41) However, the citizens of Reims built and reinforced the city's defences before Edward and his army arrived.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Patourel1984189-42) Edward besieged the city for five weeks, but the defences held and there was no coronation.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2007326-41) Edward moved on to Paris, but retreated after a few skirmishes in the suburbs. Next was the town of [Chartres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chartres "Chartres"). Disaster struck in a freak [hailstorm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hailstorm "Hailstorm") on the encamped army, causing over 1,000 English deaths – the so-called [Black Monday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Monday_/(1360/) "Black Monday (1360)") at Easter 1360. This devastated Edward's army and forced him to negotiate when approached by the French.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-43) A conference was held at Brétigny that resulted in the [Treaty of Brétigny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Br%C3%A9tigny "Treaty of Brétigny") (8 May 1360).[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Patourel198432-44) The treaty was ratified at Calais in October. In return for increased lands in Aquitaine, Edward renounced Normandy, Touraine, Anjou and Maine and consented to reduce King John's ransom by a million crowns. Edward also abandoned his claim to the crown of France.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-45) ### First peace: 1360–1369 \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=19 "Edit section: First peace: 1360–1369")\] [![Image 14](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/Map-_France_at_the_Treaty_of_Bretigny.jpg/250px-Map-_France_at_the_Treaty_of_Bretigny.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Map-_France_at_the_Treaty_of_Bretigny.jpg) France at the [Treaty of Brétigny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Br%C3%A9tigny "Treaty of Brétigny"), English holdings in light red The French king, [John II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France"), was held captive in England for four years. The [Treaty of Brétigny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Br%C3%A9tigny "Treaty of Brétigny") set his ransom at 3 million crowns and allowed for hostages to be held in lieu of John. The hostages included two of his sons, several princes and nobles, four inhabitants of Paris, and two citizens from each of the nineteen principal towns of France. While these hostages were held, John returned to France to try to raise funds to pay the ransom. In 1362, John's son [Louis of Anjou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_I_of_Anjou "Louis I of Anjou"), a hostage in English-held Calais, escaped captivity. With his stand-in hostage gone, John felt honour-bound to return to captivity in England.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuignebert1930Volume_1._pp._304%E2%80%93307-39)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911501-46) The French crown had been at odds with [Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Navarre "Kingdom of Navarre") (near southern [Gascony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gascony "Gascony")) since 1354, and in 1363, the Navarrese used the captivity of John II in London and the political weakness of the Dauphin to try to seize power.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006102%E2%80%93103-47) Although there was no formal treaty, Edward III supported the Navarrese moves, particularly as there was a prospect that he might gain control over the northern and western provinces as a consequence. With this in mind, Edward deliberately slowed the peace negotiations.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod2001384-48) In 1364, John II died in London, while still in honourable captivity.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-Backman179-49) [Charles V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V_of_France "Charles V of France") succeeded him as king of France.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuignebert1930Volume_1._pp._304%E2%80%93307-39)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-britannica1-50) On 16 May, one month after the dauphin's accession and three days before his coronation as Charles V, the Navarrese suffered a crushing defeat at the [Battle of Cocherel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cocherel "Battle of Cocherel").[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200686-51) ### French ascendancy under Charles V: 1369–1389 \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=20 "Edit section: French ascendancy under Charles V: 1369–1389")\] #### Aquitaine and Castile \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=21 "Edit section: Aquitaine and Castile")\] In 1366, there was a civil war of succession in [Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_Castile#Ascension_of_the_Trast%C3%A1mara_dynasty "Crown of Castile") (part of modern Spain). The forces of the ruler [Peter of Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_of_Castile "Peter of Castile") were pitched against those of his half-brother [Henry of Trastámara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_of_Trast%C3%A1mara "Henry of Trastámara"). The English crown supported Peter; the French supported Henry. French forces were led by [Bertrand du Guesclin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand_du_Guesclin "Bertrand du Guesclin"), a Breton, who rose from relatively humble beginnings to prominence as one of France's war leaders. Charles V provided a force of 12,000, with du Guesclin at their head, to support Trastámara in his invasion of Castile.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200269%E2%80%9370-52) [![Image 15](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Du_Guesclin_Dinan.jpg/250px-Du_Guesclin_Dinan.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Du_Guesclin_Dinan.jpg) Statue of [Bertrand du Guesclin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand_du_Guesclin "Bertrand du Guesclin") in [Dinan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinan "Dinan"), [Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany "Brittany") Peter appealed to England and Aquitaine's [Black Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Prince "Black Prince"), Edward of Woodstock, for help, but none was forthcoming, forcing Peter into exile in Aquitaine. The Black Prince had previously agreed to support Peter's claims but concerns over the terms of the treaty of Brétigny led him to assist Peter as a representative of Aquitaine, rather than England. He then led an Anglo-Gascon army into Castile. Peter was restored to power after Trastámara's army was defeated at the [Battle of Nájera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_N%C3%A1jera "Battle of Nájera").[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200678-53) Although the Castilians had agreed to fund the Black Prince, they failed to do so. The Prince was suffering from ill health and returned with his army to Aquitaine. To pay off debts incurred during the Castile campaign, the prince instituted a [hearth tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hearth_tax "Hearth tax"). [Arnaud-Amanieu VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnaud_Amanieu,_Lord_of_Albret "Arnaud Amanieu, Lord of Albret"), Lord of [Albret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albret "Albret") had fought on the Black Prince's side during the war. Albret, who already had become discontented by the influx of English administrators into the enlarged Aquitaine, refused to allow the tax to be collected in his fief. He then joined a group of Gascon lords who appealed to Charles V for support in their refusal to pay the tax.
