Charles V summoned one Gascon lord and the Black Prince to hear the case in his High Court in Paris. The Black Prince answered that he would go to Paris with sixty thousand men behind him. War broke out again and Edward III resumed the title of King of France.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006122-54) Charles V declared that all the English possessions in France were forfeited, and before the end of 1369 all of Aquitaine was in full revolt.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-55) With the Black Prince gone from Castile, Henry of Trastámara led a second invasion that ended with Peter's death at the [Battle of Montiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Montiel "Battle of Montiel") in March 1369. The new Castilian regime provided naval support to French campaigns against Aquitaine and England[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200678-53) and England backed [John of Gaunt's claim to the Castilan throne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Gaunt%27s_claim_to_the_Castilan_throne "John of Gaunt's claim to the Castilan throne"). In 1372, the Castilian fleet defeated the English fleet in the [Battle of La Rochelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_La_Rochelle "Battle of La Rochelle"). #### 1373 campaign of John of Gaunt \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=22 "Edit section: 1373 campaign of John of Gaunt")\] In August 1373, [John of Gaunt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Gaunt "John of Gaunt"), accompanied by [John de Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), Duke of Brittany led a force of 9,000 men from Calais on a _chevauchée_. While initially successful as French forces were insufficiently concentrated to oppose them, the English met more resistance as they moved south. French forces began to concentrate around the English force but under orders from [Charles V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V_of_France "Charles V of France"), the French avoided a set battle. Instead, they fell on forces detached from the main body to raid or forage. The French shadowed the English and in October, the English found themselves trapped against the [River Allier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Allier "River Allier") by four French forces. With some difficulty, the English crossed at the bridge at [Moulins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moulins,_Allier "Moulins, Allier") but lost all their baggage and loot. The English carried on south across the [Limousin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limousin "Limousin") plateau but the weather was turning severe. Men and horses died in great numbers and many soldiers, forced to march on foot, discarded their armour. At the beginning of December, the English army entered friendly territory in [Gascony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gascony "Gascony"). By the end of December, they were in [Bordeaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bordeaux "Bordeaux"), starving, ill-equipped, and having lost over half of the 30,000 horses with which they had left Calais. Although the march across France had been a remarkable feat, it was a military failure.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption2012187%E2%80%93196-56) [![Image 16](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Ofensivas_Tovar-Vienne_contra_Inglaterra_01.jpg/500px-Ofensivas_Tovar-Vienne_contra_Inglaterra_01.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ofensivas_Tovar-Vienne_contra_Inglaterra_01.jpg) The Franco-Castilian Navy, led by Admirals [de Vienne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_de_Vienne "Jean de Vienne") and [Tovar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_S%C3%A1nchez_de_Tovar "Fernando Sánchez de Tovar"), managed to raid the English coasts for the first time since the beginning of the Hundred Years' War. With his health deteriorating, the Black Prince returned to England in January 1371, where his father Edward III was elderly and also in poor health. The prince's illness was debilitating, and he died on 8 June 1376.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarber2004-57) Edward III died the following year on 21 June 1377[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod2008-58) and was succeeded by the Black Prince's second son [Richard II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_II "Richard II") who was still a child of 10 ([Edward of Angoulême](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_of_Angoul%C3%AAme "Edward of Angoulême"), the Black Prince's first son, had died sometime earlier).[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTETuck2004-59) The treaty of Brétigny had left Edward III and England with enlarged holdings in France, but a small professional French army under the leadership of du Guesclin pushed the English back; by the time Charles V died in 1380, the English held only Calais and a few other ports.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-vauchez283-60) It was usual to appoint a [regent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regent "Regent") in the case of a child monarch but no regent was appointed for Richard II, who nominally exercised the power of kingship from the date of his accession in 1377.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTETuck2004-59) Between 1377 and 1380, actual power was in the hands of a series of councils. The political community preferred this to a regency led by the king's uncle, [John of Gaunt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Gaunt "John of Gaunt"), although Gaunt remained highly influential.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTETuck2004-59) Richard faced many challenges during his reign, including the [Peasants' Revolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peasants%27_Revolt "Peasants' Revolt") led by [Wat Tyler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wat_Tyler "Wat Tyler") in 1381 and an Anglo-Scottish war in 1384–1385. His attempts to raise taxes, including [poll taxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poll_taxes_of_1376%E2%80%931381 "Poll taxes of 1376–1381"), to pay for his Scottish adventure and for the protection of Calais against the French made him increasingly unpopular.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTETuck2004-59) ##### 1380 campaign of the Earl of Buckingham \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=24 "Edit section: 1380 campaign of the Earl of Buckingham")\] In July 1380, the [Earl of Buckingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_of_Woodstock,_1st_Duke_of_Gloucester "Thomas of Woodstock, 1st Duke of Gloucester") commanded an expedition to France to aid England's ally, the [Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"). The French refused battle before the walls of [Troyes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troyes "Troyes") on 25 August; Buckingham's forces continued their _chevauchée_ and in November laid siege to [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes").[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption2012385%E2%80%93390,_396%E2%80%93399-61) The support expected from the Duke of Brittany did not appear and in the face of severe losses in men and horses, Buckingham was forced to abandon the siege in January 1381.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption2012409-62) In February, reconciled to the regime of the new French king [Charles VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_VI_of_France "Charles VI of France") by the [Treaty of Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_/(1381/) "Treaty of Guérande (1381)"), Brittany paid 50,000 francs to Buckingham for him to abandon the siege and the campaign.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption2012411-63) After the deaths of Charles V and du Guesclin in 1380, France lost its main leadership and overall momentum in the war. [Charles VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_VI_of_France "Charles VI of France") succeeded his father as king of France at the age of 11, and he was thus put under a regency led by his uncles, who managed to maintain an effective grip on government affairs until about 1388, well after Charles had achieved royal majority.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] With France facing widespread destruction, plague, and economic recession, high taxation put a heavy burden on the French peasantry and urban communities. The war effort against England largely depended on royal taxation, but the population was increasingly unwilling to pay for it, as would be demonstrated at the [Harelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harelle "Harelle") and Maillotin revolts in 1382. Charles V had abolished many of these taxes on his deathbed, but subsequent attempts to reinstate them stirred up hostility between the French government and populace.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Philip II of Burgundy, the uncle of the French king, brought together a Burgundian-French army and a fleet of 1,200 ships near the Zeeland town of [Sluis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sluis "Sluis") in the summer and autumn of 1386 to attempt an invasion of England, but this venture failed. However, Philip's brother [John of Berry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John,_Duke_of_Berry "John, Duke of Berry") appeared deliberately late, so that the autumn weather prevented the fleet from leaving and the invading army then dispersed again.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Difficulties in raising taxes and revenue hampered the ability of the French to fight the English. At this point, the war's pace had largely slowed down, and both nations found themselves fighting mainly through [proxy wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proxy_war "Proxy war"), such as during the [1383–1385 Portuguese interregnum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1383%E2%80%931385_Portuguese_interregnum "1383–1385 Portuguese interregnum"). The independence party in the [Kingdom of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Portugal "Kingdom of Portugal"), which was supported by the English, won against the supporters of the King of Castile's claim to the Portuguese throne, who in turn was backed by the French.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] ### Second peace: 1389–1415 \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=26 "Edit section: Second peace: 1389–1415")\] [![Image 17](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Apanages.svg/330px-Apanages.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Apanages.svg) France in 1388, just before signing a truce. English territories are shown in red, French royal territories are dark blue, papal territories are orange, and French vassals have the other colours. The war became increasingly unpopular with the English public due to the high taxes needed for the war effort. These taxes were seen as one of the reasons for the Peasants' Revolt.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBaker20006-64) Richard II's indifference to the war together with his preferential treatment of a select few close friends and advisors angered an alliance of lords that included [one of his uncles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_of_Woodstock,_1st_Duke_of_Gloucester "Thomas of Woodstock, 1st Duke of Gloucester"). This group, known as [Lords Appellant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lords_Appellant "Lords Appellant"), managed to press charges of treason against five of Richard's advisors and friends in the [Merciless Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merciless_Parliament "Merciless Parliament"). The Lords Appellant were able to gain control of the council in 1388 but failed to reignite the war in France. Although the will was there, the funds to pay the troops was lacking, so in the autumn of 1388 the Council agreed to resume negotiations with the French crown, beginning on 18 June 1389 with the signing of the three-year [Truce of Leulinghem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Leulinghem "Truce of Leulinghem").[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-65) In 1389, Richard's uncle and supporter, [John of Gaunt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Gaunt "John of Gaunt"), returned from Spain and Richard was able to rebuild his power gradually until 1397, when he reasserted his authority and destroyed\[_[specify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_\] the principal three among the Lords Appellant. In 1399, after John of Gaunt died, Richard II disinherited Gaunt's son, the exiled [Henry of Bolingbroke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_of_Bolingbroke "Henry of Bolingbroke"). Bolingbroke returned to England with his supporters, deposed Richard and had himself crowned Henry IV.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTETuck2004-59)[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-66) In Scotland, the problems brought in by the English regime change prompted border raids that were countered by an invasion in 1402 and the defeat of a Scottish army at the [Battle of Homildon Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Homildon_Hill "Battle of Homildon Hill").[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2008253%E2%80%93254-67) A dispute over the spoils between Henry and [Henry Percy, 1st Earl of Northumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Percy,_1st_Earl_of_Northumberland "Henry Percy, 1st Earl of Northumberland"), resulted in a long and bloody struggle between the two for control of northern England, resolved only with the almost complete destruction of the [House of Percy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Percy "House of Percy") by 1408.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-68) In Wales, [Owain Glyndŵr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owain_Glynd%C5%B5r "Owain Glyndŵr") was declared [Prince of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Wales "Prince of Wales") on 16 September 1400. He was the leader of the most serious and widespread [rebellion against England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Anglo-Welsh_wars "List of Anglo-Welsh wars") authority in Wales since the [conquest of 1282–1283](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_Wales_by_Edward_I_of_England "Conquest of Wales by Edward I of England"). In 1405, the French allied with Glyndŵr and the Castilians in Spain; a Franco-Welsh army advanced as far as [Worcester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worcester,_England "Worcester, England"), while the Spaniards used galleys to raid and burn all the way from [Cornwall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornwall "Cornwall") to [Southampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southampton "Southampton"), before taking refuge in [Harfleur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harfleur "Harfleur") for the winter.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-69) The [Glyndŵr Rising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glynd%C5%B5r_Rising "Glyndŵr Rising") was finally put down in 1415 and resulted in Welsh semi-independence for a number of years.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2008-70)\[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_\] [![Image 18](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Assassinat_louis_orleans.jpg/456px-Assassinat_louis_orleans.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Assassinat_louis_orleans.jpg) [Assassination of Louis I, Duke of Orléans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Louis_I,_Duke_of_Orl%C3%A9ans "Assassination of Louis I, Duke of Orléans"), in Paris in 1407 In 1392, [Charles VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_VI_of_France "Charles VI of France") suddenly descended into madness, forcing France into a regency dominated by his uncles and his brother. A conflict for control over the Regency began between his uncle [Philip the Bold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_the_Bold "Philip the Bold"), Duke of Burgundy and his brother, [Louis of Valois, Duke of Orléans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_of_Valois,_Duke_of_Orl%C3%A9ans "Louis of Valois, Duke of Orléans"). After Philip's death, his son and heir [John the Fearless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_the_Fearless "John the Fearless") continued the struggle against Louis but with the disadvantage of having no close relation to the king. Finding himself outmanoeuvred politically, John ordered the assassination of Louis in retaliation. His involvement in the murder was quickly revealed and the [Armagnac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armagnac_/(party/) "Armagnac (party)") family took political power in opposition to John. By 1410, both sides were bidding for the help of English forces in a civil war.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200277%E2%80%9382-71) In 1418 [Paris was taken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat_and_massacres_of_1418 "Paris coup d'état and massacres of 1418") by the Burgundians, who were unable to stop the massacre of [Count of Armagnac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_VII,_Count_of_Armagnac "Bernard VII, Count of Armagnac") and his followers by a Parisian crowd, with an estimated death toll between 1,000 and 5,000.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-72) Throughout this period, England confronted repeated raids by [pirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirate "Pirate") that damaged trade and the navy. There is some evidence that Henry IV used state-legalised piracy as a form of warfare in the English Channel. He used such [privateering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privateer "Privateer") campaigns to pressure enemies without risking open war.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-hattendorf76-73) The French responded in kind and French pirates, under Scottish protection, raided many English coastal towns.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-nolan424-74) The domestic and dynastic difficulties faced by England and France in this period quieted the war for a decade.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-nolan424-74) Henry IV died in 1413 and was replaced by his eldest son Henry V. The mental illness of Charles VI of France allowed his power to be exercised by royal princes whose rivalries caused deep divisions in France. In 1414 while Henry held court at [Leicester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leicester "Leicester"), he received ambassadors from Burgundy.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand2010-75) Henry accredited envoys to the French king to make clear his territorial claims in France; he also demanded the hand of Charles VI's youngest daughter [Catherine of Valois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_of_Valois "Catherine of Valois"). The French rejected his demands, leading Henry to prepare for war.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand2010-75) ### Resumption of the war under Henry V: 1415–1429 \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=27 "Edit section: Resumption of the war under Henry V: 1415–1429")\] #### Burgundian alliance and the seizure of Paris \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=28 "Edit section: Burgundian alliance and the seizure of Paris")\] ##### Battle of Agincourt (1415) \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=29 "Edit section: Battle of Agincourt (1415)")\] [![Image 19](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/Battle_of_Agincourt%2C_St._Alban%27s_Chronicle_by_Thomas_Walsingham.jpg/500px-Battle_of_Agincourt%2C_St._Alban%27s_Chronicle_by_Thomas_Walsingham.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Battle_of_Agincourt,_St._Alban%27s_Chronicle_by_Thomas_Walsingham.jpg) Fifteenth-century miniature depicting the [Battle of Agincourt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Agincourt "Battle of Agincourt") in October 1415 In August 1415, [Henry V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_V_of_England "Henry V of England") sailed from England with a force of about 10,500 and [laid siege to Harfleur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Harfleur "Siege of Harfleur"). The city resisted for longer than expected, but finally surrendered on 22 September. Because of the unexpected delay, most of the campaign season was gone. Rather than march on Paris directly, Henry elected to make a raiding expedition across France toward English-occupied Calais. In a campaign reminiscent of [Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cr%C3%A9cy "Crécy"), he found himself outmanoeuvred and low on supplies and had to fight a much larger French army at the [Battle of Agincourt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Agincourt "Battle of Agincourt"), north of the [Somme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somme_/(river/) "Somme (river)"). Despite the problems and having a smaller force, his victory was near total; the French defeat was catastrophic, costing the lives of many of the Armagnac leaders. About 40% of the French nobility was killed.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTETurchin2003179%E2%80%93180-76) Henry was apparently concerned that the large number of prisoners taken were a security risk (there were more French prisoners than there were soldiers in the entire English army) and he ordered their deaths before the French reserves fled the field and Henry rescinded the order.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand2010-75) ##### Treaty of Troyes (1420) \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=30 "Edit section: Treaty of Troyes (1420)")\] Henry retook much of Normandy, including Caen in 1417, and [Rouen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rouen "Rouen") on 19 January 1419, turning Normandy English for the first time in two centuries. A formal alliance was made with Burgundy, which had taken Paris in 1418 before the assassination of Duke [John the Fearless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_the_Fearless "John the Fearless") in 1419. In 1420, Henry met with King Charles VI. They signed the [Treaty of Troyes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Troyes "Treaty of Troyes"), by which Henry finally married Charles' daughter Catherine of Valois and Henry's heirs would inherit the throne of France. The Dauphin, [Charles VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_VII_of_France "Charles VII of France"), was declared illegitimate. Henry formally entered Paris later that year and the agreement was ratified by the [Estates-General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estates_General_/(France/) "Estates General (France)") ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _Les États-Généraux_).[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand2010-75) ##### Death of the Duke of Clarence (1421) \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=31 "Edit section: Death of the Duke of Clarence (1421)")\] [![Image 20](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/Clan_member_crest_badge_-_Clan_Carmichael.svg/250px-Clan_member_crest_badge_-_Clan_Carmichael.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Clan_member_crest_badge_-_Clan_Carmichael.svg) [Clan Carmichael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clan_Carmichael "Clan Carmichael") crest with a broken lance commemorating the unseating of the [Duke of Clarence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_of_Lancaster,_1st_Duke_of_Clarence "Thomas of Lancaster, 1st Duke of Clarence"), leading to his death at the [Battle of Baugé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Baug%C3%A9 "Battle of Baugé") On 22 March 1421 Henry V's progress in his French campaign experienced an unexpected reversal. Henry had left his brother and presumptive heir [Thomas, Duke of Clarence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas,_Duke_of_Clarence "Thomas, Duke of Clarence") in charge while he returned to England. The Duke of Clarence engaged a Franco-Scottish force of 5,000 men, led by [Gilbert Motier de La Fayette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_Motier_de_La_Fayette "Gilbert Motier de La Fayette") and [John Stewart, Earl of Buchan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Stewart,_Earl_of_Buchan "John Stewart, Earl of Buchan") at the [Battle of Baugé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Baug%C3%A9 "Battle of Baugé"). The Duke of Clarence, against the advice of his lieutenants, before his army had been fully assembled, attacked with a force of no more than 1,500 men-at-arms. Then, during the course of the battle, he led a charge of a few hundred men into the main body of the Franco-Scottish army, who quickly enveloped the English. In the ensuing mêlée, the Scot, John Carmichael of Douglasdale, broke his lance unhorsing the Duke of Clarence. Once on the ground, the duke was slain by [Alexander Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Alexander_Buchanan "Sir Alexander Buchanan").[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-77) The body of the Duke of Clarence was recovered from the field by [Thomas Montacute, 4th Earl of Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Montacute,_4th_Earl_of_Salisbury "Thomas Montacute, 4th Earl of Salisbury"), who conducted the English retreat.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarriss2010-78) Henry V returned to France and went to Paris, then visiting Chartres and Gâtinais before returning to Paris. From there, he decided to attack the Dauphin-held town of [Meaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meaux "Meaux"). It turned out to be more difficult to overcome than first thought. The siege began about 6 October 1421, and the town held for seven months before finally falling on 11 May 1422.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand2010-75) At the end of May, Henry was joined by his queen and together with the French court, they went to rest at [Senlis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senlis "Senlis"). While there, it became apparent that he was ill (possibly [dysentery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dysentery "Dysentery")), and when he set out to the Upper Loire, he diverted to the royal castle at Vincennes, near Paris, where he died on 31 August.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand2010-75) The elderly and insane Charles VI of France died two months later on 21 October. Henry left an only child, his nine-month-old son, [Henry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VI_of_England "Henry VI of England"), later to become Henry VI.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGriffiths2015-79) On his deathbed, as Henry VI was only an infant, Henry V had given the Duke of Bedford responsibility for English France. The war in France continued under Bedford's generalship and several battles were won. The English won an emphatic victory at the [Battle of Verneuil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Verneuil "Battle of Verneuil") (17 August 1424). At the Battle of Baugé, the Duke of Clarence had rushed into battle without the support of his archers; by contrast, at Verneuil the archers fought to devastating effect against the Franco-Scottish army. The effect of the battle was to virtually destroy the Dauphin's field army and to eliminate the Scots as a significant military force for the rest of the war.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-80) ### French victory: 1429–1453 \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=33 "Edit section: French victory: 1429–1453")\] #### Joan of Arc and French revival \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=34 "Edit section: Joan of Arc and French revival")\] [![Image 21](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Siege_orleans.jpg/500px-Siege_orleans.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Siege_orleans.jpg) The first Western image of a battle with cannon: the [Siege of Orléans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Orl%C3%A9ans "Siege of Orléans") in 1429. From _Les Vigiles de Charles VII_, [Bibliothèque nationale de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblioth%C3%A8que_nationale_de_France "Bibliothèque nationale de France"), Paris. The English laid [siege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege "Siege") to Orléans in October 1428, which created a stalemate for months. Food shortages within the city led to the likelihood that the city would be forced to surrender. In April 1429 [Joan of Arc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Arc "Joan of Arc") persuaded the Dauphin to send her to the siege, stating she had received visions from God telling her to drive out the English. She entered the city on April 29, after which the tide began to turn against the English within a matter of days.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGriffiths2015-79) She raised the morale of the troops, and they attacked the English [redoubts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redoubt "Redoubt"), forcing the English to lift the siege. Inspired by Joan, the French took several English strongholds on the Loire River.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavis200376%E2%80%9380-81) [![Image 22](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Contemporaine_afb_jeanne_d_arc.png/250px-Contemporaine_afb_jeanne_d_arc.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Contemporaine_afb_jeanne_d_arc.png) [Joan of Arc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Arc "Joan of Arc") pictured in 1429 The English retreated from the Loire Valley, pursued by a French army. Near the village of [Patay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Patay "Battle of Patay"), French cavalry broke through a unit of English longbowmen that had been sent to block the road, then swept through the retreating English army. The English lost 2,200 men, and the commander, [John Talbot, 1st Earl of Shrewsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Talbot,_1st_Earl_of_Shrewsbury "John Talbot, 1st Earl of Shrewsbury"), was taken prisoner. This victory opened the way for the Dauphin to march to [Reims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reims "Reims") for his coronation as Charles VII, on 16 July 1429.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavis200376%E2%80%9380-81)[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-nrofast-82) After the coronation, Charles VII's army fared less well. An attempted French [siege of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Paris_/(1429/) "Siege of Paris (1429)") was defeated on 8 September 1429, and Charles VII withdrew to the Loire Valley.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJaques2007777-83) #### Henry's coronations and the desertion of Burgundy \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=35 "Edit section: Henry's coronations and the desertion of Burgundy")\] [Henry VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VI_of_England "Henry VI of England") was crowned king of England at Westminster Abbey on 5 November 1429 and king of France at Notre-Dame, in Paris, on 16 December 1431.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGriffiths2015-79) Joan of Arc was captured by the Burgundians at the [siege of Compiègne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Compi%C3%A8gne "Siege of Compiègne") on 23 May 1430. The Burgundians then transferred her to the English, who organised a trial headed by [Pierre Cauchon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Cauchon "Pierre Cauchon"), Bishop of Beauvais and a collaborator with the English government who served as a member of the English Council at Rouen.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-84) Joan was convicted and burned at the stake on 30 May 1431[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavis200376%E2%80%9380-81) (she was rehabilitated 25 years later by [Pope Callixtus III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Callixtus_III "Pope Callixtus III")). After the death of Joan of Arc, the fortunes of war turned dramatically against the English.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1998145%E2%80%93147-85) Most of Henry's royal advisers were against making peace. Among the factions, the Duke of Bedford wanted to defend Normandy, the Duke of Gloucester was committed to just Calais, whereas [Cardinal Beaufort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Beaufort "Cardinal Beaufort") was inclined to peace. Negotiations stalled. It seems that at the [congress of Arras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Arras_/(1435/) "Treaty of Arras (1435)"), in the summer of 1435, where the duke of Beaufort was mediator, the English were unrealistic in their demands. A few days after the congress ended in September, [Philip the Good](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_the_Good "Philip the Good"), [duke of Burgundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Burgundy "Duke of Burgundy"), deserted to Charles VII, signing the [Treaty of Arras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Arras_/(1435/) "Treaty of Arras (1435)") that returned Paris to the King of France. This was a major blow to English sovereignty in France.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGriffiths2015-79) The Duke of Bedford died on 14 September 1435 and was later replaced by [Richard Plantagenet, 3rd Duke of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Plantagenet,_3rd_Duke_of_York "Richard Plantagenet, 3rd Duke of York").[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1998145%E2%80%93147-85) [![Image 23](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/Vigiles_du_roi_Charles_VII_32.jpg/500px-Vigiles_du_roi_Charles_VII_32.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vigiles_du_roi_Charles_VII_32.jpg) The French victory at the [Battle of Formigny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Formigny "Battle of Formigny") (1450) The allegiance of Burgundy remained fickle, but the Burgundian focus on expanding their domains in the Low Countries left them little energy to intervene in the rest of France.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1991562-86) The long truces that marked the war gave Charles time to centralise the French state and reorganise his army and government, replacing his feudal levies with a more modern professional army that could put its superior numbers to good use. A castle that once could only be captured after a prolonged siege would now fall after a few days from cannon bombardment. The French artillery developed a reputation as the best in the world.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1998145%E2%80%93147-85) By 1449, the French had retaken [Rouen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rouen "Rouen"). In 1450 the [Count of Clermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counts_of_Clermont-en-Beauvaisis "Counts of Clermont-en-Beauvaisis") and [Arthur de Richemont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_de_Richemont "Arthur de Richemont"), Earl of Richmond, of the Montfort family (the future [Arthur III, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "Arthur III, Duke of Brittany")), caught an English army attempting to relieve Caen and defeated it at the [Battle of Formigny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Formigny "Battle of Formigny") in 1450. Richemont's force attacked the English army from the flank and rear just as they were on the verge of beating Clermont's army.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTENicolle201226%E2%80%9335-87) #### French conquest of Gascony \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=37 "Edit section: French conquest of Gascony")\] [![Image 24](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/71/KarlVII.jpg/250px-KarlVII.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:KarlVII.jpg) [Charles "the Victorious"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_VII_of_France "Charles VII of France") by [Jean Fouquet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Fouquet "Jean Fouquet"). [Louvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvre "Louvre"), Paris. After Charles VII's successful Normandy campaign in 1450, he concentrated his efforts on Gascony, the last province held by the English. Bordeaux, Gascony's capital, was besieged and surrendered to the French on 30 June 1451. Largely due to the English sympathies of the Gascon people, this was reversed when John Talbot and his army retook the city on 23 October 1452. However, the English were decisively defeated at the [Battle of Castillon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Castillon "Battle of Castillon") on 17 July 1453. Talbot had been persuaded to engage the French army at Castillon near Bordeaux. During the battle the French appeared to retreat towards their camp. The French camp at Castillon had been laid out by Charles VII's ordinance officer [Jean Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Bureau "Jean Bureau") and this was instrumental in the French success as when the French cannon opened fire, from their positions in the camp, the English took severe casualties losing both Talbot and his son.[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200679-88) Although the Battle of Castillon is considered the last battle of the Hundred Years' War,[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200679-88) England and France remained formally at war for another 20 years, but the English were in no position to carry on the war as they faced unrest at home. Bordeaux fell to the French on 19 October and there were no more hostilities afterwards. Following defeat in the Hundred Years' War, English landowners complained vociferously about the financial losses resulting from the loss of their continental holdings; this is often considered a major cause of the [Wars of the Roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Roses "Wars of the Roses") that started in 1455.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1998145%E2%80%93147-85)[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-webster39-89) The Hundred Years' War almost resumed in 1474, when the duke [Charles of Burgundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Burgundy "Charles of Burgundy"), counting on English support, [took up arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgundian_Wars "Burgundian Wars") against [Louis XI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XI "Louis XI"). Louis managed to isolate the Burgundians by buying [Edward IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_IV "Edward IV") of England off with a large cash sum and an annual pension, in the [Treaty of Picquigny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Picquigny "Treaty of Picquigny") (1475). The treaty formally ended the Hundred Years' War with Edward renouncing his claim to the throne of France. Kings of England (and later of Great Britain) continued to [claim the title](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_claims_to_the_French_throne "English claims to the French throne") until 1803, when they were dropped in deference to the exiled Count of Provence, titular King [Louis XVIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XVIII "Louis XVIII"), who was living in England after the [French Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution "French Revolution").[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTENeillands2001290%E2%80%93291-90) ### Historical significance \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=40 "Edit section: Historical significance")\] [![Image 25](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/Map_France_1477-en.svg/250px-Map_France_1477-en.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Map_France_1477-en.svg) Burgundian territories (orange/yellow) and limits of France (red) after the Burgundian War The French victory marked the end of a long period of instability that had begun with the [Norman Conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Conquest "Norman Conquest") (1066), when [William the Conqueror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_the_Conqueror "William the Conqueror") added "King of England" to his titles, becoming both the vassal to (as Duke of Normandy) and the equal of (as king of England) the king of France.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJanvrinRawlinson201615-91) When the war ended, England was bereft of its continental possessions, leaving it with only Calais on the Continent (until 1558). The war destroyed the English dream of a joint monarchy and led to the rejection in England of all things French, although the [Anglo-Norman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Norman_language "Anglo-Norman language"), which had served as the language of the ruling classes and commerce there from the time of the Norman conquest, left its mark in English vocabulary. English became the official language in 1362 and French was no longer used for teaching from 1385.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJanvrinRawlinson201616-92) National feeling that emerged from the war unified both France and England further. Despite the devastation on its soil, the Hundred Years' War accelerated the process of transforming France from a feudal monarchy to a centralised state.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolmesSchutz194861-93) In England the political and financial troubles which emerged from the defeat were a major cause of the [Wars of the Roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Roses "Wars of the Roses") (1455–1487).[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-webster39-89) [![Image 26](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Bubonic_plague_map.PNG/250px-Bubonic_plague_map.PNG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bubonic_plague_map.PNG) The spread of the [Black Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death "Black Death") (with modern borders) Historian Ben Lowe argued in 1997 that opposition to the war helped to shape England's early modern political culture. Although anti-war and pro-peace spokesmen generally failed to influence outcomes at the time, they had a long-term impact. England showed decreasing enthusiasm for conflict deemed not in the national interest, yielding only losses in return for high economic burdens. In comparing this English cost-benefit analysis with French attitudes, given that both countries suffered from weak leaders and undisciplined soldiers, Lowe noted that the French understood that warfare was necessary to expel the foreigners occupying their homeland. French kings found alternative ways to finance the war – sales taxes, debasing the coinage – and were less dependent than the English on tax levies passed by national legislatures. English anti-war critics thus had more to work with than the French.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-94) A 2021 theory about the early formation of [state capacity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_capacity "State capacity") is that interstate war was responsible for initiating a strong move toward states implementing tax systems with higher state capabilities. For example, see France in the Hundred Years' War, when the English occupation threatened the independent French Kingdom. The king and his ruling elite demanded consistent and permanent taxation, which would allow a [standing army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standing_army "Standing army") to be financed. The French nobility, which had always opposed such an extension of state capacity, agreed in this exceptional situation. The inter-state war with England increased French state capability.[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-95) Bubonic [plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plague_/(disease/) "Plague (disease)") and warfare reduced population numbers throughout Europe during this period. France lost half its population during the Hundred Years' War,[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTETurchin2003179%E2%80%93180-76) with [Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normandy "Normandy") reduced by three-quarters and Paris by two-thirds.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELadurie198732-96) During the same period, England's population fell by 20 to 33 percent.[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTENeillands2001110%E2%80%93111-97) ### Military significance \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hundred_Years%27_War&action=edit§ion=41 "Edit section: Military significance")\] French success in the [Caroline war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War,_1369%E2%80%931389 "Hundred Years' War, 1369–1389") had been largely driven by a professional standing army that [Charles V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V_of_France "Charles V of France") had been able to create and finance in the aftermath of the disastrous experience with the mercenary [routiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_company "Free company") who had pillaged much of the country after the 1360 [peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Bretigny "Treaty of Bretigny"). This force, the first standing army in post-Roman western Europe, had been disbanded in the tumultuous regency period after 1380.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-98) [Charles VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_VII_of_France "Charles VII of France") reestablished a permanent standing army in 1445 with the _[Compagnies d'ordonnance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compagnies_d%27ordonnance "Compagnies d'ordonnance")_ which would survive until eventually replaced by the [gendarmerie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gendarme_/(historical/) "Gendarme (historical)") system in the 17th century.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-roman-99) The professional units gave the French a considerable strategic advantage as well as an edge in professionalism and discipline, being composed of paid full-time soldiers, at a time when levies could only be fielded for limited periods of time and the allegiances of the aristocratic knights could often shift to the opposing side. The standing armies of both Charles V and Charles VII had approximately 6,000 men, divided to many companies of cavalrymen.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-RolandPreston1991-100) The Hundred Years' War was a time of rapid military evolution. Weapons, tactics, army structure and the social meaning of war all changed, partly in response to the war's costs, partly through advancement in technology and partly through lessons that [warfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warfare "Warfare") taught. The feudal system slowly disintegrated as well as the concept of chivalry. By the war's end, although the heavy cavalry was still considered the most powerful unit in an army, the heavily armoured horse had to deal with several tactics developed to deny or mitigate its effective use on a battlefield.[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPowicke2009189-101) The English began using lightly armoured mounted troops, known as [hobelars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hobelar "Hobelar") whose tactics had been developed against the Scots, in the Anglo-Scottish wars of the 14th century. Hobelars rode smaller unarmoured horses, enabling them to move through difficult or boggy terrain where heavier cavalry would struggle. Rather than fight while seated on the horse, they would dismount to engage the enemy.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-RolandPreston1991-100)[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War#cite_note-rogers267-102) The closing battle of the war, the [Battle of Castillon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Castillon "Battle of Castillon"), was the first major battle won through the extensive use of [field 18.title: VGhlIFdhciBvZiB0aGUgQnJldG9uIFN1Y2Nlc3Npb24gb3IgV2FyIG9mIHRoZSBUd28gSmVhbm5lcw==
18.content:
What better way for the experienced reenactor and the one just taking their first steps into living history than with ready-made costume and armour sets? If you have to dive into the first third of the XIVth century and just need to look cool and dignified, then we have gorgeous, luxurious, stylish and, most importantly - fully finished gambesons of the relevant period. Or maybe - complete sets of costume and armour, from the undershirt to the plume on the helmet.

Our inspiration and source after the [Battle of Poitiers](https://steel-mastery.com/battle-of-poitiers?fbclid=IwAR19LrTcncXQOMKS5F_Nm5XfyxZQfCo-ebXtA21RA0c_bqvpH5f9hFT2srA) was such a stage of the Hundred Years' War called the War of the Breton Succession. Why that one in particular? Well, apart from the fact that it's its turn chronologically, the story itself is amazingly entertaining and the gambesons came out just amazing.

**Now, the gambesons...**

We're sure you recognise the [Charles de Blois gambeson](https://steel-mastery.com/arming-doublet-aketon-1360-year.html), even in the white linen with black ermine print. What we particularly love dear Charles for is not only his participation in the events below in a major role, but also the fact that his authentic gambeson has survived. You can find it in [The Textile Arts and Decorative Arts Museum](https://www.museedestissus.fr/), Lyon, France. Well, we happily and thankfully use it as an inspiration and source for many of our [gambesons](https://steel-mastery.com/gambesons), including this ones. As for the ermine print on the fabric, we can only remind you that it is the coat of arms of the Duchy of Brittany.

![Image 1](https://steel-mastery.com/image/catalog/Battle-of-Poitiers/_DSC0262.jpg)

The second white gambeson is also inspired by Charles's gambeson, but has been slightly modified by our fashion designers to embody the image of Jeanne la Flamme, who fought on the other side. It features a double print - still the same black ermine on one half and a black rampant two-tailed lion on the other.

![Image 2](https://steel-mastery.com/image/catalog/Battle-of-Poitiers/0b69-7768Women's_gambeson-0-1.jpg)

**An ermine and a lion**

So why an ermine and a lion? This marvellous story began when Arthur II Capet-Dreux de Bretagne, Duke of Brittany married twice. Times were hard, and his first wife died giving Arthur 3 sons: Jean III de Bretagne - heir to the Duchy, Guy VII de Limoges and Pierre of Avesnes. Well, when his wife died, Arthur remarried and his second wife gave him 6 more children: Jean de Montfort, Béatrix de Hédé, Jeanne de Bretagne, Alix de Bretagne, Blanche de Bretagne and Marie de Bretagne. We are interested in the eldest of these six, Jean de Montfort. When the prolific father Arthur died, his eldest son Jean III de Bretagne became Duke but he was childless. Shit happens. But the Duchy of Brittany throne was in need of an heir. As Jean’s III brothers died early enough and, by law, his half-brother Jean de Montfort was to inherit. But as it happened, one Jean didn't like the other one. He didn't like the other one so much that he even tried to prove in court that his father's second marriage was illegitimate and his children from that marriage were bastards. But that attempt was unsuccessful. And when it came to choosing a successor, Jean III de Bretagne thought a little and wrote a will in favour of his niece Jeanne de Penthièvre, known as duchesse de Bretagne or simply - Joan the Lame. But towards the end of his life he seems to have reconciled with his younger brother and made a more traditional will in favour of Jean de Montfort. Well, sort of reconciled and sort of made a will, but only sort of. When the Duke was dying, and he was pestered by his peers with the question of who was the heir after all, he replied, "Don't you dare trouble my spirit with such questions before I die!" and died. That's right, he just died without answering the sacramental question. Why? Fuck You... That's Why! (с)

So in 1341 the Duchy of Brittany was left with two heirs: Joan the Lame and her uncle Jean de Montfort. As you can guess, each of them had their own supporters and arguments as to their claim to the Duchy's throne.

**Charles of Blois' ermine gambeson**

Of particular interest to us personally is the fact that Jeanne the Lame at the time was already married to... drumroll... Charles of Blois - a man and a gambeson! Yes, that's him in the fancy ermine gambeson. Handsome, isn't he? And as well as being the nephew of the then French King Phillip VI. As you might guess, the King of France was very keen that the Duchy of Breton should go to his nephew. That's why our version of the famous gambeson is decorated with the coat of arms of Brittany (black ermine on a white field), because Charles really, really wanted to rule the Duchy of Brittany. And he fought hard for this title while his limp-wristed wife Jeanne sat at home and bore him heirs. After all, her uncle's example is a good example of the fact that it is better to have children of your own, so as not to look for heirs later on among your relatives. Because having heirs was a serious argument in such a dispute.

**Jeanne la Flamme’s ermine and lion gambeson**

Regarding the gambeson with lion and ermine, it embodies the second side of the war for Breton succession - wife of Jean de Montfor Joanna of Flanders, Duchess of Brittany, better known as Jeanne la Flamme. Brittany's ermines complemented here with the Montfor family's coat of arms - a rampant two-tailed lion. While an amazing and beautiful woman in a gorgeous gambeson was one of the famous warriors of the Hundred Years' War. Seriously, in those wild chauvinistic times she commanded town defences and combat raids. So the War of the Breton Succession also went down in history as the War of the Two Jeannes.

**War of the Two Jeannes**

Going back to history - when Jean de Montfort realized that he was unlikely to get his rights recognized by the French king (because he was not his nephew), he decided to appeal to another king - Edward III of England as King of France. You do remember that the King of England also had a claim to the French throne and started the Hundred Years War on that very occasion, don't you? Well, Jean de Montfort paid the King of England (and France according to his own version) vassal oath, and the war over the Breton succession turned into an interstate conflict, continuing the Hundred Years' War.

It must be said that at the beginning of the conflict, luck was on the side of Joan the Lame and Charles of Blois. Indeed, in 1341 there was still an armistice between England and France, and Edward III of England could not send troops to help Jean de Montfort. In 1345 Jean de Montfort died, and his widow Joanna of Flanders became the Montfort party leader. Seriously, this woman did not just sit back and bear children. Oh no! She donned armour, took up arms and urged the other ladies to "cut their skirts and take their safety in their own hands" and personally led the defence of Hennebont. Moreover, she guided the soldiers in an attack outside the town walls and burned down the enemy’s camp. It was after this that she became known as Jeanne la Flamme, and not only for her fiery character and inflammatory speeches before the defenders of the city. Froissart described her as a lady "with the heart of a lion, and in her hand she wielded a sharp glaive, wherewith she fought fiercely". During another attack, when her troops were frightened and retreated, this lady turned her horse and galloped towards the enemy herself. Her knights were then ashamed and joined the attack, following the intrepid Jeanne. Defending the rights of her son John V to the Breton succession, she continued the war. In 1347, Jeanne la Flamme's troops even captured Charles of Blois in battle. She later, however, had to escape to England where she was declared insane under unexplained circumstances and locked up in Tickhill Castle for the rest of her life. She died there in 1374. It must be said that she outlived the other three war participants. For while her husband Jean de Montfort died in 1345, Charles of Blois in 1364 and his wife Joan the Lame in 1365.

The War of the Breton Succession itself lasted until 1364. Although much of the time luck in this war was with Charles of Blois, after his death by the treaty of Guérande in 1365, Jeanne la Flamme and Jean de Montfort son John V was recognized as the rightful Duke of Brittany and had married Mary Plantagenet, daughter of Edward III of England. And then...

And then there were many more interesting and enlightening stories, both in Brittany and elsewhere. And we'll tell you about them in the next parts. Stay tuned :)

Author: Katarina Ziborova, writer, reenactor [https://www.facebook.com/katarina.ustymenko](https://www.facebook.com/katarina.ustymenko)

Izickaa Tonya, re-enactor [https://www.facebook.com/antoninaizickaa](https://www.facebook.com/antoninaizickaa)

23.title: V2FyIG9mIHRoZSBCcmV0b24gU3VjY2Vzc2lvbg==
23.content:
If you are looking for the page with the statistics about this event you can find it here:[All Statistics](https://phersu-atlas.com/metrics_summary/event/5144.html)

Was a conflict between the Counts of Blois and the Montforts of Brittany for control of the Sovereign Duchy of Brittany, then a fief of the Kingdom of France. The conflict became also a proxy war between England and France.

Chronology
----------

* * *

Interactive Chronologies with maps are available in the section [Changes Navigation](https://phersu-atlas.com/data/event_changes/5144)

*   _April 1365:_ In 1365, under the first Treaty of Guérande, the king of France recognized John IV, the son of John of Montfort, as duke of Brittany.
*   _June 1342:_ Battle of Quimperlé.
*   _January 1345:_ Victorious siege of the city of Quimper by Charles of Blois in 1344.
*   _May 1342:_ Battle of Quimperlé.
*   _August 1352:_ Battle of Mauron.
*   _January 1343:_ Siege of Vannes.
*   _June 1345:_ Battle of Cadoret.
*   _October 1341:_ Battle of Champtoceaux: John of Montfort, the leader of one faction, was made prisoner.
*   _September 1364:_ Battle of Auray.
*   _June 1342:_ The Siege of Hennebont in 1342 was part of the Breton War of Succession. The town was defended by Jeanne de Clisson and her husband Olivier de Clisson against the forces of Charles of Blois, who claimed the Duchy of Brittany. The siege was ultimately unsuccessful, with the town holding out until the arrival of reinforcements.
*   _June 1341:_ John de Montfort settled in Nantes, the capital of the Duchy of Brittany, and seized the ducal treasury at Limoges.
*   _August 1341:_ Jean de Montfort carried out a great ride in his duchy to secure control of the strongholds (Rennes, Malestroit, Vannes, Pontivy, Hennebont, Quimperlé, La Roche-Piriou, Quimper, Brest, Saint-Brieuc, Dinan and Mauron).
*   _May 1342:_ Meanwhile the French took Rennes.
*   _July 1342:_ The Siege of Hennebont in 1342 was part of the Breton War of Succession. The town was defended by Jeanne de Clisson and her husband Olivier de Clisson against the forces of Charles of Blois, who was supported by the French crown. The siege ended with the town successfully holding out and the territory going to Montfort County.
*   _September 1342:_ Battle of Morlaix.
*   _October 1342:_ Battle of Morlaix.
*   _June 1346:_ Battle of Saint-Pol-de-Léon.
*   _July 1346:_ Battle of Saint-Pol-de-Léon.
*   _April 1354:_ Battle of Montmuran.
*   _May 1354:_ Battle of Montmuran.
*   _July 1357:_ Siege of Rennes.

From 1370 to his death, he was Constable of France for King Charles V. Well known for his Fabian strategy, he took part in six pitched battles and won the four in which he held command. _**(Intro from Wikipedia)**_ **January(?) 1(?), 1320 - Motte-Broon, Brittany -** Bertrand du Guesclin is born. [![Image 1: War of the Breton Succession - Wikipedia](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!D4Pr!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7936b0f0-688a-498f-90fd-9a368f21eb28_565x364.jpeg)](https://medievalstudies.thinkific.com/courses/hundred-years-war)

I once heard that the Hundred Years’ War broke out because the French court mocked the English king’s accent so ruthlessly that it prompted him to declare war. Vanity, however, was not the cause of the Hundred Years’ War, nor was the other often cited trope: the succession to the French crown. The truth is actually far stranger.

You see, on the eve of the outbreak of war in 1337, Edward III had not yet claimed the French crown; nor would he do so for another three years. He even paid homage to the new French king, Phillip VI, in 1329, putting the matter to proverbial bed. This tells us that contesting the French crown was not the original motivating factor behind his first campaign in France (though it did later become a matter of political expediency). Instead, modern historians have come to agree that the war had its roots in French aggression.

England and France had fought several small-scale wars in the preceding decades, many of which involved England’s claim to the region of Aquitaine through their Angevin line. King Phillip VI decided to settle this long-standing matter, which was a frequent source of costly conflicts, by simply annexing it in 1337. Edward was none too pleased.

Now, there was a succession controversy that rocked France in 1328, and it needs to be mentioned. Edward did have a claim to the French throne on his mother’s side, and in English law, that would have given him a fighting chance to become king. However, French law did not permit kings to come from the female line, so Edward was denied the right to petition. Given that Edward was sixteen or so when this all happened, it’s hard to say whether he truly understood what was at stake, and he did not press the issue. He did, however, keep the resentment in his back pocket for later.

It could be said that part of Phillip’s motivation to annex Aquitaine stemmed from the earlier succession struggle. Some historians have proposed he was peeved that Edward even tried to contest him. In truth, his reasons were more economic, and I discuss those factors further [in my course on the Hundred Years' War](https://medievalstudies.thinkific.com/courses/hundred-years-war).

The first years of the war followed the same unremarkable cadence of the wars of the previous eighty years. A few sea battles, clashes in Flanders and Aquitaine, and a meandering campaign in northern France did little to impress. What's more, wars at the time were expensive and slow, and for monarchs whose revenue systems were still shaky at best (France was even considered to have been in an economic depression), even these small, unimpressive engagements took their toll. By 1340, Edward and Phillip signed their first truce to allow time to refill their war chests.

Had nothing else happened, the war might have ended there. Each monarch might have gone his separate way, and historians might have chalked up the conflict as another one for the books. But it would not be so. No, a small, irreducible region in Western France was sitting on a time bomb that would fan the flames of war for the next 123 years. Brittany, still a semi-independent duchy that played both sides in the conflict between France and England, experienced its own succession struggle. The trouble was, despite their semi-independence, their nobility was intermarried with half the continent.

When Duke John III of Brittany died on 30 April 1341, he had no clear successor. Two claimants emerged: Charles of Blois and John of Montfort. Charles’ claim stemmed from his marriage to Joan of Penthièvre, the niece of Duke John III and the daughter of his younger brother, Guy. John’s claim stemmed from his being Duke John III’s half-brother, making his a male-line claim.

Now, Charles had a slight advantage insofar as he was also Phillip VI’s nephew. Naturally, Phillip supported his claim. But herein lay the incendiary problem: Edward had been denied a right to claim the throne of France because Capetian Salic Law did not allow succession through the female line. But Phillip was now pressing his advantage in Brittany despite Charles having a claim through a woman. Edward, of course, took great offense to Phillip’s hypocritical move, and that festering resentment over the female succession controversy took hold. He thus supported John.

However, he did so not just out of principle, but also because there were a lot of damn sheep at stake. Forgive my expletive, but sheep were really important. How important? They were so immensely, tremendously, stupendously valuable that any shift in who controlled them stood to become the next hegemon of Western Europe. And they powered England’s war machine. Wool from England was sent to the Low Countries to be spooled, refined, and dyed, and then sent to France to feed its textile industry, which sold into the rest of the world. At the time, the textile industry was THE defining industry of the European economy, akin to today’s AI giants as a share of the global economy.

Therefore, whoever controlled Brittany, a net wool exporter, stood to gain substantially. And they might use those gains for…you know…more wars. Moreover, Edward had taken massive loans against England’s wool exports to fund his war effort, and adding Brittany as a vassal would help him make his interest payments. Brittany possessed other valuable assets as well, including strategic ports that ensured the movement of goods and troops between England and Aquitaine, as well as commodities such as salt. Phillip’s hypocrisy was one thing, but the chance for Edward to wrestle away one of Phillip’s most critical vassals was something completely different.

The War of Breton Succession thus poured rocket fuel on an already smoldering fire, leading to the renewed outbreak of hostilities between England and France that would persist long after everyone involved was dead. Still, it’s neat to think that the small region of Brittany, which the Romans had considered a waste of space (the peninsula was depopulated during the Gallo-Roman period), was in large part responsible for turning the broader conflict we today call the Hundred Years’ War into something more than a mere continuation of the sporadic disputes of the previous century.
