**Joan of Penthièvre** ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _Jeanne_; c. 1319 – 10 September 1384), sometimes called **Joan the Lame**, reigned as [Duchess of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchess_of_Brittany "Duchess of Brittany") together with her husband, [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois"), between 1341 and 1364. Her ducal claims were contested by the [House of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montfort_of_Brittany "Montfort of Brittany"), which prevailed only after an extensive civil war, the [War of the Breton Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession "War of the Breton Succession"). After the war, Joan remained titular Duchess of Brittany to her death. She was [Countess of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counts_and_dukes_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Counts and dukes of Penthièvre") in her own right throughout her life.

Joan was the only child of [Guy of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Guy of Penthièvre") (brother of [John III, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany")) and Joan of Avaugour.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990372-1) Through her father she became Countess of Penthièvre in [her own right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Her_own_right "Her own right") and established her ducal claims.

War of the Breton Succession
----------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: War of the Breton Succession")\]

Joan was one of the protagonists of the [War of the Breton Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession "War of the Breton Succession"). The issue of succession to the ducal crown would involve the issue of whether a child could, regardless of gender, claim the right of "representation" of a deceased parent, and Joan would then inherit her father's rights as the second brother of the late [Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Brittany "Duke of Brittany"), or the next eldest male heir in a partially-parallel lineage outranked all others. In the Breton succession, the collateral claimant was Joan's half-uncle [John, Count of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort"), born from the second marriage of Joan's grandfather [Arthur II, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "Arthur II, Duke of Brittany") to [Yolande of Dreux, Queen of Scots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yolande_of_Dreux,_Queen_of_Scots "Yolande of Dreux, Queen of Scots"). Joan's uncle John III had been alienated from Yolande, his stepmother, and sought to prevent his half-brother John from succeeding him, which included an abortive attempt to annul his father's second marriage and so render his half-siblings illegitimate.[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre#cite_note-3)

In December 1335, negotiations were made for a marriage between Joan and [John of Eltham, Earl of Cornwall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Eltham,_Earl_of_Cornwall "John of Eltham, Earl of Cornwall"), the brother of King [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England");[\[b\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre#cite_note-5) however, it appears that the arrangements did not result in an official betrothal. In 1337, Joan was betrothed to [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois") in Paris, and they were living together by 1338 or 1339.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraham-Goering202040-6) In 1341, on the death of John III, the couple assumed the rule of the [Duchy of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brittany "Duchy of Brittany"), Charles having been granted permission to perform homage by King [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") by the _arrêt_ of [Conflans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conflans-Sainte-Honorine "Conflans-Sainte-Honorine") on 7 September 1341. They appeared to be supported by most of the local nobility and administration. However, John of Montfort did not agree to let go of his own claim, and war ensued.[\[c\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre#cite_note-7) Ironically, while the initial argument of the _Montfortist cause_ actually relied very strongly on the idea that Brittany should follow French successorial practice, subsequent generations the line would vigorously enforce the notion that the Duchy of Brittany should remain independent from its royal neighbour.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones19724-8)

When Joan's half-uncle John died in 1345 during the succession war, his wife, [Joanna of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), took arms to protect the rights of their son [John IV the Conqueror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany") from the party led by Joan and her husband, Charles. Joanna organized [resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resistance_movement "Resistance movement") and used diplomatic means to protect her family's position.[\[d\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre#cite_note-9)

After those initial successes, Joan's husband, Charles of Blois, was taken prisoner by the English in 1347. [Thomas Dagworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Dagworth "Thomas Dagworth") was the official captor of her husband.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers2005127-10) Charles was released nine years afterwards for a ransom of about half a million [écus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89cu "Écu") and resumed the war against the Montforts. Charles died in the [Battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray"), which determined the end of the war and the victory of the Montforts, leaving Joan a widow.[\[e\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre#cite_note-11)

The contest between the two claimants was then settled in 1365 by the [First Treaty of Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_/(1365/) "Treaty of Guérande (1365)"), whose terms had Joan receive a substantial pension (payments of which continued until 1372) in compensation for her claims, the right to maintain the ducal title for life and all her family lands of Penthièvre and Avaugour and an exemption from homage to the new duke for those territories. Most critically for future events, her male heirs would recover the duchy if John IV had no male posterity, and women were now formally prohibited from inheriting the duchy.

In 1379, when John IV had been forced into exile in England, King [Charles V of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V_of_France "Charles V of France") attempted to annex Brittany to the French royal domain. Joan was shocked by the violation of her her sons' rights, as laid out in the Treaty of Guérande. Both her supporters and those of the Montfort line united to invite John IV back from his exile in England and retake control of the duchy.

After the death of Charles V, she ratified on 2 May 1381 the Second Treaty of Guérande, which essentially reinstated the terms of the First Treaty. From the legal perspective of the Treaties of Guérande, the issue of succession to the ducal crown appeared settled, but Joan's descendants provoked various conflicts with John IV and future dukes from the House of Montfort.

Joan died on 10 September 1384 and was buried at the church of the Friars Minor of [Guingamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guingamp "Guingamp").

Joan had lost the ducal title and powers of Brittany for her descendants, and despite attempts to reclaim the ducal crown the loss was permanent. However, her descendants were appointed from time to time to high administrative posts in Brittany under the future Kings of France. Her title and rights as Countess of Penthièvre were inherited, only to be lost from time to time to the Duke of Brittany, as her descendants continued their conflicts with the House of Montfort.

Joan and Charles had the following children:

*   Marguerite, married in 1351 [Charles de la Cerda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_la_Cerda "Charles de la Cerda") (d. 1354)
*   [Marie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_of_Blois,_Duchess_of_Anjou "Marie of Blois, Duchess of Anjou") (c.1340–1404),[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraham-Goering202033-12) Lady of [Guise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guise "Guise"), married in 1360 [Louis I, Duke of Anjou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_I,_Duke_of_Anjou "Louis I, Duke of Anjou")
*   [John I, Count of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I,_Count_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "John I, Count of Penthièvre") (1345–1404)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones1995486-13) - also known as John of Blois
*   Guy (d. 1385)
*   Henry (d. 1400)
*   Charles (d. before 1364)

1.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre#cite_ref-3)** The issue of 'representative' versus 'cadet' inheritance[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilkinson2000108-2) was related also to the question of whether the ducal line of Brittany would adhere to French royal tradition (cadet succession) or its own local custom (representative).
2.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre#cite_ref-5)** Edward III appointed "_Willielmi d´Aubeneye militis et Joannis Caupegorge_" as proxies to negotiate the marriage between "_Joannem comitem Cornubiæ fratrem nostrum_" and "_Johannam filiam Guidonis de Britannia neptem et hæredem \[Johanne Duce Britanniæ consanguineo nostro\]_" by a charter dated 31 December 1335.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre#cite_note-4)
3.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre#cite_ref-7)** The reverberating theme in the history of Brittany has been its strong preference for independence. See, for example, the expression of that theme in the life of [Francis II, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "Francis II, Duke of Brittany").
4.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre#cite_ref-9)** Supposedly, in the [Siege of Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont "Siege of Hennebont"), an isolated account states that she took up arms and, dressed in armour, conducted the defence of the town. In that version, Joanna even led a raid of knights outside the walls that successfully set fire to and destroyed one of the enemy's rear camps. She then popularly became known as "Jeanne la Flamme". However, Joanna was eventually forced to retreat to England, where she became [mentally ill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mentally_ill "Mentally ill"), which her young son in the care of the English court. Joan and Charles now controlled most of the Duchy of Brittany.
5.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre#cite_ref-11)** His supporters led a movement to canonise him as a saint for his devotion to religion, but despite the apparent support of Pope [Gregory XI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregory_XI "Gregory XI"), no final canonisation was achieved. He was eventually beatified in 1904.

**Charles** (born 1319—died Sept. 29, 1364, Auray, Fr.) was a [rival](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/rival) [duke](https://www.britannica.com/topic/duke) of Brittany, a son of the French king [Philip VI’s](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Philip-VI) sister Margaret.

Quick Facts

Byname:

Charles Of Blois

_(Show more)_

Born:

1319

_(Show more)_

Died:

_(Show more)_

Role In:

[Combat of the Thirty](https://www.britannica.com/event/Combat-of-the-Thirty)

[War of the Breton Succession](https://www.britannica.com/event/War-of-the-Breton-Succession)

_(Show more)_

[See all related content](https://www.britannica.com/facts/Charles-duke-of-Brittany)

Show More

Charles’s claim to Brittany through his marriage to Joan the Lame of Penthièvre, niece of Duke [John III](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-III-duke-of-Brittany) of Brittany, led to a conflict with the other claimants, [John of](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-IV-duke-of-Brittany-died-1345) Montfort and later his son Duke John IV of Brittany, in the 20-year War of the Breton Succession, which also involved the kings of England and [France](https://www.britannica.com/place/France). When John of Montfort began to win most of Brittany, Charles appealed to Philip, who had the peers of France recognize Charles as sole heir to the duchy; meanwhile, John had sought the aid of [Edward III](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Edward-III-king-of-England) of England. On Nov. 1, 1341, Charles seized the city of Nantes and imprisoned John for four years. When Edward attacked Nantes, Pope [Clement VI](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Clement-VI) intervened in 1343 to conclude a truce. The war was renewed, however, and Charles was captured at La Roche-Derrien in January 1347 and incarcerated in the Tower of London; he paid a [ransom](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/ransom) and promised to hold Brittany, under vassalage to Edward. On July 12, 1363, Charles finally agreed on a partition of Brittany with Duke [John IV](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-IV-duke-of-Brittany-1340-1399) of Brittany but was persuaded by his wife to break the treaty. At the [Battle of Auray](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Battle-of-Auray) (Sept. 29, 1364), Charles was killed and his army defeated.

This article was most recently revised and updated by [Encyclopaedia Britannica](https://www.britannica.com/contributor/encyclopaedia-britannica/12989892).

What better way for the experienced reenactor and the one just taking their first steps into living history than with ready-made costume and armour sets? If you have to dive into the first third of the XIVth century and just need to look cool and dignified, then we have gorgeous, luxurious, stylish and, most importantly - fully finished gambesons of the relevant period. Or maybe - complete sets of costume and armour, from the undershirt to the plume on the helmet.

Our inspiration and source after the [Battle of Poitiers](https://steel-mastery.com/battle-of-poitiers?fbclid=IwAR19LrTcncXQOMKS5F_Nm5XfyxZQfCo-ebXtA21RA0c_bqvpH5f9hFT2srA) was such a stage of the Hundred Years' War called the War of the Breton Succession. Why that one in particular? Well, apart from the fact that it's its turn chronologically, the story itself is amazingly entertaining and the gambesons came out just amazing.

**Now, the gambesons...**

We're sure you recognise the [Charles de Blois gambeson](https://steel-mastery.com/arming-doublet-aketon-1360-year.html), even in the white linen with black ermine print. What we particularly love dear Charles for is not only his participation in the events below in a major role, but also the fact that his authentic gambeson has survived. You can find it in [The Textile Arts and Decorative Arts Museum](https://www.museedestissus.fr/), Lyon, France. Well, we happily and thankfully use it as an inspiration and source for many of our [gambesons](https://steel-mastery.com/gambesons), including this ones. As for the ermine print on the fabric, we can only remind you that it is the coat of arms of the Duchy of Brittany.

![Image 1](https://steel-mastery.com/image/catalog/Battle-of-Poitiers/_DSC0262.jpg)

The second white gambeson is also inspired by Charles's gambeson, but has been slightly modified by our fashion designers to embody the image of Jeanne la Flamme, who fought on the other side. It features a double print - still the same black ermine on one half and a black rampant two-tailed lion on the other.

![Image 2](https://steel-mastery.com/image/catalog/Battle-of-Poitiers/0b69-7768Women's_gambeson-0-1.jpg)

**An ermine and a lion**

So why an ermine and a lion? This marvellous story began when Arthur II Capet-Dreux de Bretagne, Duke of Brittany married twice. Times were hard, and his first wife died giving Arthur 3 sons: Jean III de Bretagne - heir to the Duchy, Guy VII de Limoges and Pierre of Avesnes. Well, when his wife died, Arthur remarried and his second wife gave him 6 more children: Jean de Montfort, Béatrix de Hédé, Jeanne de Bretagne, Alix de Bretagne, Blanche de Bretagne and Marie de Bretagne. We are interested in the eldest of these six, Jean de Montfort. When the prolific father Arthur died, his eldest son Jean III de Bretagne became Duke but he was childless. Shit happens. But the Duchy of Brittany throne was in need of an heir. As Jean’s III brothers died early enough and, by law, his half-brother Jean de Montfort was to inherit. But as it happened, one Jean didn't like the other one. He didn't like the other one so much that he even tried to prove in court that his father's second marriage was illegitimate and his children from that marriage were bastards. But that attempt was unsuccessful. And when it came to choosing a successor, Jean III de Bretagne thought a little and wrote a will in favour of his niece Jeanne de Penthièvre, known as duchesse de Bretagne or simply - Joan the Lame. But towards the end of his life he seems to have reconciled with his younger brother and made a more traditional will in favour of Jean de Montfort. Well, sort of reconciled and sort of made a will, but only sort of. When the Duke was dying, and he was pestered by his peers with the question of who was the heir after all, he replied, "Don't you dare trouble my spirit with such questions before I die!" and died. That's right, he just died without answering the sacramental question. Why? Fuck You... That's Why! (с)

So in 1341 the Duchy of Brittany was left with two heirs: Joan the Lame and her uncle Jean de Montfort. As you can guess, each of them had their own supporters and arguments as to their claim to the Duchy's throne.

**Charles of Blois' ermine gambeson**

Of particular interest to us personally is the fact that Jeanne the Lame at the time was already married to... drumroll... Charles of Blois - a man and a gambeson! Yes, that's him in the fancy ermine gambeson. Handsome, isn't he? And as well as being the nephew of the then French King Phillip VI. As you might guess, the King of France was very keen that the Duchy of Breton should go to his nephew. That's why our version of the famous gambeson is decorated with the coat of arms of Brittany (black ermine on a white field), because Charles really, really wanted to rule the Duchy of Brittany. And he fought hard for this title while his limp-wristed wife Jeanne sat at home and bore him heirs. After all, her uncle's example is a good example of the fact that it is better to have children of your own, so as not to look for heirs later on among your relatives. Because having heirs was a serious argument in such a dispute.

**Jeanne la Flamme’s ermine and lion gambeson**

Regarding the gambeson with lion and ermine, it embodies the second side of the war for Breton succession - wife of Jean de Montfor Joanna of Flanders, Duchess of Brittany, better known as Jeanne la Flamme. Brittany's ermines complemented here with the Montfor family's coat of arms - a rampant two-tailed lion. While an amazing and beautiful woman in a gorgeous gambeson was one of the famous warriors of the Hundred Years' War. Seriously, in those wild chauvinistic times she commanded town defences and combat raids. So the War of the Breton Succession also went down in history as the War of the Two Jeannes.

**War of the Two Jeannes**

Going back to history - when Jean de Montfort realized that he was unlikely to get his rights recognized by the French king (because he was not his nephew), he decided to appeal to another king - Edward III of England as King of France. You do remember that the King of England also had a claim to the French throne and started the Hundred Years War on that very occasion, don't you? Well, Jean de Montfort paid the King of England (and France according to his own version) vassal oath, and the war over the Breton succession turned into an interstate conflict, continuing the Hundred Years' War.

It must be said that at the beginning of the conflict, luck was on the side of Joan the Lame and Charles of Blois. Indeed, in 1341 there was still an armistice between England and France, and Edward III of England could not send troops to help Jean de Montfort. In 1345 Jean de Montfort died, and his widow Joanna of Flanders became the Montfort party leader. Seriously, this woman did not just sit back and bear children. Oh no! She donned armour, took up arms and urged the other ladies to "cut their skirts and take their safety in their own hands" and personally led the defence of Hennebont. Moreover, she guided the soldiers in an attack outside the town walls and burned down the enemy’s camp. It was after this that she became known as Jeanne la Flamme, and not only for her fiery character and inflammatory speeches before the defenders of the city. Froissart described her as a lady "with the heart of a lion, and in her hand she wielded a sharp glaive, wherewith she fought fiercely". During another attack, when her troops were frightened and retreated, this lady turned her horse and galloped towards the enemy herself. Her knights were then ashamed and joined the attack, following the intrepid Jeanne. Defending the rights of her son John V to the Breton succession, she continued the war. In 1347, Jeanne la Flamme's troops even captured Charles of Blois in battle. She later, however, had to escape to England where she was declared insane under unexplained circumstances and locked up in Tickhill Castle for the rest of her life. She died there in 1374. It must be said that she outlived the other three war participants. For while her husband Jean de Montfort died in 1345, Charles of Blois in 1364 and his wife Joan the Lame in 1365.

The War of the Breton Succession itself lasted until 1364. Although much of the time luck in this war was with Charles of Blois, after his death by the treaty of Guérande in 1365, Jeanne la Flamme and Jean de Montfort son John V was recognized as the rightful Duke of Brittany and had married Mary Plantagenet, daughter of Edward III of England. And then...

And then there were many more interesting and enlightening stories, both in Brittany and elsewhere. And we'll tell you about them in the next parts. Stay tuned :)

died 1309)​ * [Isabella of Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_of_Castile,_Queen_of_Aragon "Isabella of Castile, Queen of Aragon") ​ ​ (m. 1310; died 1328)​ * [Joan of Savoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Savoy "Joan of Savoy") ​ (m. 1329)​ | | [House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynasty "Dynasty") | [Dreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Dreux "House of Dreux") | | Father | [Arthur II, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "Arthur II, Duke of Brittany") | | Mother | [Marie, Viscountess of Limoges](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marie,_Viscountess_of_Limoges&action=edit&redlink=1 "Marie, Viscountess of Limoges (page does not exist)") | **John III _the Good_** (in [Breton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_language "Breton language") _Yann III_, in [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language") _Jean III_; 8 March 1286 – 30 April 1341) was [Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Brittany "Duke of Brittany"), from 1312 to his death and 5th [Earl of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Richmond "Earl of Richmond") from 1334 to his death. He was the son of [Arthur II, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "Arthur II, Duke of Brittany"), and his first wife Marie, Viscountess of Limoges.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorvan2009table_2-1) John was strongly opposed to his father's second marriage to [Yolande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yolande_of_Dreux,_Queen_of_Scotland "Yolande of Dreux, Queen of Scotland") and attempted to contest its legality. In 1297, John married Isabella of Valois,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones1988210-2) eldest child of [Charles, Count of Valois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Valois "Charles of Valois") and his first wife [Margaret of Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_of_Naples "Margaret of Naples"). At the time of their marriage John was eleven years old and his bride five. She died childless in 1309. In 1310, John married his second wife, [Isabella of Castile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_of_Castile,_Duchess_of_Brittany "Isabella of Castile, Duchess of Brittany").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorvan2009table_2-1) She died childless in 1328. In 1329, John married his third wife [Joan of Savoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Savoy "Joan of Savoy").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorvan2009table_2-1) He predeceased his third wife by three years and died childless. He was unwilling to cede the [Duchy of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brittany "Duchy of Brittany") to his half-brother [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort"), son of his hated step-mother Yolande. He wished to leave the duchy to the French [King Philip VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"), but his nobles objected. The marriage of his niece [Joanna of Dreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joanna_of_Dreux "Joanna of Dreux") to [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois") gave Charles a plausible claim to the duchy, but the matter was unresolved at John's death. After his death, John of Montfort claimed his rights as duke of Brittany, but King Philip VI supported the Blois faction, and the [Breton War of Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_War_of_Succession "Breton War of Succession") (1341–1364) was triggered. The Breton Civil War was fought between the [House of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Blois "House of Blois") and the [House of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montfort_of_Brittany "Montfort of Brittany"). It became part of the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War"), as England supported the Montfort faction, which won, against the House of Blois, which was supported by France. | Siege of Hennebont | | --- | | Part of the [Breton Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_War_of_Succession "Breton War of Succession") | | [![Image 1: A colourful Medieval depiction of men in armour fighting in front of the gate of a fortified town](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9c/Si%C3%A8ge_d%27Hennebont.jpg/330px-Si%C3%A8ge_d%27Hennebont.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Si%C3%A8ge_d%27Hennebont.jpg) An incident during the siege from a near-contemporary manuscript | |
DateLate May – late June 1342
Location

Brittany

47°48′14″N 3°16′48″W﻿ / ﻿47.80389°N 3.28000°W
ResultMontfort victory
| | Belligerents | | * [House of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Blois "House of Blois") * [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France") | * [House of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lords,_counts_and_dukes_of_Montfort-l%27Amaury "Lords, counts and dukes of Montfort-l'Amaury") * [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") | | Commanders and leaders | | [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I,_Duke_of_Brittany "Charles I, Duke of Brittany") | [Joanna of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort") | | [![Image 2: Map](https://maps.wikimedia.org/img/osm-intl,10,47.803888888889,-3.28,270x200.png?lang=en&domain=en.wikipedia.org&title=Siege_of_Hennebont&revid=1292985669&groups=_be85820b9de7ebaf0b168363d340039cb176f732&parser=legacy)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Map/10/47.803888888889/-3.28/en) | | | The **siege of Hennebont** took place between late May and late June 1342 when the forces of [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany "Charles, Duke of Brittany") conducted an unsuccessful siege of the fortified port of [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont"), commanded by [Joanna of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort").[\[note 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-2) The conflict was a part of the [Breton Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession "War of the Breton Succession"), a dynastic dispute between two claimants to the [Duchy of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brittany "Duchy of Brittany") which had broken out the previous year. A complicating factor was the pre-existing [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") between [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France") and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England"). [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") was supporting Charles of Blois, his nephew; [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") had promised military assistance to Joanna, the wife of the rival claimant, [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort"). A [truce between France and England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Espl%C3%A9chin "Truce of Espléchin") was in place when the siege started but it expired in June. Charles's French army overran eastern Brittany and captured John of Montfort. Joanna took up the cause and concentrated her resources in Hennebont. In late May 1342 Charles moved on the town. On arrival part of his army advanced against orders and attacked some of the town's defenders who were formed up outside its gate. More troops were pulled into this fight before the French were pushed back in a disorderly retreat. The Montfortists pursued, inflicting many casualties and burning the French camp. Two days later the French launched a series of better-planned assaults, but all were repulsed. The main French force moved on, leaving a detachment to attempt to starve the town into surrender. In late June, after a small English force had reinforced the town by sea, this too left. In July Charles was strongly reinforced and returned; the Montfortists abandoned Hennebont and redeployed further west, hoping for English reinforcements. [Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany "Brittany") was a province of France. Although the dukes of Brittany were [vassals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vassal "Vassal") of the French kings, they governed the duchy as all but independent rulers.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption199017,_34%E2%80%9335-3)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200662-4)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones19888%E2%80%9311-5) Nevertheless, when the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") broke out in 1337 between France and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") the Duke of Brittany, [John III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany"), fought alongside his [feudal lord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudal_lordship "Feudal lordship") the [King of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kings_of_France "Kings of France"), [Philip VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"). John died on 30 April 1341, leaving a disputed succession: both his niece, [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre"), and his younger half-brother, [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort"), claimed the dukedom; Joan was married to [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany "Charles, Duke of Brittany"), a well-connected and militarily oriented French nobleman who was also a nephew of the King of France.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990370%E2%80%93371-6)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199966%E2%80%9367-7)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraham-Goering202047%E2%80%9349-8) John had the stronger legal claim but the [aristocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristocracy "Aristocracy") and [clergy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clergy "Clergy") knew little about him and mostly preferred Charles. John's support came mostly from the lower levels of society in the countryside, and the [bourgeoisie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourgeoisie "Bourgeoisie") in the towns.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990371,_374-9)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007202-10)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200660-11) Starting in early June 1341 John seized most of the fortified places in Brittany and by mid-August had all but made good his claim to the duchy. Philip initially disregarded the situation but, correctly suspecting that John was negotiating with the English, had Charles declared the rightful heir on 7 September. The French king liked the idea of the new duke being related to him as it would bring the traditionally semi-autonomous province more firmly under royal control. He was willing to commit considerable military resources to achieve this and despatched an army, commanded by his eldest son, [John, Duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John,_Duke_of_Normandy "John, Duke of Normandy"), to support Charles. This led to the outbreak of the [Breton Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_War_of_Succession "Breton War of Succession").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand200114-12)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990377%E2%80%93378-13)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007203-14) French and English intervention ------------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Siege_of_Hennebont&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: French and English intervention")\] A map of Brittany, with modern administrative boundaries, showing the locations of some of the places mentioned in the text This French army overran all of eastern Brittany apart from [Rennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes "Rennes") in the six months from September 1341 and captured John of Montfort. John surrendered on the granting of a [safe conduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safe_conduct "Safe conduct") to Paris and back by John of Normandy, who escorted him. In Paris Philip proposed to John that he repudiate all claim to Brittany and his possessions there in favour of Charles of Blois, receiving an [annuity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annuity "Annuity") and land in France in exchange. John declined, at which Philip withdrew his son's promised safe conduct and had John imprisoned.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990388%E2%80%93391-15)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-16) John's wife, [Joanna of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), was in Rennes with their two-year-old son, also named [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), and the ducal treasury when news of John's capture arrived. Modern historians consider her to have been an energetic and effective leader, and she acted decisively and aggressively. She recalled the field army from western Brittany, joined it with some of the troops in Rennes and took command. She stormed the town of [Redon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redon,_Ille-et-Vilaine "Redon, Ille-et-Vilaine") and then moved to [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont"). This was a small but strongly walled town with access to the sea. From there Joanna retained control of most of western Brittany and set up her infant son as the faction's figurehead and heir to his father's claim to the duchy.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990389%E2%80%93390,_409-17)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199967-18)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVisserSnijder201433%E2%80%9334-19) At the time the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") between France and England had been underway for five years; therefore Joanna despatched her senior counsellor, [Amaury of Clisson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amaury_de_Clisson "Amaury de Clisson"), to [Edward III in England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") with a large sum in cash to encourage English military intervention.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990390-20) The Montfortist cause was soon being supported by Edward III as an extension of the war with France.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod199017-21) This was the start of Edward's "provincial strategy", by which he sided with French vassals of Philip in their disagreements with him: this promoted Edward's claim to be the rightful king of France and potentially created military allies.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod199017-21) Strategically Edward had the opportunity to set up a ruler in Brittany at least partially under his control, which would provide access to Breton ports, greatly aiding England's naval war and giving ready entry to France for English armies.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand200114-12) However, English reinforcements took a long time to reach Brittany.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-16) This was partly because the [Truce of Espléchin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Espl%C3%A9chin "Truce of Espléchin") was in force between France and England. Ostensibly halting all fighting, in practice it prevented either country from deploying their main field armies, but was otherwise ill observed. It was due to expire on 24 June 1342.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006122%E2%80%93123-22)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990358%E2%80%93359,_379%E2%80%93380,_383-23) On 15 April Charles moved on Rennes. The populace seized the commander Joanna had left in charge and surrendered to the French army. A little later a small English force of 234 men under Sir [Walter Mauny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Manny,_1st_Baron_Manny "Walter Manny, 1st Baron Manny") arrived at [Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brest,_France "Brest, France") in western Brittany. They were despatched ahead of the main English force to garrison the main Breton ports; Mauny was probably under orders not to attack French forces until after the truce expired.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990393-24) Edward planned to land in Brittany himself in June with a substantial force, but had extreme difficulty in assembling ships.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011109%E2%80%93112-25)[\[note 2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-28) Mauny's force skirmished in the west to little effect, while Charles detached a force to besiege Vannes and marched the rest of his army on Hennebont.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990393%E2%80%93394-29) [![Image 3: A colourful Medieval depiction of several ladies leaving a walled town](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Jeanne_de_Flandre.jpg/250px-Jeanne_de_Flandre.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jeanne_de_Flandre.jpg) Joanna and her ladies greet the English relief force The town contained a large garrison and [morale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morale#Military "Morale") was high. The French army arrived in late May. Some of the Spanish and Italian mercenaries pushed forward against orders and engaged a group of defenders formed up in front of the town gates. Charles's men got the worst of this fight but were unable to retreat; he was forced to send more men forward in small groups as they became available in an attempt to temporarily push back the Montfortists and allow his impetuous troops to retreat. The Montfortists also fed additional troops into the fight through the gate and Charles's attempt to facilitate an organised retreat failed; the whole attack was thrown back in disorder with many killed. The Montfortists pursued the French and burnt down most of their freshly established camp.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-16) According to a contemporary account Joanna rode through the suburbs in full armour encouraging the fighting men.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-16) She was later given the soubriquet "Flame of Brittany".[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVisserSnijder201433-30) The next day Charles probed the town's defences and on the second day after arriving he repeatedly ordered assaults on the town; they were all repulsed with losses.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVisserSnijder201436-31) In early June the French dug in for a regular siege, in the hope that starvation would force the town's surrender. Charles moved his main force to [Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auray "Auray"), leaving a small force of mercenaries, mostly Spanish, and several [siege engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_engine "Siege engine") to carry on the siege at Hennebont under the command of [Louis of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_de_la_Cerda "Luis de la Cerda"), an expatriate Spaniard who had previously been the [admiral of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Admiral_of_France "Admiral of France").[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990394%E2%80%93395-32) Charles promised pardons and financial incentives in an attempt to win the Montfortists back to France. Some were inclined to seek what terms they could,[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007205-33) but the majority of Joanna's council held firm. The betrayal by Philip of the safe conduct given to John of Montfort by Duke John caused a deep distrust of such pledges. At some point in June Mauny took his force up the estuary to resupply and reinforce Hennebont. By late June the besiegers had broken up their engines and left. Charles also pulled back from his siege of Auray.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007205-33)[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990395-34) The French mobilised more than 10,000 men, possibly many more, in late June for the campaigning season and most of them were allocated to renewing the offensive in Brittany. By early July their impact was felt: the Montfortists in Auray ran out of food and abandoned the town at night, Vannes agreed terms of surrender and fell to the French, and many other places also went over to the French. Joanna considered her position in Hennebont unsustainable and left it for Brest, where by August Charles was again besieging her.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990398-35) More than 2,000 English troops [landed at Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Brest_/(1342/) "Siege of Brest (1342)") on 18 August, relieving the town and causing Charles to withdraw his army from western Brittany. The English then marched on [Morlaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morlaix "Morlaix"), a town on the north coast with strong fortifications and a secure harbour 50 kilometres (30 mi) from Brest, and besieged it.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199970-36)[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990400%E2%80%93401-37) Charles was now aware that his force greatly outnumbered the English and he attempted to relieve Morlaix, but was defeated on 30 September at the [battle of Morlaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix "Battle of Morlaix").[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990401-38)[\[note 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-41) [Edward III landed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III%27s_Breton_campaign "Edward III's Breton campaign") in Brest with a further 3,000 men on 26 October, marched to and besieged Vannes, only to agree the [Truce of Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit "Truce of Malestroit") on 19 January 1343.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich1980174-42)[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200245-43) Hostilities did not recommence until June 1345.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006207-44) Joanna travelled to England and took no further part in the war and died in September 1374. She stayed in Tickhill Castle and it was given out at the time that she had gone insane; this is accepted by most historians although it has been suggested that she was confined for political reasons, rather than because of mental illness.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990409-45)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESarpy2019section_%22political_prisoner%22-46) Her husband predeceased her in 1345.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998139-47) The Breton Civil War continued as a disjointed and inconclusive series of sieges, skirmishes and truces, frequently as part of the Hundred Years' War. The eastern and southern parts of Brittany were mostly held by the French, who continued to strongly support Charles of Blois, while western and northern Brittany continued to be largely Montfort or English controlled.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200237-39) Charles of Blois was killed in 1364 at the [Battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray") and his army decisively defeated. The next year his widow, [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre"), signed the [Treaty of Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_/(1365/) "Treaty of Guérande (1365)"), recognising John of Montfort's son as Duke of Brittany, which ended the war.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich1980174-42)[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200245-43)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones1999106-48)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200692%E2%80%9393-49) The Hundred Years' War continued until 1453, when it ended in a French victory.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006l-50) Notes, citations and sources **John of Montfort** ([Middle Breton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Breton_language "Middle Breton language"): _Yann Moñforzh_, [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _Jean de Montfort_) (1295 – 26 September 1345),[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-1) sometimes known as **John IV**,[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-2) was [Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Brittany "Duke of Brittany") and [Earl of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Richmond "Earl of Richmond") from 1341 to 1345 in dispute with his niece [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre") and her husband [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois"). He was also [Count of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Montfort-l%27Amaury "Count of Montfort-l'Amaury") from 1322. He was the son of [Arthur II, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "Arthur II, Duke of Brittany"), and his second wife, [Yolande of Dreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yolande_de_Dreux,_Queen_of_Scotland "Yolande de Dreux, Queen of Scotland"). His contesting of the inheritance of the Duchy of Brittany with his niece Joan led to the [War of the Breton Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession "War of the Breton Succession"), which in turn evolved into being part of the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") between England and France. John's patron in his quest was King [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrevit%C3%A9-Orton1978877-3) He died in 1345, 19 years before the end of the war, and the victory of his son [John IV, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), over Joan of Penthièvre and Charles of Blois.

[![Image 2: Jean of Montfort's coat of arms.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Arms_of_Jean_de_Montfort.svg/250px-Arms_of_Jean_de_Montfort.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Arms_of_Jean_de_Montfort.svg "Jean of Montfort's coat of arms.")

Jean of Montfort's coat of arms.

John of Montfort was born in 1295, the only son to Arthur II of Brittany and his second wife Yolande of Dreux.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) In 1322 he inherited from his mother the title of count of Montfort-l'Amaury,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorvan2009table_2-5) and in 1329 he married [Joanna of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort") in [Chartres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chartres "Chartres").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) Joanna was the daughter of [Louis I, Count of Nevers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_I,_Count_of_Nevers "Louis I, Count of Nevers"),[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) and [Joan, Countess of Rethel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan,_Countess_of_Rethel "Joan, Countess of Rethel"). They had:

*   [John IV, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany") (1339–1399), married (1) [Mary of Waltham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_of_Waltham "Mary of Waltham") (1344–1362), daughter of King [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England"), in 1361 in Oxfordshire;[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) (2) [Joan Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Holland,_Duchess_of_Brittany "Joan Holland, Duchess of Brittany") (1350–1384) in 1366 in London;[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) (3) [Joan of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Navarre,_Queen_of_England "Joan of Navarre, Queen of England") (1370–1437), daughter of King [Charles II of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_Navarre "Charles II of Navarre"), in 1386 in Saillé-près-Guérande.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones1988123-6)
*   [Joan of Brittany, Baroness of Drayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Brittany,_Baroness_of_Drayton "Joan of Brittany, Baroness of Drayton") (1341–1402), married before 21 October 1385 to [Ralph Basset, 3rd Baron Basset of Drayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Basset,_3rd_Baron_Basset_of_Drayton "Ralph Basset, 3rd Baron Basset of Drayton")[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChibnall1965130-7)

Succession to Duke John III
---------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_of_Montfort&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Succession to Duke John III")\]

On 30 April 1341, [John III, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany"), died without a male heir. His half-brother, John of Montfort, was a candidate for the succession, which was also claimed by Joan of Penthièvre, niece of John III and wife of Charles of Blois, himself a nephew of the [Philip VI, King of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"). The King was, of course, favourable to his nephew.

The Duchy of Brittany historically had a "semi-Salic" mode of inheritance; male primogeniture was followed unless no direct male descendants remained. At that point the closest female descendant inherited as duchess, with her husband serving as duke by "right of representation". The position of John of Montfort was legally founded on the belief that a brother (even a half-brother) was a closer heir than a beneficiary niece, and that the Salic form of inheritance adopted by the Kingdom of France should be followed. This argument was based on the fact that since 1297 Brittany had been a _duché-pairie_ ("member and part of the crown"), and that the legislation of the suzerain kingdom should therefore be applied.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeguayMartin198299-8) Challenges to the [Salic law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salic_law "Salic law") of the Franks had historically been rejected for the Kingdom of France, allowing Philip V to gain the throne in 1316, and Philip VI most recently. This made Philip VI's support of Joan of Penthièvre quite ironic, in that the argument for Philip VI to inherit the Kingdom of France was based on the opposing philosophy that the crown should not be able to descend through the female line to Edward III.

A civil war, termed the War of the Breton Succession, then began and lasted 23 years. This conflict was also called _La guerre de deux Jeanne_, after the French names of the two duchesses in competition: Jeanne de Penthièvre and Jeanne de Flanders, wife of John of Montfort.

Early stages of the War (1341)
------------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_of_Montfort&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early stages of the War (1341)")\]

After the funeral of John III, Charles of Blois returned to the Court of France and John of Montfort returned to his Breton estate in [Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gu%C3%A9rande "Guérande"). Then, incited by his wife (according to tradition), he went with a small army to [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes") where he was well received by the inhabitants who swore their loyalty. John then went to [Limoges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limoges "Limoges") where he managed to obtain the ducal treasury. John returned to Nantes and was recognised as Duke in May 1341 by an assembly composed of members of the towns and minor nobles, but shunned by the major vassals with the exception of Hervé VII, Count of Léon. Thanks to the ducal treasury, he recruited mercenaries which allowed him to perform in June and July a 'great ride in Brittany' (as described by Arthur de la Borderie) and take control of the duchy. John first gained [Rennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes "Rennes"), then [Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes "Vannes") and the places surrounding the [Château de Suscinio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_de_Suscinio "Château de Suscinio"), [Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auray "Auray"), [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont"), and then [Quimperlé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quimperl%C3%A9 "Quimperlé"). Having failed to take the domains of [Rohan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Rohan "House of Rohan"), he submitted [Quimper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quimper "Quimper") and [Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brest,_France "Brest, France") before descending to [Carhaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carhaix "Carhaix"), and then went back northward and captured [Saint-Brieuc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Brieuc "Saint-Brieuc"), [Lamballe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamballe "Lamballe"), [Jugon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jugon-les-Lacs_/(delegated_commune/) "Jugon-les-Lacs (delegated commune)"), [Dinan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinan "Dinan"), [Dol-de-Bretagne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dol-de-Bretagne "Dol-de-Bretagne"), and returned to Nantes via [Ploërmel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plo%C3%ABrmel "Ploërmel").

Always accompanied by Hervé VII of Léon, John obtained the submission, if not the support, of some of the major nobles who possessed several of these strongholds and had been loyal to Charles of Blois. However it would probably require getting [Josselin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josselin "Josselin"), or the support of the high secular clergy and great lords, or more, to control the domains of the Penthièvres and the House of Rohan, which represented about two-thirds of Brittany.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_la_Borderie1975425%E2%80%93429-9) John also went to England and met with Edward III of England in Windsor, who promised him military assistance and invested him with the [Honour of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honour_of_Richmond "Honour of Richmond").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeguayMartin1982100-10)

Charles of Blois then made an appeal to Philip VI, who summoned John of Montfort to a Court of Peers session in Conflans in September 1341. In this context by the judgment of Conflans, the Duchy of Brittany was attributed to Charles of Blois. Philip VI agreed to receive _l'hommage lige_ of Charles of Blois on behalf of his wife, and confiscated from John of Montfort the French lands of the County of Montfort-l'Amaury, as well as the Viscounty of Limoges that he held more unduly.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_la_Borderie1975430%E2%80%93432-11)

In October 1341, Charles of Blois and [John II, Duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France") (later King of France), put together an army and penetrated into Brittany. They managed to retrieve a number of strongholds which had been lost, including Nantes, which relented on 21 November 1341 after three weeks of siege. John of Montfort was captured and imprisoned in the [Louvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvre "Louvre") in Paris. Despite the change of camp of Hervé VII de Leon (due to criticisms from John regarding his handling of the siege of Nantes), Joanna, the wife of John of Montfort, continued the armed struggle supported by his allies.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_la_Borderie1975441%E2%80%93449-12)

Subsequent stages of the War (1342–1345)
----------------------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_of_Montfort&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Subsequent stages of the War (1342–1345)")\]

After a winter break that ended on 15 April 1342, Charles of Blois resumed the fight and regained a large part of Brittany between May and September 1342. King Edward III of England decided to intervene on behalf of the House of Montfort. Charles de Blois failed to take Hennebont, which was defended by [Joanna of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), while [Robert III of Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_III_of_Artois "Robert III of Artois") was mortally wounded besieging Vannes in vain leading an English contingent. In January 1343, through [Pope Clement VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_VI "Pope Clement VI"), a truce was signed at [Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malestroit "Malestroit") to bring peace and the liberation of John of Montfort. The latter was released in September 1343 and retired to England 27 March 1345. His return to the struggle with reinforcements provided by King Edward III of England put an end to the truce. John of Montfort unsuccessfully laid siege to Quimper, then fell ill and died in Hennebont on 26 September 1345.

Tomb of John of Montfort
------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_of_Montfort&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Tomb of John of Montfort")\]

He was buried in the convent of the Dominicans of Quimperlé[\[b\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-13) where his tomb, which had already been desecrated, was found again in December 1883.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_la_Villemarqu%C3%A91884278%E2%80%93297-14) His remains are now in the Church of Sainte-Croix de Quimperlé.
