[![Image 1](https://i0.wp.com/thefreelancehistorywriter.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/202112-2_countess-jeanne-de-montfort.jpg?resize=338%2C450&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/thefreelancehistorywriter.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/202112-2_countess-jeanne-de-montfort.jpg?ssl=1)

**Jeanne “la Flamme”, Duchess of Brittany ~ A guest post by Simon Duits**

The Freelance History Writer is pleased to welcome historian Simon Duits as a guest on the blog with an article on French/Breton history. He writes extensively about the Middle Ages over at [MedievalReporter.com](https://medievalreporter.com/).

During the chaos and confusion of the early Hundred Years’ War, a woman of fiery character led the Duchy of Brittany into battle. Strong-willed and courageous, her ferocious personality earned her the epithet “la Flamme” or, “the Flame”. Her name was Jeanne. She eventually even had the rare honor of having a war named after her, as the War of the Breton Succession also became known as the “War of the Two Jeannes” – one of them, of course, being Jeanne la Flamme. She spent much of her life pouring her energy into this cruel contest.

At the time, succession struggles were all the rage across late medieval Europe. Only four years before the Breton War erupted, the Hundred Years’ War had kicked off. [Claimants from the Houses of Plantagenet and Valois](https://thefreelancehistorywriter.com/2016/04/15/salic-law-and-the-exclusion-of-women-from-the-crown-of-france/) went to war over the right to rule France. The late French king, Charles IV “the Fair”, had died without issue in 1328. Both his cousin – King Edward III of England (Plantagenet) – as well as his nephew – Count Philip (Valois) – claimed the French throne.

In 1341, the War of the Breton Succession erupted against this backdrop. The same thing that had happened to the French crown happened to the Duchy of Brittany: its ruler died without direct male descendants. Again, two factions went to war over the spoils of succession. Because the Hundred Years’ War was already raging across France, the Breton succession struggle soon became a proxy conflict of the larger theater of war between the English and the French. Both London and Paris intervened heavily in Brittany’s affairs during this period – and thus in Jeanne la Flamme’s life.

**The War of the Breton Succession**

Jeanne was born as Joanna of Flanders, daughter of the count of Nevers in western Burgundy and the countess of Rethel in northern Champagne. She carried the Flemish name on account of her brother, who became Count of Flanders in 1328 and steered the county into a pro-French course. Later, he was duly killed in the famous Battle of Crécy by the English.

In 1329, Jeanne married John of Montfort, the half-brother of the Breton duke. When this duke died childless, a contentious succession dispute dragged the entirety of Brittany into open war. The reason for this was that, for a long time, the late duke had declared his niece Jeanne de Penthièvre as heir. She was married to Charles of Blois, who would thus become the next Duke of Brittany. But, just before passing away, the dying duke indicated that his half-brother John of Montfort – Joanna of Flanders’ husband – should be his successor.

Upon the duke’s death in April, 1341, John and Jeanne predictably pressed their claim. Charles of Blois and Jeanne de Penthièvre naturally did the same. The stage for the War of the Two Jeannes was set.

John of Montfort and Jeanne of Flanders moved as quickly as they could. They secured the ducal treasury, hired some mercenaries, and – with this makeshift army – managed to subdue several castles and cities. Rennes, Vannes, Hennebont, Brest, Dol-de-Bretagne, and other strategic sites declared for the Montfortist cause. On top of that, an assembly of the citizens and lower nobility of the important city of Nantes acknowledged John as Duke of Brittany. John and Jeanne enjoyed a clear first mover advantage.

[![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/thefreelancehistorywriter.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/202112-2_jeanne-and-john-at-court.jpg?resize=809%2C942&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/thefreelancehistorywriter.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/202112-2_jeanne-and-john-at-court.jpg?ssl=1)

Jeanne and John are declared Duchess and Duke of Brittany by the inhabitants of Nantes. (15th century, Public Domain)\]

However, the high nobility, who controlled roughly two-thirds of the duchy, had not chosen sides yet. One of the major Breton houses were the Penthièvres – the House of the “other Jeanne”, wife of the opposing claimant Charles of Blois. To make matters even more complicated, Charles of Blois was a cousin of Philip of Valois – the new King of France and the very reason for the commencement of the Hundred Years’ War. In response, John of Montfort made a fateful decision that plunged the Breton dispute into the larger Anglo-French conflict, and sought the assistance of the king of England to balance things out.

**The English Connection**

John met with Edward III at Windsor. The English king pledged to support the Montfortist cause with troops and money in return for Brittany recognizing Edward as its lawful suzerain. This was precisely what the French feared. King Philip VI was not prepared to engage in a protracted proxy war over the Breton peninsula. The Hundred Years’ War already had enough fronts as is. Therefore, the French king summoned both John of Montfort and Charles of Blois to Paris. Philip VI wanted to settle this dispute without spilling any more blood.

The two claimants met during the Court of Peers meeting that King Philip VI had assembled. Quite unsurprisingly, neither side was willing to concede their point. So, the French king took a simple yet significant decision: he imprisoned John on the grounds of conspiring with the English and attributed the Duchy of Brittany to his cousin, Charles of Blois. One could be forgiven for thinking that this was an effective “quick and dirty” solution to one of the many challenges facing the French king at the time. Before the first English soldier had set foot on Breton soil, the succession war seemed already concluded.

But, in a spectacular turn of events, John of Montfort escaped his Paris prison, fled to Brittany and gathered his army. The French dreaded the idea of the English landing in Brittany, so Philip VI responded posthaste. He dispatched Charles of Blois to Brittany to settle the issue militarily once and for all. A French army over 7,000 strong appeared in front of the city walls of Nantes before the year 1341 was out.

The French made it very clear what they would do to treasonous Bretons if they didn’t surrender. They executed Montfortists taken prisoner in sight of the walls and catapulted the decapitated heads inside the city. The assembly that had declared for John only months earlier was enraged at the course of recent events and forced John to surrender. He gave in and was – once again – imprisoned in the Louvre in Paris.

Thanks to friends in high places, Charles of Blois had won the day. His uncle, the King of France, had personally made him Duke of Brittany. John’s brief stint as duke and his rapid downfall caused Montfortist morale to drop to an all-time low. Many members were considering the cause lost and regarded it futile to defy the French any longer. But Jeanne of Flanders, who had not been present at the siege of Nantes, was quite unwilling to surrender.

With her husband in prison once again, it fell upon her to lead the Montfortist cause. As one contemporary chronicler put it, “\[with\] the courage of a man and the heart of a lion”, Jeanne lifted her soldiers’ spirits and reassured them of the rightfulness of her husband’s claim. Bellicose as ever, under her leadership, the House of Montfort geared up for another round of fighting.

**A Flame Erupts**

With winter approaching (Charles of Blois conquered Nantes in November, 1341), hostilities ceased for the moment. This gave Jeanne of Flanders ample time to prepare for the next year of campaigning. She based much of her hope on the English reinforcements still making their way to Brittany. Consequently, she decided she would buy as much time as possible. Looking for a place to stall the advance of Charles of Blois into Brittany proper, she picked the castle of Hennebont on the southern Breton coast.

[![Image 3](https://i0.wp.com/thefreelancehistorywriter.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/202112-2_jeanne-at-hennebont_1.jpg?resize=564%2C814&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/thefreelancehistorywriter.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/202112-2_jeanne-at-hennebont_1.jpg?ssl=1)

Jeanne at Hennebont

Throughout the 1341-1342 winter, the House of Montfort supplied, strengthened and reinforced the fort. In April, 1342, when the warm weather had returned, Charles of Blois duly besieged Hennebont castle. Jeanne of Flanders had successfully lifted troop morale over the winter, but when the French army appeared in front of the walls, she felt the need for steeling her army’s resolve.

Until then, she had strutted about, dressed as a duchess. Now, she took up arms, donned armor and personally led the castle’s defense to inspire population and garrison alike. Upping the ante, she personally spoke to the women of the castle, calling on them to “cut their skirts and take their safety into their own hands”. Immediately, they began breaking up the pavements and carried the stones to the battlements to be used as ammunition.

Over the following days and weeks, Jeanne kept a close eye from the castle walls on everything that happened inside the Blois camp. At a certain point during the siege, Jeanne noticed that it was lightly guarded. Most French soldiers happened to be scattered over the nearby woods, foraging. Spotting an opportunity to turn the tide, she gathered 300 cavalrymen and rode out on a great courser. Her force quickly overwhelmed the camp’s defenders, destroyed the tents of Charles of Blois, and torched the place.

This was probably the moment when Jeanne earned the nickname “la Flamme”. However, at least one Frenchman managed to sound the alarm and thousands of soldiers hurried back from the forest to defend their camp. As the fire raged all around, they managed to cut off Jeanne’s retreat route to Hennebont. With a stroke of genius, she turned her force around, left Hennebont for what it was, and retreated to Brest – on the western end of the Breton peninsula.

Charles of Blois immediately gave pursuit, but his larger force on foot could not keep up with Jeanne’s horseback pace. She thus arrived at Brest much earlier than Charles, gathered supplies and around 500 fresh troops, and went back to Hennebont by a different route. The French, to their chagrin, quickly realized what happened and returned to the castle to restart the siege. But Jeanne la Flamme had managed to resupply her army, destroy the enemy’s camp, and – most importantly – scored a crucial moral victory.

**His Majesty’s Naval Service**

Her theatrics thus bought Jeanne crucial weeks of time. But as the powerful French catapults kept hammering away at Hennebont’s walls day after day, the _esprit de corps_ declined again. The initial effects of Jeanne’s antics, impressive as they might have been, faded. Once more locked up inside Hennebont castle, her advisors started to pressure her to surrender by the end of spring. In one of the keep’s upper chambers, a heated discussion erupted, as captain after captain tried to make the steadfast Jeanne change her mind.

Her officers were desperate to the point of rebellion, but when La Flamme looked out the window, a smile appeared on her lips. Ships had appeared on the horizon: the Admiral of the Northern Seas arrived at the head of an English navy. Jeanne would not need to surrender just yet. Evidently, the French had taken up too much time to capture Hennebont and now the window of opportunity had closed. Jeanne la Flamme’s sally and feigned retreat to Brest had undone much of the siege’s progress.

[![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/thefreelancehistorywriter.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/202112-2_jeanne-at-hennebont_2.jpg?resize=809%2C1044&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/thefreelancehistorywriter.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/202112-2_jeanne-at-hennebont_2.jpg?ssl=1)

_Whilst her captains are desperate to the point of insubordination, Jeanne witnesses the English fleet arriving and knows the tide has turned._

As the ships docked at Hennebont, King Philip’s nightmare had come true: the English landed in Brittany. The War of the Breton Succession had turned into a proxy conflict of the Hundred Years’ War. Overwhelmed by the arrival of the English, the French army lifted the siege and retreated. The tide of the war turned in favor of House Montfort again. But with her husband still in prison and two-thirds of Brittany loyal to her rival Jeanne de Penthièvre, the War of the Two Jeannes was far from over.

Jeanne la Flamme decided she needed more help and went to England herself. King Edward III was a bit preoccupied with hosting feasts and tournaments, but – after a long wait – finally granted Jeanne an audience and promised her further assistance. She set sail back to Brittany with a fine collection of English men-at-arms. However, near Guernsey, they were beset upon by a French fleet that had been lying in ambush. The French grappled the English ships and fierce hand-to-hand combat ensued. Fortunately for the English, Jeanne la Flamme was aboard: she raged across the decks with a glaive and allegedly slew many enemies. By the end of the day, the fight had failed to deliver a clear result and the French retreated. Jeanne and her allies continued towards Brittany.

**Edward, The King**

Around this point in time, the role England began to play in the War of the Breton Succession became a mixed blessing for the Montforts. Although it had been John of Montfort himself, and – after him – Jeanne la Flamme too, who had personally requested reinforcements from king Edward III, the Breton conflict now assumed proportions greater than ever intended. English commanders – not in the least Edward himself – increasingly influenced Breton affairs, relegating Jeanne la Flamme to a background role.

For instance, King Edward landed at Brest and, over the following years, basically took over the Breton conflict. The king enjoyed mixed results in the duchy, however, and a truce was concluded in 1343. Tellingly, the treaty failed to deliver a definitive answer to the underlying question of the Breton succession. At least, the truce allowed John of Montfort to be released from the Louvre prison. Jeanne and John could reunite after two eventful years.

They went to England to make further preparations for continuing their struggle when the truce ran out. When hostilities resumed in 1345, John of Montfort gathered another English army, fought against the French and died – of all places – at Hennebont. Jeanne la Flamme and her infant son were still in England, ready to carry on the succession struggle, but now Edward had had enough. With John of Montfort out of the way, the English king wanted the Breton front for himself. He ordered Jeanne la Flamme to be confined to Tickhill Castle, in northern England.

She was charged with mental illness, although no evidence of that ever surfaced. In essence, Edward used her as a figurehead claimant to augment his own offensive. The king carried Jeanne’s claim in theory, but – in practice – wanted to conduct the war without Montfortist meddling.

**La Flamme’s Legacy**

Over the next two decades, the English steadily gained the upper hand in their Breton theater of war. In the end, Edward allowed Jeanne la Flamme’s (now adult) son John to leave Tickhill and move to Brittany. To further illustrate the balance of power, Edward III instructed him not to marry or wage war – fundamentally, not to do anything – without consulting him first. Perhaps taking after his strong-willed parents, John tried to strike a deal with Charles of Blois anyway by proposing to divide Brittany between them. But the “other” Jeanne, Charles’ wife, would have nothing of it and implored her husband to crush the young Montfort claimant.

Matters quickly came to a head after that. In 1364, an Anglo-Breton force of around 6,000 strong clashed with a French army of roughly 4,000 in strength. Jeanne la Flamme’s son commanded the English center; Charles of Blois the French. Men-at-arms and knights of both sides marched towards each other and, without any maneuvering or tactical tricks, engaged in ferocious and sanguine direct combat. After more than twenty years of war, both armies wanted a decisive result there and then. John, as well as Charles, gave orders not to take any prisoners and to leave as few survivors as possible.

The setup worked, as Charles of Blois was killed in the ensuing melee. His wife Jeanne de Penthièvre tried to carry on his claim like Jeanne la Flamme had done for the Montfortists, but the Blois cause collapsed soon after the battle. The next year, a comprehensive peace treaty was concluded to end the War of the Breton Succession. The son of John of Montfort and Jeanne la Flamme was finally and universally recognized as John IV, Duke of Brittany.

Still locked up in Tickhill Castle, Jeanne la Flamme only learned of these developments sometime later. With her son now wearing the Breton ducal crown, she was of no value to the English king anymore. Edward did not allow Jeanne to leave. Despite having fought so hard for the Montfortist cause, Jeanne la Flamme never set foot in Brittany again. But her efforts were not in vain: she spent the last 10 years of her life – albeit under house arrest – in the knowledge that her son’s rule over the duchy was safe and secure.

Further reading: “The True Chronicles of Jean le Bel, 1290 – 1360” by Jean le Bel (transl. Nigel Bryant); “Joanna of Flanders: Heroine and Exile” by Julie Sarpy; “Women of Medieval France”, Chapter IX, by Pierce Butler; “The Creation of Brittany: A Late Medieval State” by Michael Jones; “Princely Power in Late Medieval France. Jeanne de Penthièvre and the War for Brittany” by Erika Graham-Goering; “The Hundred Years War, Vol 1: Trial by Battle” by Jonathan Sumption.

Battle of Morlaix
=============== 

[British Battles](https://www.britishbattles.com/)

You are here: [Home](https://www.britishbattles.com/) / [100 Years War](https://www.britishbattles.com/one-hundred-years-war/) / Battle of Morlaix

Battle of Morlaix
=================

**_The first land battle between the English and the French of the Hundred Years War fought in Brittany on 30th September 1342_**

[![Image 1: Siege of Hennebont: Battle of Morlaix 30th September 1342 in the Hundred Years War](https://www.britishbattles.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Siege_dHennebont-870x1024.jpg)](https://www.britishbattles.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Siege_dHennebont.jpg)

**Siege of Hennebont: Battle of Morlaix 30th September 1342 in the Hundred Years War**

**The previous battle of the Hundred Years War is [the Battle of Sluys](https://www.britishbattles.com/one-hundred-years-war/battle-of-sluys/)**

**The next battle of the Hundred Years War is [the **Battle of Auberoche**](https://www.britishbattles.com/one-hundred-years-war/battle-of-auberoche/)**

[**To the 100 Years War index**](https://www.britishbattles.com/one-hundred-years-war/)

**Date of the Battle of** **Morlaix**: 30th September 1342

**Place of the Battle of** **Morlaix**: in the North-West of Brittany in France.

**Combatants at the Battle of** **Morlaix**: An English army against a Breton/French army.

[![Image 2: Charles of Blois: Battle of Morlaix 30th September 1342 in the Hundred Years War](https://www.britishbattles.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Charles-of-Blois.jpg)](https://www.britishbattles.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Charles-of-Blois.jpg)

**Charles of Blois: Battle of Morlaix 30th September 1342 in the Hundred Years War**

**Commanders at the Battle of** **Morlaix**: The Earl of Northampton commanded the English army. Charles of Blois, the claimant Duke of Brittany, commanded the Breton/French army.

**Size of the armies at the Battle of** **Morlaix**: The English army comprised around 3,000 men. The army of Charles of Blois is said to have been several times larger than the English.

**Uniforms, arms and equipment at the Battle of** **Morlaix**: The English army comprised a core of knights and men-at-arms with a strong force of archers.

Increasingly during the 14th Century soldiers in an English army in France were all mounted to enable the army to move at speed.

The Battles of Bannockburn in 1314 and Halidon Hill in 1333, both fought against the Scots, moulded English tactics, causing them to abandon the headlong mounted charge and form their armies with knights and men-at-arms as a dismounted central core with the archers pushed forward on the flanks,

The French continued to believe that battles would be won by a massed mounted charge of nobles, knights and men-at-arms delivered against the opposition’s line.

The English had learnt to their considerable cost at Bannockburn the dangers of a mounted attack against a dismounted line armed with spears.

At the battles of Dupplin Moor in 1332 and Halidon Hill in 1333 the English used their archers to strike down the Scots attacks, the stratagem they then pursued so successfully against the French throughout the Hundred Years War.

The weapon of the English archer was a six-foot yew bow discharging a feathered arrow a cloth metre in length. Arrows were fired with a high trajectory, descending on the approaching foe at an angle. The rate of fire was up to one arrow every 5 seconds. For close quarter fighting the archers used hammers or daggers to batter at an adversary’s armour or penetrate between the plates.

the particular strength of the English army lay in its archers with their life-time of training in the use of the longbow, enabling them to deliver a storm of arrows at a high rate of fire.

**Winner of the Battle of** **Morlaix**: The English army repelled at least two French attacks. After the battle both sides initially remained on the battlefield before retreating, the French having suffered significantly more casualties than the English.

**Background to the Battle of Morlaix:**

The 100 Years War between England and France began in 1337. There were a number of issues between the Kings of the two countries. Among them were the security of Gascony for the English King, the encouragement the French Kings gave the Scots to attack England, the English encouragement of rebellion against the French King in the regions of north-eastern France and above all the English Kings’ claim to the throne of France.

During the course of this long war there were periods of French civil war, particularly over the accession to some of the great estates, which the English King exploited by allying himself to one of the sides.

The first of these disputed accessions was over the Dukedom of Brittany.

In April 1341 Duke John of Brittany died leaving no direct heir with his succession in doubt.

The two claimants to the dukedom were Charles, Count of Blois, married to the deceased duke’s niece, Joan of Ponthièvre and John de Montfort, the deceased duke’s step-brother by his father’s second wife, the widow of King Alexander II of Scotland.

Charles of Blois was the nephew of King Philip VI of France, who strongly supported his claim to the Duchy of Brittany.

The claim of John de Montfort was consequently supported by King Edward III of England.

The two parties began a war to take Brittany.

In November 1341, Charles of Blois with a strong Breton/French army captured the city of Nantes and with it John de Montfort, who was imprisoned in Paris.

The resistance on behalf of John de Montfort was continued by his wife, the redoubtable Joan of Flanders.

After some successes, Joan of Flanders was besieged by Charles of Blois in the estuary town of Hennebont in the south-west of Brittainy.

[![Image 3: Joan of Flanders: Battle of Morlaix 30th September 1342 in the Hundred Years War](https://www.britishbattles.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Jan_z_Montfortu-870x1024.jpg)](https://www.britishbattles.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Jan_z_Montfortu.jpg)

**Joan of Flanders: Battle of Morlaix 30th September 1342 in the Hundred Years War**

Joan of Flanders appealed to King Edward III of England for help and a force was dispatched from England under Sir Walter Manny, finally arriving in May 1342 and relieving the now hard-pressed Hennebont garrison, before beginning a campaign against the supporters of Charles of Blois.

On 14th August 1342 another English army landed at Brest on Cape Finisterre, the north-west point of Brittany, comprising 3,000 men commanded by the Earl of Northampton.

Charles of Blois was besieging Brest and was forced by the arrival of Northampton’s army to raise the siege and withdraw to Guingamp, 40 miles to the east.

Northampton advanced to Morlaix and made an unsuccessful attempt to storm the town, before beginning a regular siege.

[![Image 4: Map of the Battle of Morlaix 30th September 1342 in the Hundred Years War: battle map by John Fawkes](https://www.britishbattles.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/MorlaixA-708x1024.jpg)](https://www.britishbattles.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/MorlaixA.jpg)

**Map of the Battle of Morlaix 30th September 1342 in the Hundred Years War: battle map by John Fawkes**

**Battle of** **Morlaix**:

Charles of Blois, invoking his support among the French speaking nobles of northern Brittany, assembled a powerful army, before advancing on 29th September 1342 to relieve Morlaix and give battle to Northampton’s English army.

On hearing of the approach of the French army, the Earl of Northampton left his siege lines outside Morlaix and advanced to meet him.

Northampton’s army took up a position on the road from Morlaix in front of a wood through which the road passed.

The road inclined away from the English position to the east, before rising to the village of Lanmeur, some 2 miles from the wood.

The English army formed a line across the road, its knights and men-at-arms dismounted in the centre with the archers on each flank.

The English dug a trench in front of their line as a trap for the French.

Burne states that the English will particularly have had in mind the effectiveness of the pits dug by the Scots at Bannockburn in 1314.

The trench is said to have been concealed with branches and grass.

As the English can only have been in position a matter of hours before the French attack it must be questioned whether there was time to dig much of a trench.

The French army marched through the village of Lanmeur and began its attack on the English positions at around 3pm.

Charles of Blois’ army was formed in three large bodies of troops, in all several times the size of the English force facing it.

The first body leading the advance west along the Morlaix road was formed of dismounted Breton peasants armed with whatever weapons were available to them.

This body, in reality little more than an armed mob, advanced on the English position.

A single discharge of arrows was sufficient to put the peasant body in swift retreat before it reached the concealed trench.

There was a confused pause, while Charles of Blois contemplated the summary repelling of his first attack, before the second was launched.

The second French attack was made by the knights and mounted men-at-arms, who charged the English line.

This charge was brought up short by the concealed trench, into which the leading ranks fell, under further discharges of English longbow arrows.

A small party of some 200 French horsemen continued the charge beyond the trench but were overcome by the dismounted English men-at-arms, their leader Geoffrey de Charni being taken prisoner.

After a further pause, the third French body of mounted knights and men-at-arms began to advance, spreading out to outflank the now revealed and largely blocked trench and the English line.

His archers short of arrows, Northampton’s army fell back to positions along the edge of the wood. Skirmishing took place, with the French troops spilling around the English flanks.

But the attack on the English positions was not pressed.

Much of the French army had by now left the field, including its Genoese crossbowmen.

As night fell Charles of Blois’ army fell back to Lanmeur, the plan to relieve Morlaix abandoned.

**Casualties at the Battle of** **Morlaix**: French casualties were heavy. 50 knights were killed in the mounted attack on the English line, with 150 taken prisoner, including the commander of the attack, Geoffrey de Charni.

[![Image 5: Image of the beatified Charles of Blois: Battle of Morlaix 30th September 1342 in the Hundred Years War](https://www.britishbattles.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/img-Blessed-Charles-of-Blois-1-1.jpg)](https://www.britishbattles.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/img-Blessed-Charles-of-Blois-1-1.jpg)

Image of the beatified Charles of Blois: Battle of Morlaix 30th September 1342 in the Hundred Years War

Accounts of casualties differ widely, some placing French losses in the tens of thousands. There was no frenzied pursuit so it seems unlikely the French casualties were more than the high hundreds or low thousands, with English casualties perhaps as low as less than a hundred.

Almost certainly the ‘armed peasant’ section of Charles of Blois’ army dispersed to their homes after the battle, making it difficult to assess French losses from the battle as opposed to by desertion.

**Follow-up to the Battle of** **Morlaix**: Charles of Blois was enabled to continue his campaign to take Brittany after a short period of recovery after the battle.

Northampton was unable to take Morlaix and abandoned the siege.

**Anecdotes and traditions from the Battle of** **Morlaix****:**

*   William de Bohun commanded the right flank of King Edward III’s army at the Battle of Halidon Hill against the Scots in 1333, becoming the First Earl of Northampton in 1337.
*   Charles of Blois maintained an ascetic religious life. Following his death in 1364, his cousin the French King Charles V began a move to have Charles of Blois canonized. He was finally beatified in 1904.

**References for the Battle of Morlaix:**

The Hundred Years War by Alfred H. Burne

Trial by Battle, Volume I of the four volume record of the Hundred Years War by Jonathan Sumption.

The Art of War in the Middle Ages Volume Two by Sir Charles Oman.

The Hundred Years War by Robin Neillands.

British Battles by Grant.

![Image 1: Battle of Morlaix](https://sevenswords.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Battle-of-Morlaix-scaled.jpg)

The [Battle of Morlaix](https://sevenswords.uk/wars-of-the-roses-every-battle/) took place on 30 September 1342 during the early phase of the Breton War of Succession, a wider conflict fought within the context of the Hundred Years’ War. English forces under William de Bohun, Earl of Northampton, clashed with French troops loyal to Charles of Blois. The encounter is notable for the English use of defensive tactics that prefigured later successes at [Crécy](https://sevenswords.uk/battle-of-crecy/) and [Poitiers](https://sevenswords.uk/battle-of-poitiers-1356/).

* * *

Background
----------

The Breton War of Succession began after the death of Duke John III of Brittany in 1341, who left no direct heir. Two rival claimants emerged: John of Montfort, supported by the English crown, and Charles of Blois, backed by France. The fighting in Brittany became an important theatre for England and France, each using it to test their military strength. Morlaix, a strategically significant town in north-western Brittany, became the site of a major clash.

* * *

Forces
------

### Commanders

| Side | Commander |
| --- | --- |
| England (Montfortist) | William de Bohun, Earl of Northampton |
| France (Blois faction) | Charles of Blois |

### Troop Estimates

*   **English and Montfortist forces**: around 1,500 men, including longbowmen, dismounted men-at-arms, and local Breton allies.
*   **French forces**: roughly 3,000 men, mainly heavy cavalry supported by Breton levies and men-at-arms loyal to Charles of Blois.

* * *

Leaders and Troop Composition
-----------------------------

*   **William de Bohun (England)**
    *   Experienced commander from the opening years of the Hundred Years’ War.
    *   Troops:
        *   English longbowmen armed with yew longbows
        *   Dismounted men-at-arms with [arming swords](https://sevenswords.uk/arming-sword/) and [falchions](https://sevenswords.uk/falchion/)
        *   Breton allies with spears and crossbows
*   **Charles of Blois (France)**
    *   Nephew of King Philip VI of France and claimant to Brittany.
    *   Troops:
        *   French knights with longswords and lances
        *   Breton men-at-arms with arming swords and axes
        *   Levies with polearms and shields

* * *

Arms and Armour
---------------

*   **English Forces**
    *   Longbowmen with yew bows, bodkin arrows capable of piercing mail
    *   Dismounted men-at-arms in mail and transitional plate, wielding arming swords, falchions, and poleaxes
    *   Use of earthworks and pits dug in front of their line to blunt cavalry charges
*   **French Forces**
    *   Heavily armoured knights in mail and plate, wielding [longswords](https://sevenswords.uk/longsword/), lances, and maces
    *   Breton retainers with shields and spears
    *   Cavalry relying on shock tactics against fortified English positions

* * *

The Battle
----------

The French army under Charles of Blois attempted a direct cavalry assault on the English lines. Northampton had prepared the ground by digging concealed pits and ditches in front of his position. As French knights charged, many horses stumbled into the pits, causing confusion. The English longbowmen poured arrows into the disrupted cavalry, while dismounted men-at-arms held their ground.

Despite their numerical advantage, the French could not break the English defensive line. After repeated failed assaults, Charles of Blois withdrew, leaving the English in control of the battlefield.

* * *

Archaeology
-----------

Archaeological traces near Morlaix suggest defensive earthworks and filled pits consistent with medieval battlefield preparations. Finds in the surrounding area include fragments of arrowheads, consistent with bodkin types used by English longbowmen, and pieces of horse armour attributed to French cavalry. While the precise battlefield site remains debated, these discoveries reinforce contemporary accounts of the engagement.

* * *

Battle Timeline
---------------

*   **1341**: Death of John III of Brittany sparks war of succession.
*   **Mid 1342**: Charles of Blois campaigns across Brittany with French support.
*   **September 1342**: William de Bohun arrives with English reinforcements.
*   **30 September 1342**: Battle of Morlaix fought. English defensive tactics blunt French cavalry.
*   **Aftermath**: English victory secures Montfortist position in Brittany, though the wider conflict continues.

* * *

Contemporary Quotes
-------------------

Jean Froissart, the chronicler, later wrote of the battle:

*   _“The French found themselves confounded, their horses cast into the pits, and the English archers shooting so fiercely that none could advance without peril.”_

A Breton account described the confusion of the French charge:

*   _“The charge was brave but broken by ground unseen, and many a noble fell not by sword but by earth.”_

* * *

Legacy
------

The Battle of Morlaix demonstrated the growing effectiveness of English defensive tactics. The use of concealed pits combined with longbow fire foreshadowed later triumphs at Crécy and Poitiers. For Brittany, the battle prolonged the war of succession, ensuring that the region remained a contested battleground for years to come.

Joan of Penthièvre (c. 1319 – 10 September 1384), known as [Joan the Lame](https://grokipedia.com/page/Joan_the_Lame) due to a congenital [physical disability](https://grokipedia.com/page/Physical_disability), was a [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) noblewoman who served as Duchess of Brittany from 1341 to 1364 alongside her husband, Charles of Blois.\[1\]\[2\] As the only child of Guy, Count of Penthièvre, and great-niece of the childless [John III, Duke of Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany), she inherited a strong claim to the duchy upon his death in 1341, which her marriage to Charles—her cousin and a claimant backed by the [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) [crown](https://grokipedia.com/page/The_Crown)—transformed into a joint assertion of rule.\[3\]\[1\] This sparked the [War of the Breton Succession](https://grokipedia.com/page/War_of_the_Breton_Succession) against rival claimant [John of Montfort](https://grokipedia.com/page/John_of_Montfort) and his consort [Joan of Flanders](https://grokipedia.com/page/Joanna_of_Flanders), a protracted civil conflict intertwined with the [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War) that divided [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) loyalties and drew in English and [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) interventions.\[1\]\[2\] Despite Charles's captures at La Roche-Derrien (1347) and [Poitiers](https://grokipedia.com/page/Poitiers) (1356), Joan maintained administrative control over northern [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany), mobilized resources, and exhibited strategic resilience until the decisive Blois defeat at the [Battle of Auray](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_Auray) in 1364, where Charles perished.\[1\] Through subsequent negotiations, she secured the Treaty of Guérande (1365), retaining her ancestral Penthièvre estates, a substantial [pension](https://grokipedia.com/page/Pension), and safeguards for her heirs, thereby preserving family influence amid the Montfort victory and averting total dispossession.\[1\] Her tenure defined an era of [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) turmoil, underscoring the duchy’s precarious sovereignty between Capetian and Plantagenet powers, while her post-war diplomacy ensured the Penthièvre line's enduring regional prominence.\[3\]\[1\]

Origins and Family
------------------

### Birth and Parentage

Joan of Penthièvre was born circa 1320 as the only child of [Guy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Guy), Count of Penthièvre (c. 1287–1331), and his wife Jeanne d'Avaugour (c. 1290–1327).\[4\]\[5\] Her father, a [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) nobleman and third son of [Arthur II, Duke of Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Arthur_II,_Duke_of_Brittany) (1261–1312), held the county of Penthièvre and other lordships, positioning Joan as a potential claimant to the ducal throne through the male line following the anticipated extinction of her uncle [John](https://grokipedia.com/page/John) III's legitimate issue.\[5\]\[1\] Guy's mother was Marie de Limoges, Viscountess of Limoges (d. 1290), Arthur II's first wife, which further embedded Joan within the ducal House of Dreux-Montfort.\[5\]\[1\] Jeanne d'Avaugour descended from [Norman](https://grokipedia.com/page/Norman) [nobility](https://grokipedia.com/page/nobility) as the daughter of Henri IV d'Avaugour, linking the family to regional lordships in [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) and beyond.\[5\] As Guy predeceased John III without sons, Joan's birth secured the Penthièvre branch's inheritance prospects, though the precise location and circumstances of her birth remain undocumented in surviving records.\[6\]

### Early Upbringing and Inheritance Prospects

Joan, also known as Jeanne de Penthièvre, was born circa 1320 as the only surviving child of Guy de Penthièvre, younger brother of Duke John III of [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany), and his wife Jeanne d'Avaugour, who died in 1327.\[4\] Her father held the county of Penthièvre, a prominent lordship in northern [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany), which positioned the family as key players in ducal politics.\[5\] Details of Joan's upbringing remain sparse in contemporary records, typical for noblewomen of the era whose lives centered on familial estates and preparation for dynastic roles; she was likely raised at family holdings in Penthièvre, such as [Guingamp](https://grokipedia.com/page/Guingamp), under the influence of her father's court.\[1\] With her mother deceased early and no siblings, her early environment emphasized her status as heiress to Penthièvre lands and titles, fostering awareness of [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) noble obligations amid tensions with the ducal house. Guy de Penthièvre's death on 27 March 1331 elevated Joan, then about 11 years old, to Countess of Penthièvre and inheritor of his patrimonial claims, including potential rights to the duchy through her uncle John III, who remained childless despite two marriages.\[5\] This inheritance strengthened her prospects, as [Salic law](https://grokipedia.com/page/Salic_law) customs favored male-line descent, making her the closest legitimate heir via her father; John III initially supported her claim over rivals from his half-siblings' lines, though he later wavered toward John de Montfort, son of his half-sister [Beatrice](https://grokipedia.com/page/Beatrice).\[7\]\[1\] By her early teens, these dynamics cast Joan as a pivotal figure in succession planning, with her marriage negotiations reflecting efforts to secure her ducal aspirations against mounting collateral challenges.

Marriage and Initial Claim
--------------------------

### Union with Charles of Blois

In 1337, Joan of Penthièvre, co-heiress of the county of Penthièvre and a niece of the childless [Duke](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duke) John III of Brittany, contracted marriage with Charles of Blois, a nephew of King [Philip VI of France](https://grokipedia.com/page/Philip_VI_of_France) through his mother, [Margaret of Valois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Margaret_of_Valois), sister to the king.\[5\]\[1\] The union, solemnized on 4 June 1337 in [Paris](https://grokipedia.com/page/Paris), was strategically arranged to fortify Joan's prospective inheritance rights to the duchy, as her father Guy de Penthièvre was a son of Duke Arthur II, positioning her among the senior female-line claimants in the event of John III's death without male issue.\[5\]\[8\] Charles, born around 1319 as the son of [Guy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Guy) I, Count of [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois), brought military and noble connections from the House of Châtillon, enhancing the alliance's viability against potential rivals such as [John of Montfort](https://grokipedia.com/page/John_of_Montfort), whose claim derived from a junior branch.\[1\] The couple cohabited shortly thereafter, around 1338 or 1339, and produced at least five children, including [John](https://grokipedia.com/page/John) I, Count of Penthièvre (born 1340), who later inherited significant holdings.\[5\] This marital partnership vested [Charles](https://grokipedia.com/page/Charles) with a derivative claim to [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) jure uxoris, aligning their interests with French royal support and setting the stage for the ensuing succession conflict upon John III's death in April 1341.\[8\]

### Ducal Succession Dispute

Upon the death of [John III, Duke of Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany), on 30 April 1341, without surviving legitimate children, the duchy faced a contested succession under [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) [customary law](https://grokipedia.com/page/Customary_law), which permitted inheritance by females and through representation of a deceased parent but favored male heirs where possible.\[8\] [Joan of Penthièvre](https://grokipedia.com/page/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre), daughter and heir of John III's full brother Guy, Count of Penthièvre, claimed the title _suo jure_ by representing her father as the duke's next senior male relative, positioning herself ahead of more distant male lines; her marriage to [Charles de Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Charles_de_Blois), a nephew of [King Philip VI of France](https://grokipedia.com/page/Philip_VI_of_France), aligned her faction with [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) interests seeking to maintain influence over the duchy as a [French peerage](https://grokipedia.com/page/Peerage) since 1297.\[1\] [John of Montfort](https://grokipedia.com/page/John_of_Montfort), John III's legitimate half-brother via their father Arthur II's second marriage to [Beatrice of Clermont](https://grokipedia.com/page/Beatrice_of_Clermont), countered with a claim as the closest surviving male agnate, asserting that Brittany's status as an apanage precluded female succession or representation, drawing parallels to the exclusionary principles of [Salic law](https://grokipedia.com/page/Salic_law) recently invoked in [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) royal disputes.\[9\] Montfort acted decisively post-mortem, arriving in Nantes by early May 1341 to secure oaths of [fealty](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fealty) from local nobles and seize control of key strongholds, including [Rennes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rennes) and several ports, thereby gaining [de facto](https://grokipedia.com/page/De_facto) authority over much of northern [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) before French intervention.\[8\] Joan and [Charles](https://grokipedia.com/page/Charles), initially slower to mobilize, appealed to Philip VI, who viewed Montfort's pretensions as a threat to Capetian oversight and Breton loyalty amid rising tensions with [England](https://grokipedia.com/page/England).\[1\] The Penthièvre-Blois claim gained traction among Breton [estates](https://grokipedia.com/page/The_Estates) favoring ties to France, while Montfort cultivated English support from [Edward](https://grokipedia.com/page/Edward) III, who asserted ancient Plantagenet [suzerainty](https://grokipedia.com/page/Suzerainty) over [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) to counter French expansion.\[10\] The legal resolution tilted toward Joan when Philip VI convened the [Parlement of Paris](https://grokipedia.com/page/Parlement_of_Paris) at Conflans, which on 7 September 1341 issued the Judgment of Conflans, affirming her right to the duchy and designating [Charles](https://grokipedia.com/page/Charles) as consort duke, while summoning Montfort to renounce his title under penalty of [confiscation](https://grokipedia.com/page/Confiscation); the decision emphasized representation through Joan but vested governance in her husband to align with male-preference norms.\[11\] Montfort's defiance, including his capture of additional territories, rendered the ruling unenforceable without military enforcement, exposing the interplay of [customary law](https://grokipedia.com/page/Customary_law), [royal prerogative](https://grokipedia.com/page/Royal_prerogative), and geopolitical rivalry in the dispute's origins.\[1\]

The War of the Breton Succession
--------------------------------

### Outbreak and Early Conflicts

Upon the death of Duke John III of Brittany on 30 April 1341, without surviving sons, the duchy faced a succession crisis pitting Joan of Penthièvre—John III's niece—and her husband Charles of Blois against the duke's half-brother, John of Montfort.\[12\] Philip VI of France, favoring the Blois-Penthièvre claim due to feudal ties and legal arguments privileging Joan's lineage, dispatched forces to enforce their rights, while Edward III of England backed Montfort to counter French influence in the region amid the ongoing Hundred Years' War.\[13\] Montfort acted decisively, seizing the ducal capital of Nantes in May 1341 to access the treasury and rallying local support, followed by captures of Rennes—where the governor Henri de Spinefort surrendered after a sally—Dinan, and Champtoceaux by June, thereby controlling most of southern and western Brittany by summer's end.\[12\] The war erupted in late summer 1341 as Charles of Blois, reinforced by a [French army](https://grokipedia.com/page/French_Army) under John of Normandy, invaded from the [Loire valley](https://grokipedia.com/page/Loire_Valley) in October, targeting Montfort's gains.\[13\] French forces swiftly recaptured Champtoceaux by late October and besieged [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes), where Montfort had fortified his position.\[12\] After weeks of resistance, the city surrendered in November 1341; Montfort, emerging under assurances of [safe conduct](https://grokipedia.com/page/Safe_conduct) for negotiations, was seized by Charles's troops and imprisoned in [Paris](https://grokipedia.com/page/Paris) by December, effectively neutralizing his leadership.\[13\] These initial clashes highlighted the proxy nature of the conflict, with French numerical superiority—bolstered by royal levies—overturning Montfort's localized [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) alliances. By [February](https://grokipedia.com/page/February) 1342, Charles of Blois had consolidated hold over francophone eastern [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany), though Montfort's wife [Joanna](https://grokipedia.com/page/Joanna) maintained resistance in strongholds like Hennebont, appealing to English aid and prolonging the stalemate.\[12\]\[13\]

### Charles of Blois's Capture and Joan's Regency

In June 1347, during the ongoing [War of the Breton Succession](https://grokipedia.com/page/War_of_the_Breton_Succession), Charles of Blois laid siege to the town of La Roche-Derrien, which was held by an English garrison loyal to the rival Montfort claimants.\[14\] On the night of June 20, an Anglo-Breton relief force under Sir Thomas Dagworth surprised Charles's camp, leading to a chaotic melee in which Charles was wounded and captured after attempting to rally his troops.\[14\] \[15\] He was transported to [England](https://grokipedia.com/page/England) and imprisoned, remaining in captivity for approximately nine years until his release in 1356 following the payment of a 500,000-écu ransom as part of broader Anglo-French negotiations.\[1\] \[16\] With Charles incapacitated, Joan of Penthièvre assumed effective control of their faction's territories, establishing a regency centered in [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes), the stronghold of Blois-Penthièvre loyalty.\[1\] She issued administrative charters and mandements to manage ducal finances, bureaucracy, and local governance, demonstrating continuity in princely authority despite the absence of her husband.\[17\] Joan appointed key military captains, including the Viscount of Rohan and Robert de Beaumanoir, to maintain discipline among pro-Blois forces and coordinate defenses against Montfort incursions.\[1\] Militarily, Joan actively mobilized support by traveling through Breton towns and fortresses to rally troops and affirm her sons—Jean and [Guy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Guy)—as rightful heirs, thereby sustaining the war effort against Joanna of Flanders and her English allies.\[1\] Diplomatically, she petitioned [Pope Clement VI](https://grokipedia.com/page/Pope_Clement_VI) for aid and explored negotiations with [Edward III of England](https://grokipedia.com/page/Edward_III_of_England), including potential alliances or marriages to secure her position, though these yielded limited immediate results amid the broader [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War).\[5\] \[18\] Her leadership preserved Blois-Penthièvre holdings in northern and eastern Brittany, preventing total collapse of their claim during a critical phase of the conflict.\[1\]

### Key Military Engagements

During Joan's regency following Charles de Blois's capture, her forces engaged in sporadic but intense conflicts, often characterized by sieges, raids, and chivalric combats rather than large-scale pitched battles, reflecting the guerrilla tactics employed to defend Breton strongholds against English-backed Montfort incursions. A prominent example was the [Combat of the Thirty](https://grokipedia.com/page/Combat_of_the_Thirty) on 27 March 1351 near Ploërmel, where 30 [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) and [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) knights loyal to Joan challenged an equal number of English and Anglo-[Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) combatants from the Ploërmel garrison commanded by Sir Robert Knolles. The encounter, agreed upon during a truce to settle local disputes, devolved into a brutal [melee](https://grokipedia.com/page/Melee) fought on foot with swords, maces, battle-axes, and daggers after initial mounted charges; it lasted several hours, resulting in 11 deaths and numerous wounds among Joan's supporters, compared to 12 English killed in action and 8 captured after surrender. This victory bolstered morale among Blois partisans and highlighted the martial skill of Joan's adherents, though it had limited strategic impact amid ongoing truces.\[19\]\[20\] Joan's military efforts also involved coordinating defenses of key fortresses, such as [Rennes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rennes), which withstood multiple English sieges, including a notable attempt in 1356–1357 led by Montfortist forces under Jean de Montfort's son. Her captains, financed through Joan's administrative measures like taxing clergy and nobility, conducted counter-raids; for instance, [Bertrand du Guesclin](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bertrand_du_Guesclin), operating under her authority, led harassment operations against English garrisons in eastern [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany), capturing outposts and disrupting supply lines despite setbacks like his own temporary capture at the Battle of Mauron in 1352. These actions preserved Blois control over substantial territories, including [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) and much of the interior, by leveraging local loyalties and French reinforcements, though they failed to decisively expel Montfort claimants.\[1\]

### Defeat at Auray and War's End

The [Battle of Auray](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_Auray) occurred on September 29, 1364, near the town of [Auray](https://grokipedia.com/page/Auray) in [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany), marking the decisive clash of the [War of the Breton Succession](https://grokipedia.com/page/War_of_the_Breton_Succession).\[21\] Forces loyal to Joan of Penthièvre and her husband Charles of Blois, numbering around 5,000 including French reinforcements under [Bertrand du Guesclin](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bertrand_du_Guesclin), marched to relieve the besieged Montfort-held castle of [Auray](https://grokipedia.com/page/Auray).\[22\] Opposing them were approximately 2,000-3,000 troops led by John de Montfort's son, the future John V, with significant English support commanded by [Sir John Chandos](https://grokipedia.com/page/John_Chandos), totaling effective combat strength that overwhelmed the Bloisist army through superior tactics and archery.\[21\] \[23\] The engagement began with Montfortist forces crossing the Auray River and forming lines, prompting a fierce assault by [Charles](https://grokipedia.com/page/Charles) of Blois's knights that initially breached the enemy center but faltered against [English longbow](https://grokipedia.com/page/English_longbow) fire and reserves.\[22\] [Charles](https://grokipedia.com/page/Charles) himself was struck down by multiple wounds during the [melee](https://grokipedia.com/page/Melee), dying on the field alongside heavy [casualties](https://grokipedia.com/page/The_Casualties) among his supporters, while du Guesclin was captured after prolonged resistance.\[21\] \[22\] This rout shattered the Blois-Penthièvre faction's military capacity, with survivors scattering and key allies like du Guesclin ransomed later to the English side.\[23\] Joan's cause collapsed with Charles's death, as she lacked viable forces to continue the fight and faced isolation from French royal support amid the broader [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War) dynamics.\[8\] In the immediate aftermath, she negotiated terms, renouncing her ducal claim in exchange for retaining the County of Penthièvre and a [courtesy title](https://grokipedia.com/page/Courtesy_title) of duchess for life.\[8\] The war formally concluded in April 1365 with the first Treaty of Guérande, wherein King Charles V of France recognized John V de Montfort as Duke of [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) under English [suzerainty](https://grokipedia.com/page/Suzerainty), ending over two decades of conflict that had claimed thousands of lives and devastated [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) lands.\[21\]

Post-War Settlement
-------------------

### Treaty of Guérande and Territorial Compromises

The First Treaty of [Guérande](https://grokipedia.com/page/Gu%C3%A9rande), signed on 12 April 1365 at [Guérande](https://grokipedia.com/page/Gu%C3%A9rande), formally ended the [War of the Breton Succession](https://grokipedia.com/page/War_of_the_Breton_Succession) by recognizing John IV de Montfort as the sole Duke of Brittany, following his forces' victory at the [Battle of Auray](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_Auray) six months earlier.\[24\] Joan of Penthièvre, who had claimed the duchy through her inheritance from Duke John III, renounced her ducal rights in exchange for retaining personal control over key ancestral territories, thereby averting her total exclusion from Breton power structures.\[1\] Under the treaty's territorial terms, Joan preserved the County of Penthièvre—encompassing lands in northern [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) such as [Lamballe](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lamballe) and Goëlo—and the lordship of Avaugour during her lifetime, allowing her family to maintain economic and feudal influence in these regions without subordination to the new duke.\[1\] She was explicitly exempted from rendering homage to John IV, a concession that preserved her semi-autonomous status and avoided symbolic acknowledgment of Montfort superiority.\[1\] Additionally, Joan received an annual pension of 12,000 _livres tournois_, funded from the revenues of [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes), providing financial security amid the loss of broader ducal authority.\[1\] These compromises reflected pragmatic balancing: John IV gained uncontested ducal sovereignty and Brittany's nominal neutrality in the Anglo-French conflicts of the [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War), while the Penthièvre line secured a foothold for potential future claims, as the treaty did not fully bar their heirs from ducal succession prospects.\[24\] The arrangements were later reaffirmed in the Second Treaty of [Guérande](https://grokipedia.com/page/Gu%C3%A9rande) on 2 May 1381, after tensions with John's son, but the 1365 accord marked the decisive shift in territorial control post-war.\[1\]

### Administration of Remaining Holdings

Following the First Treaty of [Guérande](https://grokipedia.com/page/Gu%C3%A9rande) on 4 April 1365, Joan retained lifelong possession of the counties of Penthièvre and [Guingamp](https://grokipedia.com/page/Guingamp), including associated ancestral lands in Avaugour, which formed the core of her post-war domains. These territories, centered around key sites such as [Lamballe](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lamballe) in Penthièvre and the fortified town of [Guingamp](https://grokipedia.com/page/Guingamp), generated revenues through feudal dues, market tolls, and jurisdictional rights, enabling her to sustain a semi-independent seigneurial regime exempt from homage to Duke [John](https://grokipedia.com/page/John) V de Montfort. The treaty stipulated an annual pension of 12,000 francs from the ducal treasury, supplementing local income and funding household and administrative functions without ducal interference.\[1\] Joan administered these holdings via a delegated network of retainers and officials, issuing confirmations of local privileges and resolving disputes to maintain [order](https://grokipedia.com/page/Order) and [loyalty](https://grokipedia.com/page/Loyalty) among [estates](https://grokipedia.com/page/The_Estates) that had backed her during the succession war. While she increasingly resided in [Paris](https://grokipedia.com/page/Paris) after 1365, prioritizing courtly ties with the [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) [crown](https://grokipedia.com/page/The_Crown), her oversight preserved autonomy in [justice](https://grokipedia.com/page/Justice) and [finance](https://grokipedia.com/page/Finance), with charters often emanating from [Guingamp](https://grokipedia.com/page/Guingamp) or Penthièvre residences. This structure reflected pragmatic adaptation to reduced power, focusing on economic stability amid Brittany's fragile peace.\[17\] Occasional frictions with the Montfort duke prompted assertions of treaty rights, such as her 1373 protest during John V's exile to [England](https://grokipedia.com/page/England), yet Joan prioritized regional stability by acquiescing to his 1378 recall under Charles V's pressure. The Second Treaty of [Guérande](https://grokipedia.com/page/Gu%C3%A9rande) on 2 May 1381 restated the original terms, securing her domains until her death on 10 September 1384, after which they reverted to the duchy, passing initially to her son John, Count of Penthièvre.\[25\]

Later Life and Death
--------------------

### Family Alliances and Descendants

Joan married Charles de Blois-Châtillon on 4 July 1337 in [Paris](https://grokipedia.com/page/Paris), uniting the Penthièvre lineage with the Châtillon family of [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois), whose ties to the French Capetian-Valois dynasty—through Charles's mother, [Margaret of Valois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Margaret_of_Valois), sister of King Philip VI—reinforced their pro-French orientation in the Breton succession dispute and the ongoing [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War).\[26\] This strategic alliance contrasted with the rival Montfort claimants' alignment with [England](https://grokipedia.com/page/England), leveraging Blois's regional influence in [Champagne](https://grokipedia.com/page/Champagne) and the royal favor to sustain Joan's ducal pretensions despite military setbacks.\[1\] Joan and Charles had five children: John I (c. 1340–1404), who inherited the County of Penthièvre and pursued claims to [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) until renouncing them under the 1365 Treaty of [Guérande](https://grokipedia.com/page/Gu%C3%A9rande); Guy, who predeceased his father without notable issue; Henry (d. 1400); Marie (c. 1345–1404), who became Lady of [Guise](https://grokipedia.com/page/Guise) through Châtillon holdings; and Marguerite, who wed [Charles de La Cerda](https://grokipedia.com/page/Charles_de_la_Cerda), [Constable of France](https://grokipedia.com/page/Constable_of_France) and illegitimate son of Castile's Alfonso XI, in 1351, forging a brief trans-Pyrenean link severed by his assassination in 1354 without surviving heirs.\[27\] Following [Charles](https://grokipedia.com/page/Charles)'s death at [Auray](https://grokipedia.com/page/Auray) on 29 September 1364, Joan did not remarry, focusing instead on guardianship of her heirs amid regency duties.\[26\] The primary descendants emanated from John I, whose marriages—to first Bonne of Brittany (d. 1370) and then Joanna of Navarre—yielded issue including Olivier (d. 1404) and later branches that retained Penthièvre titles as appanages under Montfort dukes, evolving into the House of Guéméné by the [15th century](https://grokipedia.com/page/15th_century) and influencing [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) nobility until French royal absorption.\[26\] Daughters Marie and Marguerite's lines faded without perpetuating the ducal contention, underscoring the patrilineal focus of medieval [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) inheritance amid feudal fragmentation.\[27\]

### Final Years and Burial

After the second Treaty of [Guérande](https://grokipedia.com/page/Gu%C3%A9rande) on 4 April 1365, Joan retained the lifelong title of Duchess of [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany), her counties of Penthièvre and Goëlo, the viscounty of [Limoges](https://grokipedia.com/page/Limoges), and associated lands such as Avaugour, while receiving an annual pension of 12,000 livres from the Breton treasury; she was also exempted from homage to John V de Montfort, the recognized duke.\[26\] Her political role in the duchy proper diminished, but she continued administering her northern [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) estates, focusing on financial recovery from war debts and maintaining her court's diplomatic ties.\[17\] Residing primarily at [Guingamp](https://grokipedia.com/page/Guingamp) and nearby La Roche-Derrien within her Penthièvre holdings, Joan supported the canonization process for her husband Charles de Blois, promoting his cult as a [martyr](https://grokipedia.com/page/Martyr) until papal proceedings stalled around 1381.\[26\] In 1379, amid tensions over French influence during the [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War), she joined Breton barons in efforts to preserve ducal independence against encroachments on John V's authority.\[26\] These activities reflected her ongoing commitment to her lineage's prestige and regional autonomy, though without reigniting open conflict. Joan died on 10 September 1384 at [Guingamp](https://grokipedia.com/page/Guingamp), as recorded in contemporary necrologies including that of Notre-Dame de Beauport abbey.\[26\] She was interred in the church of the Couvent des Cordeliers (Friars Minor) in [Guingamp](https://grokipedia.com/page/Guingamp), the traditional burial site for the Penthièvre family, alongside her husband Charles de Blois, father Guy de Penthièvre, and mother Marie de Bourbon.\[28\] The [monastery](https://grokipedia.com/page/Monastery), founded in the early [13th century](https://grokipedia.com/page/13th_century), housed multiple Penthièvre tombs until its suppression during the [French Revolution](https://grokipedia.com/page/French_Revolution).\[28\]

Legacy and Assessments
----------------------

### Evaluation of Rule and Leadership

Jeanne de Penthièvre exercised princely authority through a combination of administrative oversight and diplomatic maneuvering during the Breton War of Succession from 1341 to 1365, particularly as [regent](https://grokipedia.com/page/Regent) while her husband, Charles of [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois), was imprisoned by the English from 1347 to 1356. She managed ducal finances by negotiating loans collateralized against properties, sustained military efforts amid mounting war debts, and issued charters to affirm governance in territories under Blois control, demonstrating resilience in preserving administrative continuity via consistent councilors and legal instruments.\[29\] Her leadership model emphasized co-seigneurie with [Charles](https://grokipedia.com/page/Charles), blending joint estate management—encompassing taxation and transactions across [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany), [Limoges](https://grokipedia.com/page/Limoges), and [Mayenne](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mayenne)—with independent actions, such as her use of personal seals to legitimize decisions and garner support from [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) assemblies. This adaptability allowed her to balance [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany)'s precarious position between [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) and English overlords, shifting alliances as needed while resisting a rigid [hierarchy](https://grokipedia.com/page/hierarchy) of power.\[29\]\[30\] Assessments portray Jeanne as an active and determined ruler whose effectiveness lay in contextual flexibility rather than singular dominance, enabling her to prolong the [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois) claim until the 1364 defeat at [Auray](https://grokipedia.com/page/Auray) and secure concessions in the Treaty of Guérande, including retention of Penthièvre, which bolstered her family's subsequent resurgence under her son Joan V.\[31\]\[29\]\[32\]

### Debates on Succession Legitimacy

Joan's claim to the [Duchy of Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duchy_of_Brittany) derived from her position as the sole legitimate heir of her father, Guy of Penthièvre, the younger full brother of Duke John III, who had predeceased him without male issue, positioning her as the closest direct descendant under principles of lineal [primogeniture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Primogeniture) upheld in Breton customary law.\[33\] This inheritance right was reinforced by historical precedents of female rulers in [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany), including Duchess Alix of [Thouars](https://grokipedia.com/page/Thouars) (r. 1203–1221) and earlier countesses, which demonstrated that ducal authority could be exercised by women without male co-rulers, countering arguments analogizing [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) to kingdoms under male-only [Salic law](https://grokipedia.com/page/Salic_law).\[17\] Supporters of Joan, including the [Parlement of Paris](https://grokipedia.com/page/Parlement_of_Paris) in its 1341 ruling, emphasized her "representation" of her father's line as binding under feudal customs, rejecting broader testamentary overrides that might favor collateral male relatives.\[34\] John of Montfort's competing claim relied on his status as John III's surviving half-brother through their shared mother, [Beatrice of Navarre](https://grokipedia.com/page/Beatrice), invoking a [preference](https://grokipedia.com/page/Preference) for [male](https://grokipedia.com/page/Male) [agnatic succession](https://grokipedia.com/page/Succession) and an alleged 1340 will by the duke—following a [reconciliation](https://grokipedia.com/page/Reconciliation)—that purportedly named Montfort as heir to prevent female rule and preserve ducal continuity.\[13\] Critics of this will, including Joan's legal advocates, contested its validity and scope under [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) traditions, arguing that a duke's testamentary freedom did not extend to disinheriting a direct brother's established line, particularly absent explicit revocation of prior arrangements favoring Joan, and that such a document could not unilaterally alter customary inheritance norms without estate assembly consent.\[17\] Montfort's partisans, however, portrayed female succession as disruptive to the duchy's quasi-sovereign stability, drawing on evolving French legal trends that prioritized male heirs to avoid [partition](https://grokipedia.com/page/Partition) or foreign influence, though this view clashed with Brittany's distinct Celtic-influenced [customs](https://grokipedia.com/page/Customs) that historically tolerated heiresses.\[34\] The debates intensified through 1341 legal proceedings, where the Estates of Brittany initially acclaimed Joan as duchess before Montfort's seizure of [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) shifted momentum, highlighting tensions between customary law's emphasis on [blood](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blood+) proximity and the duke's personal will as a tool for political favoritism.\[33\] Foreign interventions further complicated legitimacy: King [Philip VI of France](https://grokipedia.com/page/Philip_VI_of_France) backed Joan via her husband Charles of [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois) (his nephew), prioritizing Capetian ties and aversion to English-aligned Montfort, whose 1343 alliance with [Edward](https://grokipedia.com/page/Edward) III invoked ancient Breton-English pacts but undermined claims of internal Breton consensus.\[13\] Papal efforts at [arbitration](https://grokipedia.com/page/Arbitration), including appeals to [Avignon](https://grokipedia.com/page/Avignon), ultimately deferred to arms, but underscored unresolved questions on whether ducal power inhered in the office's social and jurisdictional persona—amenable to [female](https://grokipedia.com/page/Female) exercise—or strictly patrilineal [blood](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blood+), with Joan's sustained [administration](https://grokipedia.com/page/Administration) during Charles's [captivity](https://grokipedia.com/page/Captivity) (1347–1356) later bolstering retrospective arguments for her [de facto](https://grokipedia.com/page/De_facto) legitimacy.\[35\] Despite military outcomes favoring Montfort's line by 1365, the [succession crisis](https://grokipedia.com/page/Succession_crisis) exposed fractures in late medieval princely authority, where custom often trumped individual intent absent overwhelming force.\[17\]
